english_scripts:
amalanādhi pirān aḍiyārkkennai āṭpaḍuttha vimalan\
viṇṇavar kōn viraiyār pozil vēṅgaḍavan\
nimalan ninmalan nīdi vānavan neezh madiḻ araṅgatthammān\
thirukkamala pādham vandhu en kaṇṇin uḻḻana okkinṟadhē
meaning: He who is devoid of all impure qualities and is responsible for creation, thereby being called the Primordial One, made him serve His servants. The Lord of the Nityasūris, whose bliss is without a second, shines as Veṅkaṭeśvara on the divine hill. He, the ruler of Paramapadam, never expects anything in return and is compassionate towards His devotees. The same Lord of all the devas is reclining in Tiruvaraṅgam, which is surrounded by lofty walls. Oh! The lotus feet of Raṅganātha have come to him and are residing in his eyes.
purport:
Śrīman Nārāyaṇa is celebrated as *Paratattva*, the Supreme Reality, who is the source, sustainer, and controller of all existence. Tiruppāṇ Āḻvār proclaims this truth through the very opening word, *amalanādhipirān*, declaring Him to be the Lord who stands above all devas and celestial powers. This title itself reveals His unsurpassed supremacy and His flawless, blemishless nature.

The significance of this opening word extends even deeper into Vedāntic thought. The sacred syllable *Praṇava* (*A-U-M*) encapsulates the essence of all Vedic wisdom. The first letter of *amalanādhipirān* corresponds to the first sound of the *Praṇava*, which denotes Nārāyaṇa Himself. This profound connection is beautifully reflected in the iconography of Śrīraṅgam, where Namperumāḷ reclines upon Ādiśeṣa beneath the *Praṇavākāra Vimāna*, signifying that He is the very meaning and embodiment of the *praṇava-rahasya*. The Āḻvār further reinforces this supremacy by addressing Him as *viṇṇavar kōn*, the sovereign Lord of the celestial realm. Even Indra, the king of the devas, derives his authority from Him and remains dependent upon His grace.

Yet, while His greatness is immeasurable, it is His compassion that captivates the hearts of devotees. The Lord does not remain distant in His majesty. Instead, He lovingly reaches out to uplift souls trapped in *saṃsāra*. When a devotee surrenders completely to Him, the accumulated burden of karma and the deep-rooted impressions of countless births are gradually removed through His grace. It is for this reason that Tiruppāṇ Āḻvār praises Him as *nimalan*, the Pure One who purifies others.

The Āḻvār's meditation then rests upon the divine feet of the Lord. These sacred feet, softer than newly blossomed lotus petals, are adorned with auspicious marks and possess incomparable beauty. They are the refuge sought by devotees, sages, and even the gods themselves. These are the very feet that measured all the worlds during the *Trivikrama-avatāra*, revealing His sovereignty over the entire cosmos. Their beauty is inseparable from their mercy, for they descend to reach those who are unable to rise by their own effort. Even Śrī Mahālakṣmī, the eternal Divine Mother, joyfully serves those feet of Her own accord, recognizing them as the source of all auspiciousness.

The teachings of the *Brahma-sūtras*, as understood in the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition, are beautifully reflected in this pāsuram. The *jīva* is an eternal conscious entity, subtle like an *aṇu*, whose intrinsic nature is to serve the Supreme Lord. This truth is echoed in the phrase *aḍiyārkku eṉṉai āṭpaḍutta*, where the Āḻvār rejoices in being placed in the service of the Lord's devotees. *Brahman*, on the other hand, is the Supreme Reality who pervades, governs, and transcends everything. This is the Lord praised as *amalanādhipirān*.

The relationship between the *jīva* and *Brahman* is one of *Śeṣa-Śeṣi-bhāva*, the relationship between the servant and the Master. Though inseparably connected, the two remain eternally distinct. The greatest obstacle preventing the *jīva* from realizing this relationship is ignorance born of ego and false identification with the material world. Bound by this misconception, the soul wanders through the cycle of birth and death. Yet the Lord, praised as *nimalan*, removes these impurities through His grace and draws the soul towards Himself.

Ultimately, the path to liberation lies not in personal strength or intellectual achievement, but in surrender. Tiruppāṇ Āḻvār experiences this directly when he declares that the *tirukkamala-pādam*, the divine lotus feet of the Lord, have entered and become firmly established within his vision. To seek refuge at those sacred feet is to attain the highest goal. They alone grant freedom from *saṃsāra* and lead the soul to its eternal destiny of loving service in the presence of the Supreme Lord.

english_scripts:
uvanda uḻḻattanāy ulagam aḻandaṇḍam uṟa
nivanda nīḻ muḍiyan anṟu nērnda niśāśararai
kavarnda veṅgaṇai kkāguttan kaḍiyār pozil araṅgattammān
araiccivanda āḍaiyin mēl śenṟadām en śindanaiyē
meaning: My Lord, who with a joyous mind measured all the worlds by growing as tall as the heavens, with a crown that reached the skies; who once, as Rāma, took the lives of the opposing Asuras with His fierce arrows; and who now rests in Araṅgam amidst fragrant forests—upon Him, his mind has settled.
purport:
The Lord draws all beings towards Himself through the irresistible charm of His auspicious qualities and His wondrous divine form, whose beauty transcends ordinary description. Every attribute of His exists solely for the welfare and delight of His devotees. There is not even a single quality in Him that could give rise to aversion or displeasure. For this reason, the scriptures describe Him as *Nirguṇa*, not in the sense of being devoid of qualities, but as being entirely free from all inauspicious attributes. He is the embodiment of limitless auspiciousness and boundless compassion. Reflecting upon this truth, the Āḻvār addresses Him as *uvaṇḍa uḷḷattaṉāy*, the One whose heart overflows with delight and affection for His devotees.

By referring to the Lord as Vāmana, the Āḻvār simultaneously recalls His manifestation as Trivikrama through the expression *ulagam aḷandaṇḍam uṟa*. The seemingly diminutive Vāmana assumed a cosmic form and measured all the worlds with His divine strides. This act was not merely a display of supreme sovereignty but also an expression of universal grace. As His sacred lotus feet traversed the worlds, every region, every being, and every realm received the sanctifying touch of those auspicious feet. Thus, the *Trivikrama-avatāra* revealed both His immeasurable greatness and His desire to bless all creation.

The Āḻvār next contemplates the beauty of Śrī Rāmacandra and describes Him through the expression *nivaṇḍa nīḷ muḍiyaṉ*. This evokes the Lord's luxuriant curly locks and His majestic bearing. The beauty of Śrī Rāma is celebrated throughout the tradition as captivating not merely human beings but all forms of life. Indeed, the very name Rāma is traditionally explained as:

He who delights and enchants all through His beauty, virtues, and conduct.

The Āḻvār therefore delights in the exquisite form of the Lord, whose outward beauty perfectly reflects His inner excellence.

The remembrance of Śrī Rāma naturally leads to His role as the upholder of righteousness. Rāvaṇa incurred destruction because of his lustful disposition and his improper attitude towards Sītā Devī, the universal mother and the eternal consort of Śrīman Nārāyaṇa. Yet the same Lord who destroyed Rāvaṇa readily accepted the *śaraṇāgati* of Vibhīṣaṇa, Rāvaṇa's own brother. In this context, the term *niśācarar* refers to the Asuras. Although both Rāvaṇa and Vibhīṣaṇa belonged to the same race, the Lord's dealings with them differed according to their disposition. Rāvaṇa was subdued through the Lord's strength and power, whereas Vibhīṣaṇa was won over through His love, mercy, and affectionate acceptance. Thus, the Lord demonstrated both His justice towards the arrogant and His boundless compassion towards those who sought refuge in Him through *prapatti*.

The Āḻvār then recalls the noble lineage into which Śrī Rāma descended. The illustrious Ikṣvāku dynasty produced many celebrated rulers and warriors, among whom Kakutstha occupied a place of great distinction. Since Rāma appeared in that revered lineage, He is praised as *kākuttan*. The people of Ayodhyā cherished Him with profound love and reverence, affectionately addressing Him as Perumāḷ. This title signifies not merely greatness but also the intimate bond of love between the Lord and His devotees. Since Raṅganātha was worshipped by Śrī Rāma Himself, the Lord of Śrīraṅgam came to be known as Periya Perumāḷ, the Supreme Lord who is adored even by the Lord who appeared as Rāma.

The pāsuram concludes with the Āḻvār's contemplation of the Lord's divine attire. His gaze, having journeyed through the Lord's qualities, incarnations, and form, now comes to rest upon the sacred garment described as *araiccivanda āḍaiyiṉ*. This refers to the Lord's *Pītāmbara*, the reddish-yellow garment that adorns His divine form. The Āḻvār becomes wholly absorbed in its beauty, for the brilliance of the garment forms a striking contrast with the Lord's dark *tirumēṉi*, which resembles a rain-laden cloud. In this harmonious union of colours, the devotee beholds yet another expression of the Lord's incomparable beauty, and his mind remains completely captivated by that enchanting vision.

english_scripts:
mandi pāy vaḍa vēṅgaḍa mā malai\
vānavargaḻ śandi śeyya ninṟān araṅgattaravin aṇaiyān\
andi pōl niṟattāḍaiyum adan mēl ayanai ppaḍaittadōr ezil\
undi mēladanṟō aḍiyēn uḻḻattin uyirē
meaning: He who stands in the mountains of the northern Tirumalā, where male monkeys leap from branch to branch, and where the Nityasūris worship Him with flowers; He who rests in Tiruvāraṅgam, reclining upon the sweet bed of Ananta (Ādiśeṣa)—upon His red garment and His most beautiful navel, from which even the creator Brahmā was born, has his innermost heart settled.
purport:
Here is the refined version, preserving the original meaning, theological intent, and devotional tone while improving grammar, flow, and readability:

Thiruppān Āḻvār is experiencing Thiruveṅgaḍamuḍaiyān of Tirumalā. Here, the Āḻvār uses the expression *Vaḍa Veṅgaḍam*, referring to the Northern Veṅgaḍam. Āḻvār Tirunagari is traditionally known as the Southern Tirumalā, and therefore the Āḻvār explicitly identifies Tirumalā through the phrase *mandhi pāy vaḍa veṅgaḍa māmalai*.

Here, *vāṉavar* refers to the residents of the upper worlds, namely the Devatas. These celestial beings descend to worship Śrīnivāsa Perumāḷ at Tirumalā, while human beings ascend the seven sacred hills to offer their worship. Thus, Śrīnivāsa stands atop the hill as a meeting place for both the Devatas and human beings, granting equal access to all who seek to render service unto Him. The very same Lord who reclines upon the serpent couch of Ādiśeṣa as Namperumāḷ in Śrīraṅgam stands upon the summit of Tirumalā as Thiruveṅgaḍamuḍaiyān. Thiruppān Āḻvār simultaneously enjoys the forms of Śrīnivāsa and Raṅganātha while describing Him through the words *vāṉavargaḷ sandhi seyya niṉṟāṉ araṅgatthu araviṉ aṇaiyāṉ*.

The Āḻvār once again turns his attention to the reddish *Pītāmbara* adorning Raṅganātha and alludes to it through the phrase *andhi pōl niṟattadaiyum adhan mēl ayaṉaip paḍaittathōr ezhil*. Above this divine garment shines the Lord's lotus navel. This is the very navel from which *Ayaṉ*, Brahmā, the creator of the universe, was brought forth. Here, the Āḻvār enjoys the Anantapadmanābha-svarūpa of the Lord. Overwhelmed by this vision, he marvels, "Is this not the very navel that gave birth to Brahmā? Now it has completely captivated my heart!" This experience is expressed through the words *undi mēladanṟō aḍiyēn uḷḷattin uyirē*.

english_scripts:
śadura mā madiḻ śūz ilaṅgaikkiṟaivan talaipattudira ōṭṭi
ōr veṅgaṇai uyttavan ōda vaṇṇan
madura mā vaṇḍu pāḍa mā mayilāḍaraṅgattammān
tiru vayiṭrudara bandam en uḻḻattuḻ ninṟulāginṟadē
meaning: He who resides in Śrīraṅgam, where bees sing sweetly and majestic peacocks dance; who, with a single fierce arrow, caused the ten heads of the lord of Laṅkā, surrounded on all four sides by lofty walls, to fall; and whose complexion is that of the cool ocean—His ornament, which He wears around His waist, has now entered his inner heart and settled there.
purport:
To the south of Bhārata lies Laṅkā, which was once ruled by Kubera. Rāvaṇa seized this magnificent city from the Yakṣa king and established his dominion over it. Laṅkā was comparable to the celestial realm of Indra in its splendour and prosperity. Surrounded by formidable fortifications and adorned with resplendent golden structures, it stood as one of the most glorious cities in existence. Thiruppān Āḻvār observes that only an exceptionally powerful ruler could govern such a kingdom and therefore refers to Rāvaṇa as *Iraivan*, the mighty sovereign of Laṅkā.

Rāvaṇa's tyranny and the disturbances he inflicted upon the worlds of the Devatas ultimately led to the descent of the Lord as Śrī Rāmacandra. The Lord effortlessly destroyed this formidable Asura, causing his ten heads to fall one after another as easily as a puppeteer manipulates and casts aside his puppets. Through the expressions *udhira oṭṭi* and *vem kaṇai uyttavan ōda vaṇṇan*, the Āḻvār delights in the Lord's *Vīrattva*, His unsurpassed valour and heroic prowess, manifested in the destruction of Rāvaṇa.

Thiruppān Āḻvār is immersed in *Viṣṇu-samleśa-bhāva*, a state of profound and intimate union with the Lord through devotion. Having reached the pinnacle of his experience of Raṅganātha, he perceives the entire environment of Śrīraṅgam as participating in divine worship. The bees hum melodiously as though chanting "Raṅga, Raṅga," while the peacocks dance in joyous response to that sacred refrain. In the Āḻvār's vision, both the bees and the peacocks celebrate the glory of Raṅga. Through the phrase *madhura māvandu pāda māmayil āḍu araṅgattu amman*, he experiences the omnipresent Lord whose presence fills and sanctifies all creation.

The Āḻvār then contemplates the celebrated Dāmodara-līlā of Namperumāḷ through the words *thiruvayiṟṟu udhara bandham en uḷḷattil niṉṟu ulagiṉṟadhe*. Namperumāḷ is the Supreme Reality, beyond the reach of even Brahmā and Rudra. Yet this very Lord allowed Himself to be bound by a simple rope in the hands of Yaśodā. This līlā reveals the incomparable love and affection that He bears towards His devotees and *Prapannas*. The rope with which He was bound left a mark upon His divine stomach, a mark that now remains vividly present within the Āḻvār's heart. As he meditates upon this sacred sign, he becomes immersed in the Lord's *Saulabhya*, His extraordinary accessibility and loving condescension towards those who seek refuge in Him.

english_scripts:
pāram āya pazavinai paṭraṟuttu
ennai ttan vāram ākki vaittān vaittadanṟi ennuḻ pugundān
kōra mādavam śeydanan kolaṟiyēn araṅgattammān
tiru āra mārvadanṟō aḍiyēnai āṭkoṇḍadē
meaning: He who removed his association with unbearable and ancient sins; who not only made him a person filled with love for Him and bound to Him, but also entered his very mind—for which he knows not when he performed such great and arduous penances—such Raṅganātha's chest, the abode of Lakṣmī, and the ornament adorning it, have made him serve Him.
purport:
Thiruppān Āḻvār speaks of how Raṅganātha Himself transformed the course of his life. From beginningless time, the Jīvātmā accumulates the results of its actions. This accumulated store of karma is known as *Sañcita Karma*. It serves as a major obstacle that prevents the Jīvātmā from attaining Mokṣa. When the Āḻvār declares *pāram āya paḻavinai paṭṟaṟuttu*, he indicates that the grace of Raṅganātha severed all connections with these accumulated karmic bonds. This idea is beautifully echoed in Rāmānujācārya's *Gadyatrayam*. In the *Śrī Raṅga Gadyam*, he states that when Raṅganātha casts His merciful glance upon His devotees, sins as vast as mountains are instantly reduced to ashes. Not only does He destroy their sins, but He also enters their hearts, enabling them to perform *Kaiṅkaryam* to Himself and to His devotees. This experience is expressed through the words *eṉṉai ttaṉ vāram ākki vaittāṉ vaittadaṉṟi eṉṉuḷ pugundhāṉ*.

The Āḻvār then marvels at the Lord's boundless compassion and wonders what extraordinary merit he could possibly have accumulated to deserve such grace. "What great austerities could have been performed by me," he asks, "for Paravāsudeva, reclining upon Ādiśeṣa as Raṅga, to destroy my sins and draw me close to Himself?" A similar sentiment is found in the works of Parāśara Bhaṭṭar, the eminent scholar and Ācārya of the Śrī Vaiṣṇava tradition. In one of his hymns, he pleads before Raṅganātha, saying, "O Lord, I am the lowest among the lowly. What will You do when one such as I enters Your temple precincts, which are themselves Vaikuṇṭha?" Both Bhaṭṭar and the Āḻvār celebrate the Lord's *Dayā-guṇa*, His infinite compassion. Even those who possess no worthiness of their own are uplifted by His grace, drawn into His presence, and made to realise the true purpose of life.

The pāsuram concludes with the Āḻvār's contemplation of Bhagavān together with His inseparable consort, Śrī Mahālakṣmī. Although Mahālakṣmī is eternally united with Bhagavān, the two together constitute the complete *Īśvara-tattva*. Therefore, she eternally resides upon His divine chest, reposing there in bliss. Her presence is associated with the auspicious mark known as *Śrīvatsam*, which adorns the Lord's chest. When the Vedas seek to identify the Supreme Reality, they glorify Brahman through countless distinguishing attributes, known as *Viśeṣaṇas*. Among all these exalted characteristics, particular emphasis is placed upon His being *Śrīyapati* and *Śrīman*—the Lord who is eternally united with Śrī, Bhū, and Nīlā Devīs. The scriptures proclaim that the Supreme Puruṣa, the creator and sustainer of all beings, is He who is never separated from Lakṣmī. Reflecting upon this truth, the Āḻvār acknowledges that it is through the *anugraha* of Mahālakṣmī that he has been blessed with the privilege of rendering service to the Lord.

tuṇḍa veṇpiṟaiyan tuyar tīrttavan
añjiṟaiya vaṇḍuvāz pozil śūz araṅga nagar mēya appan
aṇḍar aṇḍa pagiraṇḍattu
orumānilam ezumāl varai
muṭrum uṇḍa kaṇḍam kaṇḍīr aḍiyēnai uyyakkoṇḍadē
meaning: That Śrīraṅganātha, who removed the sin of Rudra, who wears the white crescent moon; who resides in Śrīraṅgam, surrounded by gardens where bees with beautiful wings dwell—His throat, which swallowed this world, the other worlds, the seven mountains, and the entire universe, has saved him, who is His servant.
purport:
As a consequence of severing one of Brahmā's heads, Rudra incurred the sin of Brahmahatyā and sought a means to free himself from its effects. Rudra, revered as one of the greatest Vaiṣṇavas, performed penance to Raṅganātha on the banks of the Candra Puṣkariṇī. Through the grace of Mahā Viṣṇu, the bearer of the white crescent moon upon his matted locks was finally relieved of his suffering and freed from the burden of that sin. This is indicated by the expression *tuṇḍa veṇpiṟaiyaṉ tuyar tīrttavaṉ*. The same compassionate Lord resides in Śrīraṅgam, the sacred city surrounded by flourishing groves filled with flowers and resonant with the humming of bees, as celebrated in the words *añjiṟaiya vaṇḍuvāḻ poḻil śūz araṅga nagar mēya appaṉ*.

Finally, the Āḻvār revels in the immeasurable glory of the Lord through the words:

The Āḻvār reflects upon the time of *Pralaya*, when the entire universe reaches dissolution. At that time, the Supreme Lord, in His form as Saṅkarṣaṇa, withdraws all creation into Himself, leaving nothing apart from His own divine existence. The worlds, the mountains, the celestial systems, and all beings, from Brahmā down to the smallest ant, are absorbed into Him, only to be brought forth again at the beginning of the next cycle of creation. Gazing upon this wondrous act, the Āḻvār becomes captivated by the Lord's divine throat, which has contained the entirety of existence within itself.

Filled with astonishment, the Āḻvār reflects, "That very Lord, who creates, sustains, and withdraws the universe, has now taken possession of me and granted me salvation." By revealing His true *svarūpa*, severing the bonds of saṁsāra, and bestowing the privilege of rendering *kaiṅkaryam* with complete joy and fulfilment, the Lord has rescued the Āḻvār from the endless cycle of birth and death. Thus, the Āḻvār delights in the Supreme Protector, who unfailingly comes to the aid of those who seek refuge in Him. His deep devotion shines through his wonder at the Lord's cosmic deeds and his profound gratitude for the personal grace that transformed his life and secured his ultimate welfare.

tamil_scripts:
கையின் ஆர் சுரி சங்கு அனல் ஆழியர் நீள் வரை போல்

ஐயனார் அணி அரங்கனார் அரவின் அணை மிசை மேய
மாயனார் செய்ய வாய், ஐயோ ! என்னைச் சிந்தை கவர்ந்ததுவே !
english_scripts:
kaiyin ār śuri śaṅganal āziyar nīḻvarai pōl
meyyanār tuḻaba viraiyār kamaz nīṇ muḍi em
aiyanār aṇi araṅganār aravin aṇaimiśai mēya māyanār
śeyya vāy aiyō ! ennai ccindai kavarndaduvē !
meaning: He who bears the conch and the flaming Cakra (Tiruvāḻi) in His divine hands; who possesses a divine body resembling a great mountain; who wears a divine crown fragrant with sweet Tiruttuḻāy (Tulasi); who is his Lord; who reclines in Śrīraṅgam, an ornament among sacred places; who rests upon the sweet bed of Ādiśeṣa (Tiruvanantāḻvān); and who performs wondrous deeds—His red lips have stolen his mind.
purport:
Bhagavān is traditionally depicted with two prominent divine weapons: Pāñcajanya, the conch, and Sudarśana, the discus. Pāñcajanya symbolizes divine knowledge, while Sudarśana represents His *Saṅkalpa-śakti*, the irresistible power of His divine will. Although the Lord has no need of weapons for His protection or victory, these eternal attendants remain ever ready to serve Him. To Asuras and Daityas such as the Hiraṇyas, they appear fearsome and destructive. The Sudarśana, whose glories are celebrated in the *Ahibudhnya Saṃhitā*, is said to destroy the Lord's enemies even before receiving an explicit command. Similarly, Pāñcajanya subdues adversaries merely through the awe and terror inspired by its resounding call. Yet to *Prapannas*, these very weapons appear not as instruments of destruction but as beautiful ornaments adorning the Lord. Through his divine vision, the Āḻvār beholds these sacred weapons and delights in the beauty of the Lord who bears them, as expressed in the words *kaiyiṉ ār śuri śaṅgaṉal āḻiyar*.

The Āḻvār then contemplates the Lord's majestic form. His physique is powerful and perfectly proportioned, while His broad chest resembles a great mountain in its grandeur and magnificence. This is the very chest that grants refuge and peace to devotees and serves as the eternal abode of Mahālakṣmī, the Mother of the universe. Adorned with fragrant garlands of *tulasī*, the Lord appears both transcendent and infinitely compassionate. For devotees, the vision of this divine form alone constitutes the highest attainment and fulfilment. The Āḻvār celebrates this beauty through the expression *meyyaṉār tuḻāba viraiyār kamaḻ nīṇ muḍi em*. This very Lord reclines upon Ādiśeṣa as Raṅganātha in the sacred city of Śrīraṅgam.

As the Āḻvār's gaze ascends further, it comes to rest upon the Lord's radiant red lips. At this point, he is overwhelmed by the intensity of the Lord's beauty. The experience becomes almost unbearable in its sweetness and charm. Captivated beyond measure, the Āḻvār instinctively exclaims, "Aiyo!" in astonishment and wonder. Those crimson lips completely conquer his mind and heart, leaving no room for any other thought. Through this experience, the Āḻvār reveals the many facets of Śrīraṅganātha: the bearer of divine weapons, the possessor of an incomparable and transcendent form, the Lord who reclines in Śrīraṅgam, and the enchanter who captivates the hearts of His devotees through His boundless beauty. The depth of the Āḻvār's devotion shines forth in his detailed contemplation of the Lord's attributes and in the ecstatic delight that arises from beholding His divine form.

tamil_scripts:
பரியன் ஆகி வந்த அவுணன் உடல் கீண்ட அமரர்க்கு
அரிய ஆதிபிரான் அரங்கத்து அமலன் முகத்துக்
கரிய ஆகிப் புடை பரந்து மிளிர்ந்து செவ்வரி ஓடி நீண்ட அப்
பெரிய ஆய கண்கள் என்னைப் பேதமை செய்தனவே
english_scripts:
pariyan āgi vanda avuṇan uḍal kīṇḍa
amararkkariya ādi ppirān araṅgattamalan mugattu
kariya āgi ppuḍai parandu miḻirndu śevvari ōḍi
nīṇḍa apperiya vāya kaṇgaḻ ennai ppēdaimai śeydanavē !
meaning: He who ripped apart the mighty body of Hiraṇya when he came against Him; who is unattainable even to the Devās; who is the origin of everything; who helps all beings; who resides in Śrīraṅgam; and who is supremely pure—His eyes, overflowing with grace, dark and wide, streaked with red lines, have made him a fool.
purport:
When Hiraṇyakaśipu received a boon from Brahmā that he would not be slain by any of Brahmā's creations, he became arrogant and unleashed chaos throughout the three worlds. However, he failed to realise that there exists One who transcends even Brahmā, the Supreme Being who grants liberation to all and within whose divine being the entire universe resides. Blinded by pride and ignorance, the foolish Daitya persecuted the young and devoted Prahlāda, who remained steadfast in his devotion to Bhagavān. Unable to tolerate the suffering inflicted upon His beloved devotee, the Lord manifested without delay as Narasiṃha. Tearing apart the tyrant, He brought an end to his atrocities and delivered the worlds from fear and oppression.

That Narasiṃha is beyond all the Devatas. What none among Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, or any other celestial being could accomplish was effortlessly achieved by Bhagavān alone. He is the Supreme Reality, unattainable even to the greatest of the gods through their own efforts. This primordial Lord, the source of all existence, now resides in Śrīraṅgam, embodying absolute purity and perfection. The Āḻvār celebrates Him through the words *pariyan āgi vanda avuṇan uḍal kīṇḍa amararkkariya ādi ppirān araṅgattamalan mugattu*.

The Āḻvār's gaze then rests upon the Lord's divine eyes, which overflow with grace, compassion, and affection. Who could behold such eyes without melting in devotion? Brahmā, the creator himself, meditates upon those eyes. Ikṣvāku lost his heart to their beauty. Yāmunācārya became a servant of the Lord through their enchanting influence, and Dhanurdāsa abandoned all worldly attachments after realising that nothing in existence was worthy of contemplation when compared to those divine eyes. After beholding the eyes of the All-seeing Lord, what else remains worthy of being seen?

Those eyes are dark, expansive, and adorned with delicate reddish streaks. The Āḻvār delights in their beauty and symbolism. Just as a fisherman attracts fish with bait, the Lord draws the minds and hearts of devotees towards Himself through the irresistible charm of His eyes. Their glance captivates, comforts, and conquers all who behold them. At this stage, the Āḻvār can no longer maintain composure. Having ascended to the heights of *Parama-bhakti*, he becomes completely overwhelmed by the Lord's beauty. The divine eyes of Raṅganātha have entirely seized his heart, leaving him intoxicated with devotion and unable to think of anything other than the Lord.

tamil_scripts:
ஆல மாமரத்தின் இலை மேல் ஓர் பாலகனாய்
ஞாலம் ஏழும் உண்டான் அரங்கத்து அரவின் அணையான்
கோல மா மணி ஆரமும் முத்துத் தாமமும் முடிவு இல்லது ஓர் எழில்
நீல மேனி ஐயோ ! நிறை கொண்டது என் நெஞ்சினையே
english_scripts:
ālamā marattin ilaimēl oru pālakanāy
ñālam ēzum uṇḍān araṅgattaravin aṇaiyān
kōlamā maṇi āramum muttuttāmamum muḍivilladōr ezil
nīla mēni aiyō! niṟai koṇḍaden neñjinaiyē!
meaning: He who was (lying as) a small child on a leaf of the giant banyan tree and swallowed all seven worlds, and who is lying on the sweet bed of Ādiśeṣa, His blue colored (dark) divine body without par in its beauty and with the beautiful and special gemmed garlands and pearl necklaces has alas, stolen the completeness of my heart.
purport:
After the dissolution of the entire universe, nothing remains except the Supreme Lord. The *Mahānārāyaṇopaniṣad* declares that from this primordial Being, who alone exists upon the cosmic waters, Brahmā, known as Hiraṇyagarbha, comes into existence. The *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* further describes how the Lord floated upon the cosmic ocean as a divine child resting upon a banyan leaf. The Āḻvār recalls this wondrous manifestation and marvels that the very same child now reclines upon Ādiśeṣa in Śrīraṅgam. This experience is expressed through the words *ālamā marattin ilaimēl oru pālakanāy ñālam ēẓum uṇḍān araṅgattaravin aṇaiyān*.

The Āḻvār's heart is now completely captivated by the *Svarūpa* of Bhagavān. Before him appears a divine blue-hued child, adorned with radiant ornaments, pearl garlands, lotus decorations, and countless celestial embellishments. His beauty is immeasurable and beyond all description. The Lord's dark blue complexion resembles a rain-laden cloud, ever ready to shower compassion and grace upon His devotees. The Āḻvār delights in this enchanting vision through the words *kōlamā maṇi āramum muttuttāmamum muḍivilladōr ezil nīla mēni aiyō! niṟai koṇḍaden neñjinaiyē!*.

Overwhelmed by this experience, the Āḻvār exclaims in wonder and amazement. The Lord's divine form has completely filled and possessed his heart, leaving no space for any other thought or attachment. In beholding such unsurpassed beauty, the Āḻvār realises with certainty that Bhagavān alone is the supreme goal of existence, the ultimate *Puruṣārtha* sought by all beings. Having experienced His beauty, compassion, and majesty, there remains nothing else worthy of pursuit. The Lord Himself stands revealed as both the means and the end, the highest treasure to be attained and eternally enjoyed.

tamil_scripts:
கொண்டல் வண்ணனைக் கோவலனாய் வெண்ணெய்
உண்ட வாயன் என் உள்ளம் கவர்ந்தானை
அண்டர்கோன் அணி அரங்கன் என் அமுதினைக்
கண்ட கண்கள் மற்று ஒன்றினைக் காணாவே
english_scripts:
koṇḍal vaṇṇanai kōvalanāy veṇṇey uṇḍa vāyan
en uḻḻam kavarndānai aṇḍar kōn aṇi araṅgan
en amudinai kkaṇḍa kaṇgaḻ maṭronṟinai kkāṇāvē
meaning: My eyes, which have seen Him who has the form of a moisture-laden cloud, who has the mouth with which He ate butter when born as a Yādava, who stole his heart, who is the Lord of the Nityasūris, who rests in Śrīraṅgam, an ornament to this world, and who is nectar to him, will not see anything else.
purport:
Tiruppāṇ Āḻvār has now beheld the complete divine form of the Lord in the previous pāsuram. Having experienced the full beauty of Raṅganātha, he no longer desires to see anything else. His eyes have attained the most precious vision that can ever be beheld. That divine form is *Aprākṛtika*, entirely beyond the realm of material existence. What could possibly be compared to such a form? The Āḻvār declares that this vision has completely stolen his heart, just as the Lord once stole butter from the homes of the Gopīs when He appeared as Yādava Kṛṣṇa. The Lord who is the master of even the Nitya Sūris, who are untouched by karma and eternally established in His service, has now captured the heart of the Āḻvār.

Overwhelmed by this experience, the Āḻvār wonders, "What remains to be seen now?" Having beheld the Supreme Being reclining upon Ādiśeṣa, the embodiment of sweetness, simplicity, and unfailing protection, nothing else appears worthy of attention. What could ever equal that divine vision? What could compare with the form that enchanted even the great ascetics and Ṛṣis, who longed to embrace Him when He appeared before them as Śrī Rāmacandra? This alone is the true nectar, infinitely superior to the celestial nectar that merely grants temporary freedom from death and suffering. The beauty and grace of Bhagavān bestow an eternal fulfilment that transcends all worldly attainments.

Having attained the culmination of divine experience, the Āḻvār now prays for Mokṣa. Responding to this heartfelt appeal, Raṅganātha bestows liberation upon him. Through the grace of the Lord's sacred lotus feet, the Āḻvār attains Paramapadam, the eternal abode that is the true goal of all spiritual endeavour. Thus ends the sublime journey of Tiruppāṇ Āḻvār, who not only experienced the unsurpassed beauty of the Lord but also revealed to the world the path that leads to Vaikuṇṭhanātha Himself. Therefore, surrender is offered unto that blessed Āḻvār, who showed the way to the eternal abode through his divine experience and sacred hymns.

tamil_scripts:

பிறப்பிலியாய்‌ இறப்பதற்கே எண்ணாது.
எண்ணும்‌ பொன்‌ உருவாய்‌ மணி உருவில்‌ பூதம்‌ ஐந்தாய்ப்‌,
புனல்‌ உருவாய்‌ அனல்‌ உருவில்‌ திகழும்‌ சோதி.
தன்‌ உருவாய்‌ என்‌ உருவில்‌ நின்ற எந்தை,
தளிர்‌ புரையும்‌ திருவடி என்‌ தலை மேலவே
english_scripts:
min uruvāy mun uruvil vēdam nāngāy 
viḻakkoḻiyāy muḻaittezunda tiṅgaḻ tānāy 
pin uruvāy mun uruvil piṇi mūppillā piṟappiliyāy iṟappadaṟkē 
eṇṇādu eṇṇum pon uruvāy maṇi uruvil pūdam aindāy 
punal uruvāy anal uruvil tigazum śōdi 
tan uruvāy en uruvil ninṟa endai 
taḻir puraiyum tiruvaḍi en talai mēlavē
meaning: He has shown him that the insentient things seen around are fleeting like lightning. He has revealed the four Vedas and is like the light of a lamp, dispelling the darkness called ignorance from him. He has given him knowledge, clear like the blemishless moon risen on the horizon, and as perceptible as the moon shining in the sky above. He has shown him that the ātmā is distinct and free from the disease, old age, and rebirth associated with the insentient things seen around. He does not deign to grant him Kaivalya. He has shown him His precious form, which cannot be cognized by anyone at any time. He possesses a human form composed of the divine elements (Śuddha Sattva). He is pleasant and refreshing to devotees like cool water, and to inimical beings, like fire. He is the effulgence within all and is supremely radiant. The sacred feet of such a One are enshrined in his heart.
purport:
Āḻvār expresses his gratitude to Bhagavān in this pāsuram. Tirunēṭuntāṇṭakam was composed by Āḻvār during the final stage of his life. Throughout his life, he had repeatedly pleaded with Bhagavān to grant him the vision of His Divya Maṅgala Rūpa. Indeed, the biography of Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār records that Bhagavān, accompanied by His divine consort, appeared before him in the form of a newly married couple and personally initiated him into the sacred Aṣṭākṣarī mantra. From that moment onward, Āḻvār became fully immersed in bhakti. Therefore, he reflects here on how Bhagavān blessed him and redirected his mind towards the Lord's lotus feet. Bhagavān revealed to Āḻvār the transient nature of this material world and the eternal nature of the ātmā, which is free from disease, suffering, and decay. This knowledge was bestowed upon him with the sudden brilliance and clarity of a lightning flash.

Similar to the opening pāsuram of Tiruvāymoḻi by Nammāḻvār, Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār also acknowledges that Bhagavān alone grants the knowledge that dispels the darkness of ignorance. What made Āḻvār even more grateful was that, in addition to imparting divine knowledge, the Lord also revealed His own divine form, which is not constituted of the elements of this material world. Unlike material substances, His Divya Maṅgala Rūpa is completely free from rajas and tamas and is therefore described as Śuddha Sattva. Just as the material world is constituted of five prākṛtika elements, the Lord's divine form is said to be constituted of five Śuddha Sattva principles, glorified in the Pañcopaniṣad mantras as Parameṣṭhi, Pumān, Nivṛtta, Viśva, and Sarva. Āḻvār is overwhelmed with gratitude that the Lord revealed such a transcendent form, a vision inaccessible even to Brahmā and Rudra. It is through the Lord's grace in bestowing both this divine knowledge and the experience of His divine form that Āḻvār was able to develop profound love and devotion towards Him.

பார்‌ உருவில்‌ நீர்‌ எரிகால்‌ விசும்பும்‌ ஆகிப்‌,

ஏர்‌ உருவில்‌ மூவருமே என நின்ற.

முகில்‌ உருவம்‌ எம்‌ அடிகள்‌ உருவந்‌ தானே
english_scripts:
pār uruvil nīr erigāl viśumbum āgi
palvēṟu śamayamumāy pparandu ninṟa
ēr uruvil mūvarumē ena ninṟa
imaiyavar tam tiruvuru vēṟeṇṇum pōdu
 ōr uruvam pon uruvam onṟu śendī
onṟu mā kaḍal uruvam ottu ninṟa
mū uruvum kaṇḍa pōdonṟām śōdi
mugil uruvam em aḍigaḻ uruvan tānē
meaning: He stands in a divine form as the Trinity. Yet, when the celestials conceive of their forms differently, one (Brahmā's) is of the nature of gold, one (Śiva's) is of the nature of red-hot fire, and one (the Lord's) is of the nature of the great ocean. Upon examining these three forms along with their associated natures, it is seen that our Master is the One who created the Pañcabhūtas, namely Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether (primary creation), and who stands pervading the innumerable and distinct orderly creations (secondary creation), which shine forth as a unified effulgence of love, bearing the nature of the clouds.
purport:
Āḻvār beautifully expounds the supremacy of Bhagavān (Paratattvam) in this passage. He first declares, "He stands in a divine form as the Trinity" (*pār uruvil nīr eri kāl viśumbum āgi*). Through this, Āḻvār conveys that Bhagavān Himself created Brahmā and Rudra and entered into them as their Antaryāmī to carry out the functions of creation and destruction respectively. Thus, the three fundamental activities of the universe—creation, preservation, and destruction—are ultimately performed by Bhagavān alone.

At first glance, it may appear that Āḻvār is equating all three members of the Trinity. However, he clarifies this in the following line. While Bhagavān enters Brahmā and Rudra as their Antaryāmī and empowers them to perform their respective functions, He also distinctly manifests as Viṣṇu. In this way, Āḻvār establishes both the Lord's indwelling presence within all beings and His unique, independent identity. Although these three forms appear different, Āḻvār speaks of Brahmā and Rudra in terms of their indwelling Self, namely Bhagavān Himself. Therefore, the One who truly possesses and governs all these forms is none other than our beloved Master.

He is the One who first brought forth the pañcabhūtas and subsequently carried out the secondary creation of all animate and inanimate entities. Yet His role does not end with creation alone. Having brought all beings into existence, He enters each of them as Antaryāmī, sustaining them from within and enabling all their activities. As their inner ruler and support, He continually provides the very life force and existence upon which they depend.

திருவடிவில்‌ ௧௬ நெடுமால்‌ சேயன்‌ என்றும்‌,

english_scripts:
tiruvaḍivil karu neḍumāl śēyan enṟum
tirēdaikkaṇ vaḻai uruvāy ttigazndān enṟum
peru vaḍivil kaḍal amudam koṇḍa kālam
perumānai kkaru nīla vaṇṇan tannai
oru vaḍivattōr uruvenṟuṇaral āgādu
ūzidōṟūzi ninṟēttal allāl
karu vaḍivil śeṅgaṇṇa vaṇṇan tannai
kaṭṭuraiyē yār oruvar kāṇgiṟpārē
meaning: It is said that the cloud-hued Lord, together with the effulgence of Lakṣmī, shone with a white body in a gigantic form as the Tortoise at the time when the nectar was obtained from the Milk Ocean (in Kṛta Yuga), and that He was of a red hue in Tretā Yuga. The great Lord of blue complexion (in Kali Yuga) cannot be conceived of as possessing any single form, nature, or color. Apart from praising Him continuously, age after age, through mere imagination, has anyone truly seen the dark-bodied, red-eyed Lord as he has seen Him?
purport:
In the first pāsuram, the Lord revealed to Āḻvār the futility of attachment to the body and the individual self, as well as the inadequacy of remaining in kaivalya. He also granted him the vision of His own incomparable beauty. In the second pāsuram, He revealed that He alone, and none other, is the sole Master of all. Having received these revelations, Āḻvār now stands like a chaste wife wholly dedicated to her husband. In this pāsuram, Āḻvār declares that he beholds the Lord in His true nature and in the full splendour of His divine form, unlike others who, throughout the ages, perceive Him only according to the limitations imposed by their surroundings and mental dispositions, shaped as they are by the three guṇas of sattva, rajas, and tamas.

During Kṛta Yuga, sattva predominates, and therefore people perceive the Lord as white, the colour traditionally associated with sattva. In Tretā Yuga, rajas becomes dominant, and the Lord is seen in red, the colour corresponding to that quality. In Dvāpara Yuga, where rajas and tamas exist in a mixed proportion, the perceived colour is understood to be intermediate in nature. In Kali Yuga, tamas predominates, and its associated colour is black. Yet, since people of this age are generally not inclined towards God and are unable to perceive Him as He truly is, the Lord remains in His natural hue, the deep blue complexion of Nilamegha Śyāma, manifesting in His own intrinsic splendour.

Āḻvār also beautifully extols the divinity of Mahālakṣmī through the phrase *kaḍalamutam koṇḍa kālam*. When the Milk Ocean was churned, not only did the devas obtain nectar, but the Lord Himself gained the supreme nectar in the form of Mahālakṣmī, who emerged from those sacred waters. Āḻvār, in turn, partakes of that same nectar through his loving glorification of the Lord and His divine consort. Thus, the episode becomes not merely an account of cosmic events, but a celebration of the inseparable union of the Divine Couple and the bliss experienced by the devotee who contemplates them.

english_scripts:
indiraṟkum piramaṟkum mudalvan tannai
iru nilam kāl tī nīr viṇ pūdam aindāy
śendiṟatta tamiz ōśai vaḍaśol āgi
tiśai nāngumāy ttiṅgaḻ ñāyiṟāgi
andarattil tēvarkkum aṟiyal āgā andaṇanai
andaṇar māṭṭandi vaitta mandirattai
mandirattāl maṟavādenṟum
vāzudiyēl vāzalām maḍa neñjamē
meaning: Obedient mind! We can live worthily in the company of the Nityasūris if we can forever, without interruption, eulogize through the Tirumantra that Protector (mantrāṁ trāyate iti mantraḥ, “the one who protects the chanter”), who is the originator of Indra and Brahmā (in secondary creation); who caused the five elements, namely Earth, Wind, Fire, Water, and Ether (in primary creation); who is accurately revealed in the Tamil Prabandham and the Sanskrit scriptures; who is the inner controller of everything in the four directions; who ordains the Moon and the Sun; who is the Immaculate One who, though dwelling in their hearts, cannot be understood even by the gods; and who is glorified in the Upaniṣads, the concluding portion of the sages' scriptures.
purport:
This pāsuram glorifies the Tirumantram, the sacred Aṣṭākṣarī mantra. Similar to the teachings found in Tiruvāymoḻi, Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār instructs the mind to contemplate the Supreme Lord through the recitation and meditation of the Tirumantram. The Nārāyaṇopaniṣad says the following about the Aṣṭākṣarī mantra:

<verse>om namo nārāyaṇāyēti ma̍ntrōpā̠sakaḥ |\
vaikuṇṭhabhuvanalōka̍-ṅgami̠ṣyati ।</verse>

This states that one who performs upāsanā on this sacred mantra ultimately attains Vaikuṇṭha, the Supreme Abode from which the jīvātmā never returns to the cycle of worldly existence. Āḻvār echoes the same truth in this pāsuram when he urges, "O mind, recite the Tirumantram so that we may dwell in the company of the Nityasūris, the eternal servants of the Lord in Vaikuṇṭha."

Addressing his own mind, and thereby instructing all devotees, Āḻvār asks it to meditate upon Bhagavān, the source of even Brahmā and Rudra. This teaching is once again affirmed in the Nārāyaṇopaniṣad as follows:

<verse>nā̠rā̠ya̠ṇādbra̍hmā jā̠yatē ।\
nā̠rā̠ya̠ṇādru̍drō jā̠yatē।</verse>

This declares that Brahmā and Rudra emerged from Nārāyaṇa. The pāsuram thus serves as a clear demonstration of how the Divya Prabandham embodies the very essence of Vedānta. This same Nārāyaṇa is the creator of the five great elements, the Pañcabhūtas, which constitute the material universe. Āḻvār further proclaims that this Supreme Lord is glorified both by the Vedas, the repository of Sanskrit revelation, and by the Prabandha Mālai, the treasure of Tamil revelation.

Āḻvār also affirms that the Moon, the Sun, and all the directions function entirely under the Lord's sovereignty. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad states the same truth:

<verse>bhī̠ṣā-'smā̠dvāta̍ḥ pavatē । bhī̠ṣōdē̍ti̠ sūrya̍ḥ । bhīṣā-'smādagni̍śchēndra̠ścha । mṛtyurdhāvati pañcha̍ma iti ।</verse>

This means that the wind blows, the sun shines, Agni and Indra perform their respective functions, and even Death itself carries out its duty out of reverential awe for Brahman. That same Brahman remains beyond the comprehension of even the devas. He cannot be fully grasped by the mind or expressed through ordinary thought, a truth echoed in the Upaniṣadic statement *aprāpya manasā saha*. Thus, the theological vision presented in this pāsuram closely mirrors the teachings of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad. Through his divine insight, Āḻvār exhorts all seekers to receive the Tirumantram through proper initiation from an Ācārya, constantly remember the Lord through its recitation, attain His eternal abode, and abide forever in unending bliss.

eṇ madiyum kaḍandaṇḍa mīdu pōgi
iru viśumbin ūḍu pōy ezundu
mēlai ttaṇ madiyum kadiravanum tavira ōḍi
tārakaiyin puṟam taḍavi appāl mikku
maṇ muzudum agappaḍuttu ninṟa endai
malar puraiyum tiruvaḍiyē vaṇaṅginēnē
meaning: One leg stopped short of sweeping the Earth and the waters with a single charming step. The other leg, beyond the imagination of the fortunate Mahābali, who beheld the Lord face to face, rose up from the sacrificial ground and penetrated the cosmic egg, reaching up to Brahmaloka beyond the vast heavens, the cool Moon, the Sun, and even the world of stars. He prostrates before the sacred feet, fresh as newly blossomed flowers, of his Father, who stood thus and took possession of all the worlds.
purport:
Āḻvār visualizes the Vāmana and Trivikrama incarnations in this pāsuram. Here, the relationship between the jīvātmā and Īśvara, namely that of servant and Master, is beautifully brought out. When Mahābali agreed to grant the dwarf brāhmaṇa a piece of land measuring three footsteps, the Lord revealed His true majesty and resolved to measure the entire universe with just two steps, thereby once again establishing His sovereignty over all creation.

With His first step, He encompassed the Earth, the waters, and all the worlds below. His second step expanded beyond all measure, reaching the very limits of the universe. At the boundary of Satyaloka, Brahmā worshipped those divine lotus feet with great reverence. It is said that Dharma Devī herself flowed as sacred water upon those feet, and from that divine contact the holy river Gaṅgā came into existence. Thus, those lotus feet became the source of one of the most sacred rivers revered throughout the worlds.

Āḻvār therefore offers his prostrations to those very feet that rose beyond the Moon, the Sun, and even Satyaloka; to those feet that bestowed eternal blessings upon Mahābali; and to those feet from which the sacred Gaṅgā emerged. The Lord's cosmic stride was not merely an act of measuring the worlds, but a revelation of His supreme lordship and boundless grace.

Through this contemplation, Āḻvār recalls that the same Trivikrama is the Supreme Īśvara, the ruler and owner of all existence. In contrast, all jīvātmās are eternally dependent upon Him and exist solely as His servants. By meditating upon the Trivikrama incarnation, Āḻvār reaffirms this fundamental truth of existence: that Bhagavān is the eternal Master, and the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the jīvātmā is loving and eternal service to Him.

meaning: The Lord of the Nityasūris, the unique Rider of Garuḍa of lovely wings, who, by nature, has hands far-flung and generous to satiety (towards His devotees), does not grace, out of anger, the rākṣasas (inimical people). Mind! Let us prostrate, eulogizing His feet through all towns relished by Him on the way, lovely Kōvalūr surrounded by tanks and with spread-out fields growing precious crops, where pearl-like droplets in mire oozing out from tall bamboo trees, brought and thrown about in the fields by the overflowing water of river Pennai are discarded (by the farmers).
purport:
Having given a magnificent description of the Lord in His Trivikrama avatāra in the previous pāsuram, Āḻvār need not lament that he was not present during that divine age to behold the Lord with his own eyes. The same Lord continues to reside at Tirukkōvaḷūr in the very form in which He manifested during that avatāra, making Himself available to devotees born in later generations. Thus, the blessings of witnessing Trivikrama are not confined to those who lived during the avatāra itself, but remain accessible to all who approach Him with devotion.

Āḻvār's mention of the Nityasūris and Garuḍa highlights the transcendental nature of Nārāyaṇa. In Paramapada, the Lord has already bestowed the highest gift upon the Nityasūris, namely Himself, and there are no hostile or inimical beings there from whom protection is required. Therefore, references to the Nityasūris and Garuḍa serve to emphasize the Lord's divine majesty while simultaneously drawing attention to His extraordinary accessibility through His avatāras and arcā manifestations in this world.

The Lord who transcends all realms willingly descends among humanity so that ordinary beings may approach Him, worship Him, and experience His grace. Reflecting upon this boundless accessibility, Āḻvār turns to his own mind and urges it to undertake a sacred pilgrimage through the Lord's temple towns. Just as a weary traveller carefully chooses hospitable resting places while avoiding barren and inhospitable regions, the devotee should seek refuge in the Divya Deśams where the Lord graciously resides. Journeying from one sacred abode to another, singing His glories along the way, the mind becomes steadily absorbed in divine contemplation and progresses towards its ultimate goal of eternal service to the Lord.

pūṅgōvalūr tozudum pōdu neñjē !
meaning: Mind! Let us go to worship lovely Kōvalūr, guarded by the chaste virgin (Durgā) residing in the Vindhyas, with fragrant tanks, broad streets and lotus ponds, where the chieftains of the hills do service, the town of the Lord who wielded the lovely axe (as Paraśurāma) annihilating the Chieftains (like Kārtavīryārjuna), and the Lord (as Kṛṣṇa) who defeated the army led by Subrahmaṇya who wielded the unique spear in the huge sea containing the mountains.
purport:
Because of his intense devotion, Āḻvār becomes concerned for the safety of the Lord, who stands before the world in all the beauty, tenderness, and charm of youthful splendour, as described in the previous pāsurams, amidst people of asuric disposition. Such is the nature of divine love that the devotee, forgetting the Lord's omnipotence, becomes anxious for His well-being and protection.

A similar sentiment is seen in the Rāmāyaṇa. When Vibhīṣaṇa approached Rāma on the seashore seeking refuge, Sugrīva strongly opposed accepting him. Since Vibhīṣaṇa had come from the hostile environment of Laṅkā, Sugrīva feared that he might intend harm to Rāma. In response, Rāma reassured him by explaining His unwavering vow to protect anyone who sought refuge in Him, His code of righteousness, and His incomparable prowess. In the same manner, Āḻvār is now made to realize the Lord's supreme ability to overcome all opposing forces, and this realization fills him with joy and reassurance.

The pāsuram alludes to two well-known episodes from the Purāṇas. According to the ancient legend, all mountains once possessed wings and moved freely through the skies. Their constant movement caused great disturbance to the worlds, prompting Indra to sever their wings. Only the mountain Maināka escaped this fate by concealing itself beneath the ocean. Later, Subrahmaṇya, also known as Skanda, the commander-in-chief of the celestial armies, discovered Maināka and cut off its wings with his spear.

Āḻvār then recalls an even greater demonstration of the Lord's supremacy. The same Skanda, together with his father Śiva, came to the aid of Bāṇāsura when Kṛṣṇa waged war against him. Despite the combined strength of these mighty allies, they were effortlessly subdued by Kṛṣṇa. Through this remembrance, Āḻvār understands that the Lord who conquered such formidable opponents has nothing to fear from any hostile force. The pāsuram therefore transforms the devotee's anxiety into delight, as Āḻvār reflects upon the Lord's boundless power, which remains ever ready to protect both Himself and His devotees.

nīragattāy ! neḍuvaraiyin ucci mēlāy !
nilāttiṅgaḻ tuṇḍattāy ! niṟainda kacci ūragattāy
oṇ tuṟai nīr vegkā uḻḻāy !
uḻḻuvār uḻḻattāy
ulagam ēttum kāragattāy ! kārvānattuḻḻāy ! kaḻvā !
kāmaru pūṅgāviriyin tenbāl mannu pēragattāy
pērāden neñjin uḻḻāy !
perumān un tiruvaḍiyē pēṇinēnē
meaning: Lord Nīrakam (of the nature of water)! Lord at the top on the lofty mountain (Tirumalai)! Lord pleasing like (full) moon shining in a small place (Nilaṭiṭiṅgal Tuṇḍan)! Lord Uraga in Kāñcī! Lord reposing at Vēṅka near the lovely stream (Lord Yathōktakāri)! Lord in the hearts of those who meditate on you! Lord at Kāraga eulogized by the world! Lord like water-laden cloud (at Karvāṇam)! Deceitful Lord! Lord at Tiruppērai on the southern side of the highly cherished and lovely Kāvēri river! Lord established in my mind without parting ever! The lofty Lord! I have adorned your sacred feet.
purport:
Āḻvār was unable to physically experience the divine beauty and glorious qualities of the Lord that he had envisioned in the preceding pāsurams. As this composition belongs to the final period of his life, he would have been advanced in age and no longer possessed the strength required to undertake such a journey. Realizing his own limitations, he turns directly to the Lord, knowing that Bhagavān is not only the ultimate goal (*upeya*) but also the means (*upāya*) to attain that goal.

With this understanding, Āḻvār appeals to the Lord through the sentiment expressed in *kūvuḍal varuḍal ceyyāy*—"Either call me to You or come to me Yourself." This is an appeal founded entirely upon divine grace (*Tiruvaruḷ*). The devotee recognizes that his own efforts are insufficient and therefore seeks the Lord's intervention, whether by drawing him into His presence or by personally granting him the desired vision.

One may wonder why Āḻvār addresses the Lord in various sacred abodes when his longing is specifically to behold Him at Tirukkōvaḷūr. The answer lies in the Lord's all-pervading presence and His equal manifestation in every Divya Deśam. Just as the Sun illuminates the entire world uniformly while remaining one and the same, the Lord graciously resides in all the places that He has chosen as His abodes. Though the forms may appear in different locations, the Lord who dwells within them is one and indivisible.

Therefore, Āḻvār understands that his plea will reach the Lord regardless of the particular shrine to which it is addressed. Whether he prays at Tirukkōvaḷūr or at any other sacred abode, the same compassionate Lord hears his appeal. This conviction deepens his dependence upon divine grace, for he knows that the Lord who resides everywhere is fully capable of responding to the yearning of His devotee and granting the longed-for union.
archavathara: Śrīnivāsa,Appakkudathān Perumāḷ,Yathoktakāri Perumāḷ,Ādi Varāha Perumāḷ,Ulagāḷanda Perumāḷ,Jagadīśa Perumāḷ,Karuṇākara Perumāḷ,Nilāttiṅgaḷ Tuṇḍattān Perumāḷ

ēzaiyēn iṅṅanamē uzidarugēnē
meaning: Lord at Māmallaipuram where precious gems are brought by ships and dumped! Lord of the town of Kāñcī with fortifications! Lord at Tiruppērai! Lord who has Śiva with Pārvatī beside him on the left and decorated by garland of fragrant honey-soaked bilva flowers on his chest, at His side! Lord of the Milk-ocean! Lord who came on the earth (in avatāras)! Lord at the top of the cool mountain (Tirumalai)! Lord Pavaḷavanna (at Kāñcī)! Looking for you all over, this fickle-minded self is wallowing in this body.
purport:
In an earlier pāsuram, Āḻvār celebrated the boundless compassion of the Lord, who extends His grace even to those who are not inclined towards Him. If such is the Lord's nature, Āḻvār wonders why He has neither summoned him to Tirukkāñūr nor come personally to grant him His presence. The only explanation he can find is the burden of his own accumulated sins, which continue to obstruct the fulfilment of his longing.

Filled with this sense of helplessness, Āḻvār laments his condition. He finds himself unable either to endure the separation from the Lord or to cast aside the body that sustains that suffering. Thus, he remains caught in a state of anguish, yearning for union with the Lord while feeling constrained by the limitations imposed by karma.

The phrase *"Vaṅkaṭṭāl māmaṇi vandu uṇḍu"* is explained through a beautiful analogy. Precious gems are often brought by ships from the depths of the ocean and deposited upon the shore. In the same way, the Lord, who eternally resides in Paramapada, has graciously descended and established Himself on the seashore at Māmallapuram for the delight and benefit of His devotees. Just as a rare jewel becomes accessible when brought from distant waters to the shore, the Lord has made Himself easily accessible to those who seek Him.

Through this imagery, Āḻvār highlights the Lord's extraordinary simplicity and accessibility. Though He is the Supreme Being who transcends all worlds, He willingly leaves His exalted abode and manifests among devotees so that they may approach Him without difficulty. Yet, despite such accessibility, Āḻvār feels unable to attain Him and therefore attributes the delay solely to his own shortcomings. This pāsuram thus becomes a moving expression of humility, longing, and the pain of separation experienced by a devotee who sees the Lord's nearness everywhere but feels himself unworthy of receiving His grace.
archavathara: Śrīnivāsa,Appakkudathān Perumāḷ,Varadarāja Perumāḷ,Pavala Vaṇṇar Perumāḷ,Sthala Śayana Perumāḷ,Vyūha Vāsudeva

meaning: You are in the south (at Tirumalirumcōlai) eulogized by the worlds. You are in the north (at Tirumalai). You are in the west (at Śrīraṅgam). You are in the east (at Kaṇṇapuram) like an elephant in rut. You are always in the forefront of the Nityasūris. You are at Tirumōlikkalam with effulgence for veneration by subsequent generations of devotees. You are the primordial Lord. My cherished Lord! Lord with the glory of protecting the seven worlds! What does this insignificant devotee, bereft of any means, know apart from saying "My Elephant! My Elephant!"
purport:
In the fourth pāsuram, Āḻvār had declared, *"Mantirattai mantirattai maṟavādu eṉṟum vāḻttiyēl vāḻalām"*—that one can truly thrive by constantly glorifying the Protector through the Tirumantram without interruption. Reflecting upon this, Āḻvār wonders whether the Lord had refrained from appearing before him because He might have mistaken this constant recitation for an act of personal sādhanā undertaken to attain Him. However, Āḻvār clarifies that this was never his intention. His purpose was merely to remind himself of the true nature of the soul, to remain absorbed in thoughts of the Lord, and to spend his time in a meaningful and beneficial manner while awaiting divine grace.

In this pāsuram, Āḻvār expresses both his own utter helplessness and the Lord's incomparable greatness. He emphasizes that attainment of the Lord is not the result of individual effort but solely of the Lord's compassion and initiative. To illustrate this truth, Āḻvār compares the Lord to a majestic elephant.

An elephant cannot be ignored because of its immense size and commanding presence. Yet, despite its strength, it can be controlled only when it willingly cooperates. A rider cannot mount an elephant through his own effort alone; the elephant itself must kneel down and make it possible. Likewise, if it so chooses, the elephant can lift a person with its trunk and place him upon its back. Through this analogy, Āḻvār conveys that the jīvātmā cannot attain Bhagavān merely through personal endeavour. The Lord Himself must graciously make Himself accessible and elevate the devotee through His own will.

Āḻvār further compares the Lord to the mighty Diggajas, the celestial elephants that are traditionally said to uphold and protect the directions of the universe. In a similar manner, the Lord stands protecting and sustaining the world through His presence in the great sacred abodes of Vēṅkaṭam, Kāṇṇapuram, Tirumalirumcōlai, and Śrīraṅgam. From these holy places, He extends His grace to all who seek Him.

Thus, although the Lord is immeasurably exalted, He remains within easy reach of His devotees. By contemplating His presence in these sacred kṣetras, Āḻvār finds solace in the assurance that the Lord who sustains the universe is also the compassionate Master who graciously makes Himself accessible to those who depend entirely upon Him.

meaning: She wears choice silk sari (to attract Him). She feels faint and sobs. She has no desire for the dolls. With her cool and drawn-out eyes filled with tears, she does not lie down. She does not stay on my lap even for a moment. She murmurs, "Where is my Lord of Tiruvāraṅgam?" When I asked the (female) soothsayer, "Tell me truly who did this to my young doe with locks of hair humming with lovely bees spitting the honey sucked by them?", she said, "The Lord of sea-hue did this. My life-companions! Who else is there to protect her (if He does not)!"
purport:
The ten pāsurams beginning with this one are spoken through the voice of the mother of a heroine who suffers the anguish of separation from her beloved after having experienced union with him. At this stage, Āḻvār has attained complete spiritual maturity. His mind is fixed exclusively upon the Lord and upon nothing else, embodying the principle of *Ananyā Śeṣatva*, the state of belonging solely to Bhagavān. This exclusive devotion is traditionally expressed through the mood of a chaste heroine whose thoughts are entirely absorbed in her beloved.

When femininity is attributed to Āḻvār in such passages, it does not refer in any way to physical characteristics. Rather, it signifies a particular spiritual disposition and emotional attitude towards the Lord. The soul, recognizing its complete dependence upon Bhagavān, assumes the role of the heroine, while the Lord is understood as the sole beloved and protector. Such imagery serves as a powerful means of expressing the intensity of divine love experienced by the devotee.

The love experienced by Āḻvār has now become so overwhelming that it leaves no room for self-control or ordinary worldly awareness. Because of the depth of this experience, the condition of Āḻvār is portrayed through the observations of a mature and concerned mother. This literary device allows the inner state of the devotee to be described from an external perspective while preserving the emotional richness of the experience.

In this pāsuram, the mother describes the condition of her daughter, the heroine, whose suffering has become evident to all around her. Seeking to discover the cause of this mysterious affliction, she approaches a godly inclined soothsayer and asks for an explanation. Upon learning that the heroine's condition arises not from any worldly cause but from her intense love for Bhagavān, the mother turns to the maidens gathered around her and reflects upon the situation.

She realizes that the Lord alone is the true protector and refuge of all souls. If the very One who exists to safeguard His devotees does not come to the aid of this love-stricken heroine, then who else could possibly offer her protection? Thus, the pāsuram becomes a poignant expression of absolute dependence upon Bhagavān, emphasizing that the soul has no refuge apart from Him and that relief from the anguish of separation can come only through His grace.

meaning: With her heart melting and eyes shedding tears, she stands languished. She sighs deeply. She has not known food or sleep. She says, "The perfectly lovely Lord sleeping on the poison-emitting Ādiśeṣa!" She says, "The youthful Lord at Tiruvāli with fields full of lovely fragrant flowers!" Again, bringing to mind the flying banner with Garuḍa of lovely feathers, she says, "Friends, shall we go to lovely Tiruvāraṅgam?" O! My sins! Having got a girl who is not under my control, I got censured by the people of this sprawling world.
purport:
In the previous pāsuram, the heroine had become so overwhelmed by her love for the Lord that she lost awareness of herself and her surroundings. However, when the soothsayer uttered the words "the sea-hued Lord," she regained a measure of consciousness and immediately burst into lamentation, as described in this pāsuram. The mention of the Lord was enough to awaken her from her state of inward absorption and intensify the pain of separation that already consumed her heart.

When the matronly woman complains that she stands censured by the people, she is not criticizing the heroine's conduct. Rather, she laments her own inability to find a remedy for the heroine's condition. Observers naturally expect a mother to comfort and restore her daughter, but finding herself powerless before an affliction born of divine love, she becomes the object of criticism and concern. Her grief arises not from embarrassment, but from helplessness.

This pāsuram explores more deeply the experience of *viraha*, the anguish of separation in devotional love. The heroine's suffering symbolizes the longing of the individual soul for union with Bhagavān. Having once tasted the sweetness of His presence, the soul finds separation unbearable and becomes incapable of taking delight in anything else. The intensity of this longing is presented not as a weakness, but as the natural consequence of profound devotion.

The reference to the "sea-hued Lord" evokes the image of Lord Viṣṇu, whose divine complexion is traditionally compared to the deep blue of the ocean. The very mention of this description stirs the heroine's heart, illustrating how even the slightest reminder of the Lord can awaken powerful emotions in a true devotee. For one whose mind is wholly absorbed in Bhagavān, a single word, image, or memory is sufficient to rekindle both joy and sorrow.

The pāsuram also beautifully illustrates *mādhurya bhāva*, the devotional mood in which the soul relates to the Lord as a beloved. In this mode of devotion, the intensity, exclusiveness, and purity associated with human love are employed to express the soul's longing for the Divine. Through the voice of the heroine, Āḻvār conveys the depth of his own devotion, portraying a love so complete that separation from the Lord becomes the soul's greatest suffering and remembrance of Him its only solace.

meaning: With tear drops trickling down her twin breasts, and feeling weary, she asks her parrot to repeat by prompting it, such as, "Lord who protected from hailstorm by lifting the hill!" "Lord Uraga at lovely and highly desired Kāñcī!" "Lord who embraced the tender arms (of Sītā) by breaking the bow!" "The Master who is reposing in Vēṅka!" "The Lord who vanquished the wrestlers at one time and made them powerless!" and, "My youthful Lord with palms that split open (the mouth) of the horse Keśī."
purport:
The mother observed that the repeated chanting of the Lord's names had a soothing effect on the heroine's distressed condition. Hoping to bring her further comfort, she brought the heroine's pet parrot and placed it beside her, expecting it to repeat the divine names as it had been taught. However, the parrot remained silent. Traditional commentators explain this silence through the analogy of a disciple who, even after receiving instruction from an Ācārya, does not display his learning independently in the presence of the teacher. Out of humility and reverence, the disciple speaks only when prompted.

Accordingly, the parrot waited in silence until the heroine herself addressed it. Once encouraged by its mistress, it began to repeat the sacred names of the Lord, thereby offering comfort to the very one who had taught it. The scene beautifully illustrates the reciprocal nature of devotion, where even a simple creature becomes an instrument of divine remembrance and consolation.

A distinctive feature of Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār's devotional experience is his profound fulfillment in the Arcāvatāra. While the other Āḻvārs frequently celebrate the Lord's transcendence in Paramapada, His accessibility through various avatāras, and His presence in Arcā forms, Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār displays a particularly intense attachment to the Arcā manifestations found in the Divya Deśams. For him, the Lord enshrined in the temple is not different from the Lord who appeared in the great avatāras described in the scriptures.

In this pāsuram, Āḻvār emphasizes the essential oneness of the Lord in both Arcā and Avatāra. While standing before the Arcā form, he recalls the deeds performed during Kṛṣṇa's earthly incarnation and addresses the Lord directly as the very same Kṛṣṇa who protected His devotees. Thus, there is no distinction between the deity worshipped in the temple and the Lord who enacted divine sports in ages past.

Āḻvār specifically recalls the Govardhana episode through the words, "You warded off the hailstones by lifting a stone aloft." Here, Govardhana Hill is deliberately referred to as merely a stone in order to highlight the effortless nature of Kṛṣṇa's act. What appears to the world as a mighty mountain is, from the perspective of the omnipotent Lord, no more difficult to lift than a small stone.

The episode also reveals the wondrous and inscrutable ways of Bhagavān. When torrential rains and hailstones threatened the inhabitants of Gokula, the Lord chose to protect them by using another stone, Govardhana itself, as their shelter. In this sense, He countered stone with stone, much as one might speak of fighting fire with fire. Through this delightful recollection, Āḻvār celebrates both the Lord's infinite power and His affectionate concern for those who seek refuge in Him.

vegkāvil tirumālai ppāḍa kkēṭṭu
vaḻarttadanāl payan peṭrēn varuga ! enṟu
maḍa kkiḻiyai kkai kūppi vaṇaṅgināḻē
meaning: After listening to the sonorous names of the Lord of Śrī at Tiruttaṅkal and Tiruvēṅka, effulgent like the rising Sun, the cloud-hued Lord at Kuruṅkuḍi, who is supreme and beyond the three types of souls (baddha, mukta and nitya) in the three worlds, the insatiable Nectar beyond scrutiny, the immaculate Lord at Śrīraṅgam, the Lord in the hearts of pure souls, the Lord who dispels ignorance like the darkness from the light of the lamp and who is pleasingly lustrous like emerald, by the obedient parrot, she folded her hands and prostrated, saying "Welcome; I am profited by bringing you up."
purport:
As explained in the previous pāsuram, the parrot began reciting the names of the Lord after being prompted by the heroine. Hearing those sacred names emerge from the bird she had lovingly nurtured and instructed, the heroine experiences immense joy. She feels that her efforts in raising and teaching the parrot have finally borne fruit, for it has now become an instrument for glorifying Bhagavān.

The phrase *"kaikkūppi vaṇaṅgināḷē"* indicates that the heroine folded her hands in reverence and saluted the parrot. At first glance, this may appear surprising. Why should the heroine offer such respect to a mere parrot, especially one that may be regarded as her own disciple? The commentators explain that the significance lies not in the bird itself, but in what it is doing. By reciting the divine names of the Lord, the parrot assumes the role of a Bhāgavata, one who glorifies Bhagavān, and thereby becomes worthy of veneration.

The deeper teaching conveyed through this episode is that all Bhāgavatas who recite and celebrate the names of the Lord deserve reverence, irrespective of their age, social position, learning, or status. The greatness of a devotee is measured not by worldly qualifications but by devotion to Bhagavān and engagement in His remembrance.

Traditional history provides many examples illustrating this principle. One such incident concerns Mahāpūrṇar, the revered Ācārya of Rāmānuja. On one occasion, Mahāpūrṇar prostrated before a group of Śrīvaiṣṇavas who were returning from their ablutions in the Kāveri under the leadership of his own disciple, Rāmānuja. Although Rāmānuja was his disciple, Mahāpūrṇar saw in that assembly not merely individuals, but devotees of the Lord who were adorned with devotion and service. Therefore, he offered them his respects without hesitation.

In the same spirit, the heroine bows before the parrot. Her reverence is directed not towards the bird as an individual creature, but towards the sacred act of chanting the Lord's names. Through this beautiful episode, Āḻvār teaches that anyone who becomes a vehicle for the glorification of Bhagavān deserves honour and respect. The pāsuram thus highlights the exalted position of the Bhāgavata and the humility with which true devotees regard those who engage in the remembrance and praise of the Lord.

meaning: With the sonorous and resonant vīṇā resting on her breasts, with a smile showing out the teeth just a little and with the soft fingers becoming red due to plucking (at the vīṇā strings), my daughter prattled variously like the parrot as, "My Elephant in rut at Pādakam in Kāñcī surrounded by tall and extensive stone fortifications!" "My Lord sweet like ripe fruit reposing in Milk-ocean!" and "My Lord standing with relish at lovely Aḷundūr bounded by wet fields and tanks where blossom lovely water lily flowers!"
purport:
With the parrot continuing to recite the names of the Lord in response to her prompts, as described in the previous pāsuram, the heroine gradually enters a state of joyful absorption. The divine names soothe her heart and transport her into a world entirely centred upon the Lord. Though outwardly separated from Him, her mind becomes so immersed in His remembrance that she begins to experience His presence everywhere around her.

In this state of ecstatic devotion, the heroine beholds the Lord in objects that would ordinarily appear mundane. Her love has reached such intensity that the distinction between remembrance and direct experience begins to fade. The longing born of separation transforms itself into an inward vision of union.

Thus, she takes up her Vīṇā and imagines it to be the Lord Himself. Embracing it closely to her bosom, she addresses it as though she were speaking directly to her beloved. What appears externally as an inanimate musical instrument becomes, in her devotional perception, a living manifestation of the Lord's presence. Through this act, she seeks solace from the anguish of separation and experiences a momentary sense of union with Him.

This episode beautifully illustrates the transformative power of divine love. For a devotee whose heart is wholly occupied by Bhagavān, every object becomes a reminder of Him, and every experience becomes an opportunity for communion with Him. The heroine's embrace of the Vīṇā is therefore not an act of imagination alone, but an expression of the depth of her absorption in the Lord.

meaning: With teardrops trickling down her twin breasts, she laments saying, "The young Bull who felt greatly elated grazing the calves!" "My ripe fruit in Kaṇṇapuram surrounded by fragrant orchards!" "Kṛṣṇa who was pleased to dance to the assembled people!" "The chief at northern Tiruvēṅkaṭam!" "The Hero who destroyed the chief (Rāvaṇa) of Khara, Dūṣaṇa etc. whom you defeated!" "Lord who is standing at Tirunaraiyūr surrounded by flower gardens!" and "My dark-bodied life companion with dense hair!"
purport:
The joy experienced by the heroine in the previous pāsuram proves to be fleeting. The union with the Lord that she seemed to enjoy was not a physical reality but an experience born of intense longing, akin to a dream. For a brief moment, she felt as though she had attained the presence of her beloved, but when that experience faded and she became aware of her continued separation, her sorrow returned with even greater force.

Realizing that the happiness she experienced was only momentary, the heroine cries out loudly to the Lord. In her anguish, she dwells especially upon His role as the protector and refuge of those who depend upon Him. Having no one else to turn to, she appeals directly to Him, expecting the compassion and protection that are intrinsic to His nature.

The commentators compare her condition to that of Sītā in Aśokavana. When Hanumān delivered Rāma's Cūḍāmaṇi to her, she experienced immense joy. The jewel was not merely an ornament; it was a tangible reminder of Rāma's love and concern. Seeing it, Sītā felt as though she had come into direct contact with Rāma Himself. Overwhelmed with emotion, she first placed the jewel upon her head in reverence and then held it close to her bosom, as though seeking relief from the burning fever of separation.

Yet that joy, too, was temporary. Once the initial elation subsided and she became conscious of her continued separation from Rāma, her grief resurfaced. Unable to contain her anguish, she cried aloud, "O Rāma! O Lakṣmaṇa! O Sumitrā!" Her lament expressed both the depth of her love and the unbearable pain of separation.

The heroine's condition in this pāsuram closely mirrors that experience. The brief sense of union that had comforted her only serves to intensify her sorrow when it vanishes. The memory of the Lord's presence makes His absence feel even more painful. Therefore, she calls out to Him with renewed urgency, emphasizing His protective nature and seeking refuge in the One who alone has the power to relieve her suffering. Through this portrayal, Āḻvār vividly expresses the alternating states of joy and anguish that characterize the highest forms of devotional love, where even a fleeting remembrance of the Lord can both console and torment the devotee.
