meaning: Her breasts, soft and juvenile and fully developed are paling with tears gushing from her eyes like two fishes fighting. She goes out and stares. Her heart melts hearing the subdued tone by which the red-footed youthful pigeon talks to its mate and she then recalls to her mind (her previous conversation when she was in union with the Lord). Hearing her speaking endearingly of Tiruttaṅkal and cool Tirukkuḍandai and lovingly singing to Kōvalūr, when I asked her "My girl full of feminine charm! Is this (your demonstrative behavior) befitting our family?", she started singing of Naraiyūr too!
purport:
Witnessing the heroine's intense distress in the previous pāsurams, the mother had attempted various means to console her. She brought the Vīṇā and the pet parrot, hoping that these familiar companions would soothe her sorrow and provide some relief from the pain of separation. For a brief period, they appeared to offer comfort. The parrot recited the Lord's names, and the Vīṇā became an object through which the heroine expressed her devotion and longing.

However, the mother soon realized that these remedies were producing the opposite effect. Rather than alleviating the heroine's suffering, they only deepened her absorption in the Lord and intensified her yearning for Him. Every sound from the parrot and every association evoked by the Vīṇā served only to remind her of the beloved from whom she remained separated. Concluding that these objects were aggravating her condition, the mother removed them from her daughter's presence.

Believing that practical and matronly counsel might succeed where other efforts had failed, the mother attempted to reason with the heroine. She advised her that such public displays of emotion were unbecoming of her dignity and inconsistent with the honourable traditions of their family. As a concerned elder, she hoped that an appeal to propriety and social decorum would restore some measure of self-control.

The heroine, however, is no longer governed by ordinary considerations. Her heart is wholly possessed by love for the Lord, and worldly conventions hold little meaning for her. Rather than accepting her mother's advice, she responds with defiance. Unwilling to suppress her emotions for the sake of social expectations, she leaves the house and openly expresses her longing for the Lord.

Indeed, she cries out even more loudly than before, as though deliberately provoking her mother. Yet this apparent defiance is not born of disrespect. It arises from the overwhelming force of divine love, which has surpassed all concern for reputation, custom, or public opinion. For one whose mind is entirely fixed upon Bhagavān, the demands of the world become insignificant when compared to the pain of separation from Him.

Through this episode, Āḻvār portrays the irresistible nature of supreme devotion. The heroine's love has reached such intensity that neither external restraints nor well-meaning advice can contain it. Her only concern is the Lord, and her cries become the spontaneous expression of a soul that can no longer conceal its longing for union with its eternal beloved.

kār vaṇṇam tirumēni kaṇṇum vāyum
kaittalamum aḍi iṇaiyum kamala vaṇṇam
pār vaṇṇa maḍa maṅgai pattar pittar
pani malar mēl pāvaikku ppāvam śeydēn
ēr vaṇṇa en pēdai en śol kēḻāḻ
em perumān tiruvaraṅgam eṅgē ennum
nīr vaṇṇan nīr malaikkē pōvēn ennum
iduvanṟō niṟai azindār niṟkumāṟē
meaning: The sacred body of the Lord is of the colour of clouds. His eyes, lips, palms and two feet are of the colour of lotuses. He is devoted to the ever-youthful Dame Earth, who shines in the worlds. He is infatuated by the Dame (Lakṣmī) on the cool lotus. I committed a sin (towards such a Lord). My daughter of lovely complexion does not heed my words. She says, "Which way is the Lord's Śrīraṅgam?" Again, she says, "I will go to Tirunīrmalai of Lord Nīrvaṇṇan (the name of the Lord there)." Is this not the fate of those who disregard their feminine dignity?
purport:
In the previous pāsuram, the mother attempted to counsel the heroine, telling her that such conduct was not in keeping with the traditions and dignity of their family. However, the heroine remains unmoved by these arguments. Far from moderating her behaviour, she becomes even more determined in her pursuit of the Lord. In this pāsuram, her longing intensifies to the point that she resolves to go personally to Śrīraṅgam and Tirunīrmalai in search of Him.

Observing this, the mother begins to regret her earlier advice. She realizes that she had committed a grave mistake by attempting to restrain a devotion that was directed towards the highest possible goal. What she had viewed as excessive behaviour now appears to her as the natural expression of an exalted spiritual state. Instead of correcting her daughter, she now understands that the fault lay in her own inability to appreciate the greatness of that devotion.

As explained in the introduction to *Periya Tirumoḻi*, the Lord revealed the essential nature of the soul, namely its eternal subservience to Him, simply through the manifestation of His incomparable beauty. Without elaborate instruction, the splendour of His divine form itself awakened in Āḻvār the realization of his true nature and purpose. In the present pāsuram, the Lord once again displays that same beauty, reminding Āḻvār of his ultimate goal (*puruṣārtha*), which is to attain His divine feet and render eternal service there.

The service envisioned by Āḻvār is not motivated by personal gain or self-interest. Rather, it is identical to the service rendered by the Lord's own divine consorts, Śrī and Bhū Devī. It is selfless, loving, and entirely centred upon the Lord's pleasure. Realizing that her daughter aspires to such a lofty ideal, the mother ceases to be embarrassed by her behaviour and instead becomes proud of her devotion.

The scriptures speak of various human goals (*puruṣārthas*), including prosperity, righteous living (*dharma*), social order, and the preservation of personal and familial honour. These are all valid pursuits within worldly life and have their own place in the scriptural scheme. The mother's earlier advice was rooted in concern for such lower-order goals, particularly family reputation and feminine dignity.

Yet the heroine has transcended these concerns. Her aspiration is directed solely towards the highest *puruṣārtha*, namely eternal service to Bhagavān in His presence, culminating in the bliss of Mokṣa. In comparison with this supreme goal, all other attainments appear secondary. Recognizing this truth, the mother comes to appreciate the greatness of her daughter's devotion and the exalted destination towards which it is directed.

muṭrārā vana mulaiyāḻ pāvai
māyan moy agalattuḻ iruppāḻ agtum kaṇḍum aṭrāḻ

peṭrēn vāy ccol iṟaiyum pēśa kkēḻāḻ
pēr pāḍi ttaṇ kuḍandai nagarum pāḍi
poṭrāmarai kkayam nīrāḍa ppōnāḻ
poruvaṭrāḻ en magaḻ um ponnum agtē
meaning: Even after seeing the Dame (Lakṣmī), with lovely breasts yet not fully developed, on the lovely chest of the Wondrous Lord, she laments, loses her decorum and sighs deep. She says, "Friends, shall we go prancing to lovely Śrīraṅgam?" She, begotten of me, does not listen to words spoken by me in the least. Eulogizing Tiruppēr and the cool town of Tirukkuḍandai, she has gone to plunge herself in the lovely lotus pond (to be in union with the Lord). My daughter has severed my company. Is your daughter also like this?
purport:
In the previous pāsuram, the heroine became so overwhelmed by her longing for the Lord that she cast aside all concern for feminine dignity and openly asked for directions to His abode. Having reached a state where worldly conventions no longer restrained her, she was determined to seek Him regardless of social expectations or personal reputation.

Anticipating the questions of the women and companions around her, the mother explains her position. They may well ask whether she had not warned her daughter that the Lord, being inseparably united with Mahālakṣmī and absorbed in Her divine charms, would not pay attention to another maiden seeking His affection. The mother replies that she did indeed offer such advice and attempted to dissuade her daughter. However, despite all her efforts, the heroine remained resolute and proceeded towards the Lord without heeding those warnings.

The expression *"umpoṇṇum anṭē"* carries the sense, "Is your daughter also like this?" Through these words, the mother turns to the women around her and wonders whether their daughters too exhibit such overwhelming devotion and disregard for worldly considerations when it comes to the Lord. The statement is both an expression of astonishment and an acknowledgment of the extraordinary nature of the heroine's love.

A deeper theological significance is also present here. Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār exhibits an exceptionally intimate identification of the Arcāvatāra with the transcendent Lord Himself. For him, the deity residing in the temple is not merely a representation or accessible manifestation of the Supreme; it is the very same Lord of Paramapada, complete with all His divine qualities, majesty, and grace. Consequently, the heroine's longing for the Arcā form is no different from longing for the Supreme Lord Himself.

This intense identification distinguishes Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār's devotional experience. Therefore, the mother's question may also be understood in a broader sense. Looking at the companions around her, she wonders whether their daughters, representing the experiences of the other Āḻvārs, have likewise become so completely captivated by the Arcāvatāra that they perceive no distinction between the Lord enshrined in the temple and the transcendent Lord of Vaikuṇṭha.

Thus, the pāsuram highlights both the irresistible attraction of the Lord's Arcā form and the extraordinary depth of Āḻvār's devotion. The heroine's actions, though appearing unconventional from a worldly perspective, arise from a vision in which the Lord of the temple and the Lord of the highest abode are one and the same, worthy of complete surrender and unwavering pursuit.

purport:
After repeatedly offering advice that proved futile, the mother now undergoes a change of heart. She no longer views her daughter's conduct as excessive or inappropriate. Instead, she begins to recognize how extraordinarily fortunate the heroine is. The devotion that once appeared to her as a cause for concern is now understood to be a rare and exalted blessing. The heroine's heart is so completely absorbed in Bhagavān that she aspires not merely for His presence, but for the privilege of serving Him in the manner of His own divine consorts.

The mother realizes that such an aspiration is not born of ordinary desire but of the highest form of devotion. To seek the Lord with the same exclusiveness, intimacy, and selfless dedication displayed by Śrī and Bhū Devī is the mark of a soul that has fully awakened to its true nature. Far from being ashamed of her daughter, the mother now regards her with admiration and reverence.

At this stage, the heroine has effectively passed beyond the protective care of her earthly guardians. The mother understands that she can no longer provide what her daughter truly seeks. Neither family affection, social customs, nor worldly comforts can satisfy a heart that longs exclusively for Bhagavān. Having outgrown all lesser forms of dependence, the heroine now seeks refuge in the Lord alone.

english_scripts:
mai vaṇṇa naṟuṅguñji kkuzal pin tāza
magaram śēr kuzai iru pāḍilaṅgi āḍa
ey vaṇṇa veñjilaiyē tuṇaiyā
ṅgē iruvarāy vandār en munnē ninṟār
kai vaṇṇam tāmarai vāy kamalam pōlum
kaṇ iṇaiyum aravindam aḍiyum agtē 
av vaṇṇattavar nilaimai kaṇḍum tōzī !
 avarai nām tēvar enṟañjinōmē !
meaning: He came to this very place accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and he stood before me. My dear Friend! His curly hair, black like collyrium and exuding fragrance, was flowing down at the back in strands. The shark-crocodile shaped ear ornaments were dangling sparkingly on both his sides. He had with Him the fiery bow ready to shoot. Palms were of the hue of lotuses. The lips were like lotus buds. The two eyes were like lotuses. The feet were also like lotus flowers. Even after seeing the nature of such a charming person, we were frightened that He might be an inaccessible Ishwara!
purport:
Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār is utterly captivated by the svarūpa of Bhagavān, especially in the divine form of Śrī Rāmacandra. In this pāsuram, Āḻvār assumes the mood of Parakāla Nāyaki and narrates her experience to her companion. She describes how the divine brothers, Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, are approaching her. The curly locks of Rāma's hair sway gracefully as He walks, a sight capable of enchanting even the Gandharvas and Apsaras. His Makara-kuṇḍalas swing gently on either side of His face, as though proclaiming, "Behold! He is the Supreme Being. He is the Puruṣārtha, the ultimate goal of our lives." In His hands rests a radiant bow, blazing with power and ever ready to destroy the Asuras and Daityas who oppose righteousness.

His eyes are especially captivating. Soft and expansive like the petals of a freshly blossomed lotus, they possess the power to attract and overwhelm even the most composed observer with divine ecstasy. Āḻvār praises those lotus eyes, *Aravinda-nayana*, in the same manner as the Purāṇas glorify them. His lips are tender and beautiful, resembling newly blossomed lotus buds. The two youthful brothers radiate extraordinary beauty and divine splendour. Though they appear outwardly as human princes, their attire, bearing, and effulgence unmistakably reveal that they transcend the realm of ordinary creation. Their very presence proclaims that they are beyond anything fashioned by Brahmā. The lotus-like feet of Rāma, which constitute the supreme goal of human existence, further reveal His true nature.

As Parakāla Nāyaki contemplates these features, she gradually realizes that these are no ordinary men. The recognition dawns upon her that the Supreme Lord Himself, the Īśvara who governs all existence, is walking towards her. At that moment, Āḻvār is overcome with awe and wonder. For an instant, he is struck by the realization that this divine person, who remains inaccessible even to Brahmā and Rudra, has nevertheless chosen to reveal Himself directly to him.

The beauty of this pāsuram lies in the harmonious blending of two profound divine qualities: *Sauśīlyam* and *Saulabhyam*. Sauśīlyam is the Lord's supreme majesty, by which the Sovereign of all worlds remains ever exalted, while Saulabhyam is His extraordinary accessibility, by which He makes Himself available to His devotees. Āḻvār experiences both simultaneously in the person of Śrī Rāma. Throughout His earthly life, Rāma identified Himself simply as Dāśarathi, the son of Daśaratha. Yet He was far more than an ideal human prince; He was Īśvara Himself, concealed beneath the appearance of humanity. He displayed unparalleled accessibility to devotees such as Hanumān and Vibhīṣaṇa, while revealing His sovereign majesty through the destruction of Rāvaṇa and the restoration of dharma.

Āḻvār's genius lies in presenting these two qualities together. Just as milk and honey, when blended, produce a sweetness greater than either possesses individually, the simultaneous experience of Saulabhyam and Sauśīlyam creates a devotional rasa of incomparable beauty. By portraying the Lord as both the approachable companion of His devotees and the majestic ruler of the universe, Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār serves a feast of divine experience. Through this exquisite combination, he enables devotees to relish the fullness of Bhagavān's nature, making this pāsuram a remarkable celebration of both His intimacy and His transcendence.

naivaḻam onṟārāyā nammai nōkkā
nāṇinār pōl iṟaiyē nayaṅgaḻ pinnum
śeyvaḻavil en manamum kaṇṇum ōḍi
 em perumān tiruvaḍikkīz aṇaiy
 ippāl kaivaḻaiyum mēgalaiyum kāṇēn
 kaṇḍēn kana magara kkuzai iraṇḍum nāngu tōḻum
 evvaḻavuṇḍem perumān kōyil enṟēṟku
 idu anṟō ezil āli enṟār tāmē
meaning: He sang in the unique rāga "Naivalam" and also made a few (suggestive) gestures pretending shyness to see me in my face. By then, my mind and eyes went out to rest at the feet of the Lord (I lost control over them to Him). I could no longer see (be aware of) my bangles and waist-belt. I could only see His prominent ear-ornaments and the four arms. When I asked Him "How far is my Lord's residence?", He said, "Is this not the lovely Tiruvaḻi?"
purport:
Parakāla Nāyaki realizes that the Lord has not come before her to display His supremacy or divine majesty, but rather to claim His beloved, namely herself. As she beholds Him, she is reminded of Kṛṣṇāvatāra, when He captivated the hearts of the Gopīs through the enchanting music of His flute. Now, before her very eyes, He stands singing in the Naivaḻam rāga. The unique quality of this rāga is that it profoundly stirs the hearts of both the singer and the listener. Such music should have completely overwhelmed her and driven her into ecstatic longing for the Lord. Yet, remembering the words of caution spoken by her mother, she strives to maintain control over her thoughts and senses.

The Lord, however, does not cease His efforts. Though He is *Svatantran*, absolutely independent and subject to none, He begins to offer subtle hints of His affection. In His divine playfulness, He even appears bashful, turning His gaze towards the sky as though concealing the advances He is making towards her. Through these gentle gestures, the Lord gradually melts the resistance that Parakāla Nāyaki had attempted to maintain.

At last, her composure completely dissolves. The notions of "I" and "mine" vanish from her mind. Her individuality is overwhelmed by the force of divine love, and she becomes incapable of bearing separation from Him any longer. Having lost all attachment to herself and everything connected with her, she longs only for union with the Lord.

Unable to contain her yearning, she asks Him where He resides. Her question is not motivated merely by curiosity. She knows that wherever the Lord chooses to dwell becomes sanctified by the presence of His devotees, and therefore His abode itself becomes an object of longing. The place where He resides is naturally filled with Bhāgavatas, divine service, and the constant celebration of His glories.

As the Lord begins to enumerate His various abodes, extending even to the supreme realm of Paramapada, Parakāla Nāyaki listens with intense eagerness. Yet her heart is fixed upon one sacred place in particular. Therefore, interrupting His description, she asks anxiously, "Is Tiruvāli among them?" Her question reveals the depth of her attachment to that Divya Deśam, for to her, any place associated with the Lord becomes infinitely precious. More importantly, it reflects her desire to remain wherever He is present, whether in this world or beyond it.

Thus, the pāsuram beautifully portrays the gradual dissolution of the soul's individuality in the presence of Bhagavān. The Lord's sweetness, accessibility, and loving initiative draw Parakāla Nāyaki beyond all self-awareness until her sole concern becomes the place where He resides and the opportunity to remain forever in His presence.

uḻ ūrum śindai nōy enakkē tandu
en oḻi vaḻaiyum mā niṟamum koṇḍār iṅgē
teḻ ūrum iḻan teṅgin tēṟal māndi
śēl ugaḻum tiruvaraṅgam nam ūr enṟa
kaḻ ūrum pain tuzāy mālai yānai
 kanaviḍattil yān kāṇban kaṇḍa pōdu
puḻ ūrum kaḻvā nī pōgēl enban
enṟālum idu namakkōr pulavi tānē
meaning: He took away, right here, my bright bangles and lovely complexion, having given me exclusively a deep-rooted mental agony. I will see in my dream, the Lord with the garland of fresh tulasī dripping honey who said that His residence was Śrīraṅgam- where fishes are intoxicated by the toddy from tender coconuts with clear water. At that time, I will tell Him, "You deceitful Lord riding Garuḍa! Do not go away from me." Even then, indeed! this (existence in this world) is a distressing feature to us.
purport:
Continuing from the previous pāsuram, the Lord, seated upon Vinateya (Garuḍa), prepares to depart, assuring Parakāla Nāyaki that they will meet again at Śrīraṅgam. Yet, alas, Parakāla Nāyaki is unable to bear even a moment of separation from Bhagavān. He had come before her, captivated her heart, claimed her mind, and now was departing. Having once experienced His presence, she finds it impossible to remain apart from Him. Such is the condition of a true Prapanna. Bhagavān is everything to those who have surrendered unto Him. He is their refuge, their protector, their wealth, their goal, and their very life.

Overwhelmed by the pain of separation, Parakāla Nāyaki longs to call out to Him and plead with Him not to depart upon Garuḍa. She wishes to beg Him to remain with her, unable to endure the thought of His leaving. Yet, at that very moment, a profound realization dawns upon her.

She recognizes the harsh reality of existence within saṁsāra. The bound souls (*baddhātmās*) remain trapped within the endless cycle of birth and death because of their accumulated karma. This karma acts like a dense cloud, obscuring the vision of the Supreme Lord and preventing the soul from constantly experiencing His presence. Even when Bhagavān reveals Himself through His grace, the limitations imposed by embodied existence continue to subject the soul to periods of separation and longing.

Parakāla Nāyaki therefore understands that, so long as one remains within saṁsāra, the pain of separation cannot be entirely avoided. Until the soul is liberated from the bondage of karma and attains Paramapada, it must endure the alternating experiences of union and separation. The devotee is left with no choice but to bear this suffering while continuing to depend upon the Lord's grace.

Reflecting upon this truth, she arrives at a deeper appreciation of the fortune enjoyed by the Nityasūris. Unlike the bound souls of this world, the Nityasūris dwell eternally in the presence of Nārāyaṇa. They never experience separation, forgetfulness, or obstruction caused by karma. Their service to the Lord is uninterrupted, their vision of Him is constant, and their bliss is everlasting.

Thus, the pāsuram concludes with a poignant contrast between the condition of the bound soul and that of the liberated and eternal servants of the Lord. Parakāla Nāyaki's sorrow arises from the realization that she must still endure the limitations of saṁsāra, while her aspiration remains fixed upon the state of the Nityasūris, who forever enjoy the unbroken company of Nārāyaṇa and render eternal service at His divine feet.

ilaṅgoli nīr perum pauvam maṇḍi uṇḍa
peru vayiṭra karu mugilē oppar vaṇṇam

en poru kayaṟ kaṇ nīr arumba ppulavi tandu
punal araṅgam ūr enṟu pōyinārē !
meaning: The Lord with huge mouth which swallowed the worlds (in pralaya) came right here, made me distressed shedding tears from my eyes which are like two fishes fighting, and went away saying that His place is water-rich Śrīraṅgam. He was like dark cloud (with lightning and thunder) richly laden with water sucked up to the grains of sand beneath from the mighty sea. He had the Conch in one hand and the Discus in the other hand and was surrounded by Nityasūris, and servents. Alas! My sins! Now my bangles do not stay in place in my two hands!
purport:
Āḻvār continues to express the agony of separation in this pāsuram. As Bhagavān prepares to depart, Āḻvār is unable to withstand the pain of being separated from Him. Overwhelmed by grief, Parakāla Nāyaki begins to shed tears incessantly. The very sight of the Lord's divine form, capable of enchanting all beings, only deepens the intensity of her longing. The more she beholds His beauty, the more unbearable His departure becomes.

Āḻvār describes the Lord as resembling a dark rain-bearing cloud appearing in the night sky. Upon that dark form shines a brilliant radiance, just as lightning illuminates a cloud. This description closely echoes the imagery of the Nārāyaṇa Sūktam: *"nī̠latō̍yada̍madhya̠sthā̠dvi̠dyullē̍khēva̠ bhāsva̍rā"*. The Lord possesses the deep hue of a dark cloud, often described as *Kṛṣṇa-piṅgalam*, while the golden splendour that shines upon Him is identified with Mahālakṣmī, who eternally resides upon His chest and is never separated from Him. Thus, the divine form manifests both majesty and tenderness through the inseparable presence of the Divine Couple.

The Lord's hands are adorned with the great Pāñcajanya conch and the Sudarśana Cakra. Yet, in Āḻvār's vision, these are not merely weapons intended for the destruction of evil. They appear as beautiful ornaments enhancing the splendour of His divine form. Everything associated with Him becomes an object of beauty and delight to the devotee. Around Him stand the Ṛṣis, Nityasūris, and Muktātmas, all engaged in His service and glorification.

Āḻvār beholds an extraordinary scene. The dark cloud-hued Lord is seated upon Garuḍa, surrounded by the eternal servants of Paramapada. The vision recalls the declaration of the Viṣṇu Sūkta: *"tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padaṃ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ"*—the enlightened ones eternally behold the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. The Lord is praised on all sides by the Nityasūris, whose eyes never tire of beholding Him and whose service never ceases. Witnessing such a vision, Āḻvār loses all awareness of himself. His heart becomes completely absorbed in Bhagavān, and his devotion rises to an even greater intensity.

Yet, with that intensification of devotion comes an equally intense experience of separation. The closer the devotee comes to Bhagavān, the more painful even a moment of separation becomes. Thus, the very vision that fills Āḻvār with ecstasy also becomes the source of profound anguish when the Lord prepares to depart.

The Lord who once swallowed the entire universe during Mahāpralaya, holding all existence within Himself, now turns to Āḻvār and declares that His abode is Śrīraṅgam. Having revealed His beauty, majesty, and accessibility, He then ascends upon Garuḍa and departs. Left behind, Āḻvār is consumed by longing. The Lord's departure transforms the joy of divine vision into the pain of separation, making this pāsuram a powerful expression of the paradox of supreme bhakti, where the experience of the Lord simultaneously grants the highest bliss and the deepest yearning.

min ilaṅgu tiru uruvum periya tōḻum
kari muninda kaittalamum kaṇṇum vāyum
tan alarnda naṟun tuzāy malarin kīzē
tāzndilaṅgum magaram śēr kuzaiyum kāṭṭi

en vaḻaiyum koṇḍennai āḻum koṇḍu
pon alarnda naṟuñjerundi ppozilin ūḍē
punal araṅgam ūr enṟu pōyinārē !
meaning: Displaying His sacred form sparkling like lightning, His broad arms, palms which subdued the elephant (Kuvalayāpīḍa), eyes, lips and matching ear-ornaments hanging low and sparkling below the garland of tulasī exuding fragrance of its own, He not only took away my character, my femininity, my mind and my bangles, but also made me His vassal and went away saying that His residence was Śrīraṅgam with copious water and groves exuding fragrance from the blossoming golden-coloured ceruṇḍi flowers.
purport:
As Bhagavān continues to depart, Parākāla Nāyaki repeatedly expresses the anguish of separation. The vision of the Lord remains vividly before her eyes, making His absence even more unbearable. He had descended before her, revealing Himself in all His splendour, with an effulgence shining like a flash of lightning. Having once beheld such beauty, she finds herself unable to endure the thought of being separated from Him.

She recalls His broad shoulders and powerful arms, the very arms with which He subdued the mighty elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa during His Kṛṣṇāvatāra. Yet, alongside this display of strength, she remembers the extraordinary tenderness of His form. His eyes and lips are soft and delicate like freshly blossomed lotus petals, capable of melting even the hardest of hearts. His Makara-kuṇḍalas sway gracefully as He moves, adding to the charm of His appearance. The divine fragrance emanating from His person mingles with the sweet scent of the tulasī garland adorning Him, enchanting all who come near. Faced with such an irresistibly beautiful form, Parākāla Nāyaki wonders how anyone could possibly remain apart from Him.

Overcome with emotion, she questions the Lord Himself. Why should He move away from her when He was the very one who had stolen her heart? He had come to her uninvited, captivated her mind, and drawn all her thoughts towards Himself. Having awakened such love within her, how could He now depart and leave her behind?

Āḻvār illustrates this sentiment through a striking analogy. It is as though a clever robber enters a house, distracts the children with attractive toys, gathers all the valuables, and then even persuades the householder himself to carry away the stolen goods. In the same manner, the Lord entered her heart, captivated her through His beauty and grace, took possession of her mind, thoughts, and affections, and then departed, leaving her utterly helpless.

Yet, as her emotions settle, Parākāla Nāyaki arrives at a deeper realization. After all, she belongs exclusively to Bhagavān. The soul is His possession by its very nature. If He chooses to claim her mind, her heart, and her very self, He is merely taking what already belongs to Him. Therefore, she cannot truly accuse Him of theft, for the owner cannot steal his own property. Recognizing this truth, her complaint gradually transforms into loving acceptance.

Remembering His final words, she takes comfort in the promise He had given her. He had assured her that they would meet again at the sacred island embraced by the waters of the Kāveri, namely Śrīraṅgam. Thus, even amidst the pain of separation, Parākāla Nāyaki finds a measure of solace in the hope of reunion. Her thoughts turn towards Śrīraṅgam, where the Lord awaits, and where the anguish of separation will ultimately be resolved through the joy of His presence.

nī maruvi añjādē ninṟōr mādu
nin nayan tāḻ enṟiṟaiyē iyambi kkāṇē
meaning: Six-footed little bee staying happily on the flower, supremely contented, along with your female companion putting into each other's mouth the honey at the time of blossoming in the honey-rich flower garden! I prostrate to you. Go right today to the Lord (Amaruviyappan) staying at lovely Aḷundūr, the Lord of the Nityasūris and the Lord who mixed with the cows and grazed them, and see that you speak a word that a certain dame is desiring Him.
purport:
The heroine had experienced immense joy during her union with the Lord. After He departed, the companions who had been guarding the entrance approached her and eagerly questioned her about the encounter. They wished to know how the Lord appeared and what He had spoken to her. The heroine answered these questions in the earlier pāsurams, describing His incomparable beauty, divine splendour, and the words He had spoken. She then explained that Garuḍa, eager to serve his Master, hastened the Lord's departure and carried Him away before she could fully enjoy His presence.

When the companions asked why she had not requested Him to remain with her, the heroine explained that He was surrounded on all sides by the Nityasūris. In the midst of that glorious assembly, she found no opportunity to speak freely to Him. Later, she described how the Lord overwhelmed her by revealing His majestic splendour, captivated her completely, took possession of her heart, and reduced her to His willing servant. Having recounted all these events, neither the companions nor the heroine have anything further to discuss. The exhilaration of union gives way to the heaviness of separation, and a profound sense of despondency settles upon her.

Reflecting upon the earlier conversation, the heroine arrives at a new resolution. Since she can no longer speak to the Lord directly, she decides to send an emissary to convey her message of longing. Yet the question immediately arises: whom should she choose for such a delicate mission? The scriptures provide examples that caution against relying merely upon intelligence or eloquence. Kṛṣṇa Himself went as a messenger to the court of Duryodhana, yet His mission did not avert the great war. By contrast, Hanumān, though only a monkey in outward appearance, successfully fulfilled his mission and brought hope to Sītā in her distress. Thus, success in divine service depends not merely upon ability but upon fitness for the task and the Lord's grace.

As she contemplates this, her attention falls upon a bee happily sporting with its mate among the flowers of the garden. Seeing it immersed in delight, she chooses it as her messenger. She praises the bee and entreats it to carry her message to the Lord. In the traditional interpretation, the bee assumes the role of an Ācārya, whose sacred function is to unite the soul with Bhagavān. Just as the Ācārya carries the yearning soul towards its divine destination, the bee is asked to serve as the intermediary between the heroine and her beloved Lord.

Addressing it as the "six-footed one," the heroine employs a term that is rich in symbolic meaning. While bees naturally possess six legs, the commentators discern a deeper significance. Śrī Parāśara Bhaṭṭar beautifully explains that the three pairs of feet symbolize the feet of the Ācārya, his wife, and his son, all of whom deserve reverence. Once the bee successfully accomplishes its mission, the heroine imagines placing those sacred feet upon her head and rejoicing in gratitude.

A further question arises. The Lord had already told the heroine that His abode was at Śrīraṅgam. Why then does she ask the bee to seek Him at Aḻundūr? The commentators offer a charming explanation. The heroine assumes that the Lord would have reached Śrīraṅgam, but upon arriving there, He would have found even that glorious abode devoid of joy without the presence of a true devotee such as herself. Unable to bear the separation any more than she can, He would already have begun His journey back towards her. Thus, she directs the bee to Aḻundūr, presuming that the Lord will be found there on His return.

The pāsuram therefore beautifully combines the themes of separation, longing, and the indispensable role of the Ācārya. Even amidst the sorrow of separation, the heroine remains sustained by hope, convinced that the Lord who captured her heart cannot remain content without reclaiming her and that the messenger she sends will ultimately bring about their reunion.

śeṅgāla maḍa nārāy ! inṟē śenṟu
tiru kkaṇṇaburam pukken śeṅgaṇ mālukku
en kādal en tuṇaivarkkuraitti āgil
idu oppademakkinbam illai
nāḻum paiṅgānam īdellām unadē āga
pazana mīn kavarnduṇṇa ttaruvan
tandāl iṅgē vandinidirundun peḍaiyum nīyum
iru nilattil inidinbam eydalāmē
meaning: Red-footed young crane! There is nothing that pleases me more than that you start right today, reach Tirukaṇṇapuram and put in a word about my love to my life-companion, the red-eyed Lord who is captivated by His devotees. I will allow you to peck the fish in the tank forever, considering all of this verdant sea-shore as yours. Then you and your female companion can come and stay with pleasure. You can indeed attain supreme bliss attainable in both the worlds.
purport:
The impatience born of intense longing does not allow the heroine to wait for the outcome of the bee's mission. Separation from the Lord has made every moment feel like an age, and she finds herself unable to remain idle until the messenger returns. Such is the nature of divine love that even the slightest delay becomes unbearable to the devotee.

Consequently, when she notices a crane nearby, she immediately chooses it as yet another messenger and sends it to the Lord. Her action reflects the urgency of her condition. She is unwilling to rely upon a single emissary when her entire being longs for reunion with Bhagavān. The commentators compare this to Śrī Rāma's efforts during His search for Sītā. Not content with a single attempt, Rāma dispatched numerous groups of monkeys in different directions to ensure that every possibility was explored. In a similar manner, the heroine sends messenger after messenger, hoping that one of them will quickly bring her beloved Lord back to her.

The phrase *"Tirukaṇṇapuram pukku"* receives a particularly beautiful interpretation. Earlier, the heroine had sent the bee as her emissary to seek out the Lord. The commentators imagine that the bee would have successfully met the Lord halfway at Aḻundūr and conveyed the heroine's message. Upon hearing of her condition, the compassionate Lord would naturally begin His journey towards her.

Thus, when the heroine now speaks of Tirukaṇṇapuram, it is understood that the Lord and the bee-messenger are already travelling together on their way to meet her, passing through Tirukaṇṇapuram. The mention of that sacred place therefore arises from her hopeful anticipation that the Lord has already begun His return journey.

This interpretation beautifully reveals the confidence underlying the heroine's sorrow. Although outwardly she appears overwhelmed by separation, inwardly she remains convinced of the Lord's compassion. She believes that once He learns of her suffering, He cannot remain indifferent. Just as she cannot bear separation from Him, He too cannot remain unmoved by the distress of a devotee who belongs exclusively to Him.

The pāsuram therefore combines longing with hope. The heroine's decision to send the crane demonstrates the impatience of love, while her expectation that the Lord is already on His way reveals her unwavering faith in His mercy. Even in the midst of separation, her heart remains sustained by the conviction that Bhagavān will not abandon His devotee and that every messenger sent in search of Him ultimately hastens the moment of reunion.

ten ilaṅgai araṇ śidaṟi avuṇan māḻa\
śenṟulagam mūnṟinaiyum tirindōr tērāl\

pōgāmai vallēnāy ppulavi eydi\
ennil aṅgam ellām vandinbam eyda\
eppozudum ninaindurugi iruppan nānē
meaning: I will be ever languishing by thinking that I would be enabled to bind Him between the mounds of my pale breasts making Him feel sorry and not capable of escaping, the Elephant, huge like a mountain, who shattered the ramparts of southern Laṅkā so as to destroy Rāvaṇa, who trod on the three worlds, and who steered the chariot to destruction in the Bhārata war fought by the famed chiefs, so as to make my limbs gratified.
purport:
In the two preceding pāsurams, the heroine sent messengers to the Lord, hoping to convey the depth of her longing. Various auspicious signs seemed to indicate that the Lord would respond favorably and come to her. Yet, as she reflected further, a troubling thought arose in her mind. Even if the Lord were to come and grant her the joy of union, would it not eventually be followed by another separation? Having already experienced the unbearable pain of parting from Him, she feared that any future union might only lead to renewed sorrow. Consequently, she resolved that when He came, she would not respond to His advances as before. Instead, she would end her life in His presence and thereby put an end to the endless cycle of union and separation.

Though these thoughts remained hidden within her heart, their effects became visible to those around her. The companion observed unmistakable signs of her distress. The heroine had become indifferent to food, dress, adornment, and all the ordinary concerns of life. Her entire being was consumed by thoughts of the Lord, and her outward neglect revealed the turmoil within.

Having understood her condition, the companion attempts to counsel her. She reminds the heroine that Bhagavān is not an ordinary lover towards whom one may behave like a disappointed maiden. He is the Supreme Lord, the ruler of all worlds and the controller of all beings. Moreover, His compassion towards those who seek Him is boundless. Did He not destroy Laṅkā for the sake of Sītā? Did He not orchestrate the events of the Mahābhārata to uphold the honour and vows of Draupadī? These examples demonstrate that the Lord never abandons those who place their trust in Him.

The companion further warns that resistance to the Lord is ultimately futile. Just as a wild elephant can effortlessly destroy barriers placed before it, the Lord can easily overcome any defenses the heroine might erect. The same Lord who shattered the mighty ramparts of Laṅkā can surely dissolve the resolve of a single devotee. The companion recalls the experience of Parāṅkuśa Nāyaki in Tiruvāymoḻi, where Nammāḻvār, assuming the role of a heroine, attempted to hide from the Lord but was ultimately won over by the irresistible force of His divine personality.

Yet the heroine remains steadfast in her resolve. She declares that however great and powerful the Lord may be, she intends to bind Him to herself, just as one would tether a wild elephant to a strong pillar. Having endured such prolonged suffering on His account, she desires that He should remain with her and witness the consequences of the pain He has caused. She imagines that, seeing her condition, He will feel remorse for the distress she has undergone.

The heroine's longing has become so intense that even her body bears the marks of separation. Āḻvār compares her weakened limbs to the hungry children of a householder during a famine, languishing from lack of nourishment. The sight of the Lord would satisfy and revive them, just as food relieves the suffering of the starving. Though her determination to bind the Lord may seem impossible, she continues to cherish this thought. The very impossibility of the desire only reveals the depth of her love, for in the world of devotion, longing often dares to imagine what reason declares unattainable.

anṟāyar kula magaḻukkaraiyan tannai
alai kaḍalai kkaḍaindaḍaitta ammān tannai
kunṟāda vali arakkar kōnai māḻa
koḍum śilaivāy ccaram turandu kulam kaḻaindu venṟānai
kunṟeḍutta tōḻinānai
viri tirai nīr viṇṇagaram maruvi nāḻum ninṟānai
taṇ kuḍandai kkiḍanda mālai
neḍiyānai aḍi nāyēn ninaindiṭṭēnē
meaning: This vassal of a dog is meditating on the lofty Lord, the compassionate Lord who is reposing in cool Kuḍandai (Kumbhakoṇam), who is standing forever with relish in Viṇṇagaram (Oppiliyappan Kōyil) of extensive tanks with waves, who once upon a time became the master of the cowherdess (Nappinnai), the Lord who churned the turbulent ocean (to obtain Lakṣmī) and also bridged it (to reclaim Sītā), the victorious Lord who discharged arrows from the fierce bow and destroyed Rāvaṇa, the chief of the powerful rākṣasas, who lifted the hill (Govardhana) with His arms.
purport:
It would have been one thing if the heroine had carried out her earlier resolve not to respond to the Lord's advances and to end her life in His presence. Such a determination at least presupposed that the Lord would appear before her. But now, He does not come at all. Faced with this reality, the heroine abandons her earlier boldness and becomes acutely aware of her utter helplessness and the immeasurable greatness of the Lord.

She now sees herself as being no different from a stray, hungry dog waiting at a doorway for a morsel of food. Such a creature possesses neither claim nor qualification; it survives solely through the compassion of another. In the same manner, the heroine realizes that she has no means of attaining the Lord through her own effort. Her only hope lies in His mercy. The confidence and determination that marked her earlier reflections give way to humility, dependence, and an earnest appeal for grace.

Accordingly, in this pāsuram she cries out to the Lord, invoking His compassion towards those who seek refuge in Him. Her appeal arises not from a sense of worthiness, but from the conviction that mercy is intrinsic to His nature. The Lord who has repeatedly shown kindness to the distressed and helpless cannot, she hopes, remain indifferent to her suffering.

This mood recalls the concluding decad of Tiruvāymoḻi, beginning with *"muṉiyē"*, where Nammāḻvār similarly pours out his heart before the Lord. Yet there is a significant difference between the two Āḻvārs. Nammāḻvār had remained detached from worldly concerns throughout his life. His appeal to Bhagavān arose from the intensity of his divine love and from the pain of separation experienced by one who had never sought anything apart from the Lord.

Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār's experience follows a different path. Earlier in life, he had been deeply involved in worldly pursuits, possessions, power, and martial achievements. Having experienced and ultimately transcended those attractions, he now recognizes the insignificance of all worldly attainments before the greatness of Bhagavān. This realization deepens his humility. Thus, he does not merely portray himself as a devotee longing for the Lord, but as one who, after exhausting worldly ambitions, now sees himself as utterly dependent upon divine grace, no more worthy than a street dog waiting for compassion.

Another distinction lies in the focus of their appeals. Nammāḻvār's concluding prayers encompass both the Lord's transcendence (*Paratva*) and His incarnations (*Avatāras*). Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār, however, remains captivated until the very end by the Lord's accessibility in His Avatāras and Arcā manifestations. His heart continually returns to the Lord who walked among men as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, and to the Lord who stands accessible in the Divya Deśams for the sake of devotees.

Thus, this pāsuram becomes a profound expression of humility. Having abandoned every trace of self-reliance, Āḻvār stands before Bhagavān as a helpless soul dependent entirely upon His mercy. The greatness of the Lord and the insignificance of the devotee are brought into sharp contrast, and it is precisely this contrast that becomes the basis for the devotee's appeal. For when all other supports have failed, only the Lord's compassion remains as the soul's refuge.

māna vēl para kālan kaliyan śonna

meaning: Those who study this garland in Tamil conforming to prosody, indited by the chieftain of Tirumaṅgai with hoary gem-like mansions, who, with the mighty spear, is like the Lord of death to the enemies and who is of great prowess, on the Lord who brought forth the precious Vedas as the Swan with the Celestials and Ṛṣis eulogizing, saying "The great Lord of the Nityasūris! The Lord benevolent like clouds gliding gracefully with lightning and copious rains! Please grace me," will of themselves be capable of rooting out the age-long "prārabdha karmas."
purport:
In the final pāsuram, Āḻvār once again glorifies the divine form of Bhagavān. His complexion is compared to a dark rain-bearing cloud ready to pour down showers of grace upon all beings. Just as a rain cloud nourishes the world without discrimination, the Lord bestows His compassion upon those who seek refuge in Him.

Āḻvār recalls the episode involving the four Kumāras. When the Kumāras approached Brahmā with profound questions concerning Yoga and the highest spiritual truths, the lotus-born creator found himself unable to provide the answers. At that time, Bhagavān Himself manifested in the form of a divine Swan (*Haṁsa*). Assuming this extraordinary form, He instructed Brahmā, the Kumāras, and the assembled Ṛṣis, revealing the truths of the Vedas and illuminating the path of spiritual wisdom. Thus, the Lord demonstrated that He alone is the ultimate source of all knowledge and the supreme teacher of both gods and sages.

This same Supreme Lord is eternally praised by the Nityasūris, who never cease to glorify His auspicious qualities and divine splendour. Āḻvār concludes with a prayer that this Lord may bestow His grace upon all devotees and bless them with the vision of His divine form.

The phalaśruti of the pāsuram extols the greatness of this sacred composition. Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār compares this Prabandham to a garland of fresh tulasī lovingly offered to Bhagavān. Just as a tulasī garland delights the Lord, these verses, woven together with devotion, knowledge, and divine experience, serve as a fragrant offering at His feet. Those who study, recite, and reflect upon this beautiful Prabandham will be blessed with true spiritual knowledge and deep devotion towards Bhagavān. Through His grace, they will gain clarity regarding the nature of the soul, the supremacy of the Lord, and the path of loving service to Him.

Thus, with praise of Bhagavān's divine form, remembrance of His role as the supreme teacher, and blessings upon future devotees, Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār brings the magnificent Prabandham known as *Tiruneduntāṇḍakam* to its conclusion.

meaning: Oh Lord! You are the primal cause who have kept and protected the three worlds within your stomach during deluge and then, made them manifest at the beginning of creation as the principal Brahman. Oh Lord residing at the great city of Srirangam! we have controlled our senses; we have indeed, leapt over the sins (and sinful deeds); and we tread on the heads of Yama and his hosts, erecting victory flagstafl's (on those heads). We are proud to say thus because of our practice of incessant chanting of your names as Sri Ranganitha, hearken!
purport:
Bhagavān holds the entire universe in His womb and hence he is called Garbhodakaśāyī Viṣṇu. As He holds the animate and inanimate within His garbha, He is also called Hiraṇyagarbha. From this Hiraṇyagarbha, everything is created. In the Pāñcarātra Āgama, the expansion of Vāsudeva, i.e., Saṅkarṣaṇa, further expands as Garbhodakaśāyī Viṣṇu, holding the entire universe within Him. Āḻvār praises the Lord for protecting us all the time, even after pralaya. Once He decides to create the universe again, with His saṅkalpa alone, He creates the lotus-born Brahmā. Due to Him being the primal cause of everything, He is the Brahman. This Supreme Brahman resides in Śrīraṅgam on the bed of Ādiśeṣa.

Our senses (Indriyas) play a primary role in performing actions. The mind among them can either distract us from the primary goal (Brahman) or attract us towards Him. Once one controls his senses, he is able to leap over all sinful activities. All the results of the pious actions the jīvatma performs are surrendered at the lotus feet of the Lord. When one becomes a Prapanna, surrendering to the divine feet of the Lord, he is able to conquer the cycle of birth and death (personified by Ālvār as treading on the head of Yama). One can only attain liberation by chanting the beautiful names of the Lord. By chanting the Thirumantram, that yogi is able to enter the Supreme above where the Nityas sing the glories of the Supreme.
