english_scripts:
ārttu vaṇḍalambum śōlai
aṇi tiruvaraṅgan tannuḻ
kār ttiraḻ anaiya mēni
kaṇṇanē ! unnai kkāṇum
mārkkam onṟaṟiya māṭṭā
maniśaril turiśanāya
mūrkkanēn vandu ninṟēn
mūrkkanēn mūrkkanēnē
meaning: Oh Lord Kṛṣṇa of charming beauty like the dense dark rainy clouds! You are dwelling as Śri Ranganatha at Srirangam beautified by the surrounding groves resounding with the humming of honey-bees. I am only a knave among human beings because I do not know the right path to perceive You in the proper perspective. Though I have come (seeking you), nevertheless I am just a wicked, and wicked alone.
purport:
The Āḻvār describes the scene in Śrīraṅgam, where beetles, intoxicated by excess honey from the lush groves, buzz and wander aimlessly. He likens their state to that of muktas (liberated souls) in Paramapada, who sing Sāma Gāna out of sheer joy after experiencing the Lord. This comparison elevates the sweetness of Śrīraṅgam to that of the divine realm.

Drawing a parallel to the Rāmāyaṇa's Sundara Kāṇḍa, where monkeys celebrate in Madhuvana after sighting Sītā, the Āḻvār notes a distinction: while he cries out for existence, the beetles cry out of joy. The phrase "vaṇḍu alambum sōlai" likens the beetles' predicament to Mārkaṇḍeya Maharṣi tossed in the great deluge, emphasizing the overwhelming nature of Śrīraṅgam's beauty.

Śrīraṅgam is described as "aṇi araṅgam", an ornament to saṃsāra. The Āḻvār alludes to Rāmāyaṇa, where a husband is considered a woman's greatest ornament, to highlight Raṅganātha's significance to the world. The Lord's form, "kārttiraḷ anaiya mēni", is compared to rain-laden clouds, not just in color but in qualities of coolness and selfless giving. The term "Kaṇṇan" is used to emphasize His accessibility, contrasting with the distant nature of clouds.

The Āḻvār laments his ignorance of the paths to attain the Lord, despite being born human. He calls himself "thurisanāya" (a thief or cheat), suggesting that compared to him, others might seem like nitya sūris (eternal devotees).
Finally, addressing his audacity in approaching the Lord, the Āḻvār describes himself as "mūrkkan" (a fool), repeating it for emphasis. He acknowledges his ignorance of both the Lord's greatness and his own lowliness, likening his approach to poisoning the pure water enjoyed by the wise. This passage beautifully intertwines devotional fervor with self-deprecation, using rich imagery and scriptural references to convey the Āḻvār's spiritual struggle and deep reverence for Raṅganātha.

english_scripts:
mey ellām pōga viṭṭu
viri kuzalāril paṭṭu
poy ellām podindu koṇḍa
pōzkkanēn vandu ninṟēn
aiyanē ! araṅganē !
un aruḻ ennum āśai tannāl
poyyanēn vandu ninṟēn
poyyanēn poyyanēnē
meaning: Oh Lord! O Śri Ranganatha! I have completely abandoned truthfulness on thought, word and deed. I have been ensnared by damsels of beautiful locks of hair, and I have experienced untold miseries. I am a shameless person abounding in falsehood, and falsehood alone. Though I am falsehood incarnate, I have come to You, with the desire to obtain your grace. Nevertheless, I spoke untruth; even now, I am only untruthful.
purport:
The Āḻvār discusses the concept of mey (truth), defining it as that which leads to good for all jīvātmās and describes things as they are. He cites the Kaiśika Māhātmyam, where Nampāduvān declares the primacy of truth in sustaining the world.

The Āḻvār confesses, "ellām pōgaviṭṭu" (I got rid of all truths), implying he lacks truthfulness even towards relatives. He laments speaking lies to the omniscient Lord Himself.
When questioned about the source of his deceit, the Āḻvār attributes it to his association with women: "viri kuḻalāril paṭṭu" (entangled with women of flowing hair). He elaborates on how impossible it is to speak truth in women's company, comparing it to the impossibility of lying in the Lord's presence. Āḻvār describes himself as a repository of falsehoods, contrasting with his earlier renunciation of all truths. Addressing himself as "pōtkanēn" (one without refuge), the Āḻvār stands before the Lord despite his unworthiness, drawn by their inseverable relationship. He refers to the Lord as "Aiyane" and "Araṅgane", acknowledging this bond and the Lord's presence in Śrīraṅgam.

The Āḻvār expresses his desire for the Lord's grace: "un aruḷ eṉṉum āsai taṉṉāl vantu niṉṟēṉ" (I came standing with the desire for your grace). He cites the Rāmāyaṇa to illustrate the Lord's compassion even towards the undeserving. Finally, the Āḻvār admits that even his confession might be false: "poyyaṉēṉ poyyaṉēṉē" (I am a liar, indeed a liar). He references the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā, suggesting that acknowledging one's faults before the Lord can yield benefits. However, he questions the sincerity of his own admission, wondering how many lies he can tell in the divine presence where only truth should be spoken. This passage beautifully captures the Āḻvār's deep introspection, his struggle with truthfulness, and his complex relationship with the divine, all expressed through rich scriptural allusions and poetic imagery.

uḻḻattē uṟaiyum mālai
uḻḻuvān uṇarvonṟillā
kaḻḻattēn nānum toṇḍāy
toṇḍukkē kōlam pūṇḍu
uḻḻuvār uḻḻiṭrellām
uḍan irundaṟidi enṟu
veḻgippōy ennuḻḻē nān
vilavaṟa ccirittiṭṭēnē !
meaning: Oh Lord Ranganatha! You are dwelling in the heart of everyone and affectionate towards all creatures. I do not have adequate knowledge even to contemp late upon You. However, I am a deceitful person. I pose my- self as your servant and so, put on the guise of doing service under You; when I am able to  recognize that You are the in-dweller, and so you are capable of gleaning the thought (idea) of every- one, being ever a companion - I feel quite ashamed and even then, I abandon You (i.e. move off from your holy shrine), and so laugh at myself as my ribs could break into pieces within my heart where, indeed, You hid yourself.
purport:
The Āḻvār contemplates the omnipresence of Emperumān, particularly His dwelling in the heart (uṟaiyum), the springboard of thoughts. He emphasizes the impossibility of deceiving the Lord, who is described as Mālai (the supreme one), knowing and controlling everything. The Āḻvār laments his lack of spiritual knowledge: "uḷḷuvān uṇarvu illā" (without the knowledge to meditate on His indwelling presence). He confesses to having no understanding of either the jīvātmā or Paramātmā, nor of the body's transient nature.
Calling himself "kaḷḷattēṉ" (a thief), the Āḻvār admits to deceiving both the foolish and the learned by feigning ignorance or humility. He acknowledges the impropriety of his attempts at service (toṇḍu), citing Śrī Rāmāyaṇa to illustrate the despicable nature of one unseen by Rāma.

Āḻvār confesses to wearing the external symbols of devotion (Ūrdhva puṇḍras, divine weapons) and reciting divine names without true belief, misleading others about his spiritual status. The realization dawns: "uḷḷuvār uḷḷiṟṟellām uḍaṉ irundu aṟidi eṉṟu" (You know all thoughts of those who think). The Āḻvār references Śakuntalā's words to Duṣyanta from the Mahābhārata, highlighting the futility of deceit before the omniscient Lord.

Overcome with shame (veḷgip pōy), the Āḻvār attempts to flee the Lord's presence, only to realize the impossibility of finding a place devoid of His presence. This realization leads to self-deprecating laughter (eṉṉuḷḷē nāṉ viḷavaṟac cirittiṭṭēṉē), so intense that his ribs metaphorically break. The passage concludes by comparing the Āḻvār's attempt to leave Emperumān's presence to one adorning oneself before committing suicide, highlighting the absurdity of trying to escape the omnipresent divine. This poignant self-realization is juxtaposed with Arjuna's moment of despair in the Bhagavad Gītā, emphasizing the Āḻvār's spiritual crisis and the profound understanding of the inescapable nature of the divine presence.

english_scripts:
tāvi anṟulagam ellām
talaiviḻākkoṇḍa endāy
śēviyēn unnai allāl
śikkena cceṅgaṇ mālē
āviyē ! amudē
en tan ār uyir anaiya endāy
pāviyēn unnai allāl
pāviyēn pāviyēnē
meaning: Oh! my supreme Lord who have encompassed all the worlds, without leaving any space, when You begged the great emperor, Mahābali, and got the three foot-steps of space from him! I am sure I won't bow to any other god except You. Oh! graceful Lord with reddish lotus-like eyes! Oh my supreme Self! Oh nectarine immortal Lord! Oh beneficent Lord similar to my rare life-birth! I will never think of any important goal other than You. Though I deem myself sinful, I do, again, sinful deeds alone.
purport:
The Āḻvār expresses his deep regret at emperumāṉ's unanticipated act of placing His divine foot upon the heads of saṃsārīs. He reflects that had emperumāṉ forewarned of His intention, the saṃsārīs, burdened with immense ego, would have refused this divine grace, commanding Him, "Do not place Your foot upon us." Just as those of sattva guṇa would have beseeched, "thiruvāṇai niṉṉāṇai" (Thiruvāimoḻi 10.10.2) to ensure emperumāṉ's divine foot rested upon their heads, these saṃsārīs would have vehemently opposed His approach. It was for this reason that emperumāṉ, in His infinite wisdom, placed His foot upon their heads without their knowledge, growing rapidly in form without causing fatigue to either Himself or the saṃsārīs.

On that day when the hierarchy between master and servitor lay in ruins, and Mahābali had seized the worlds. Not content with merely measuring the three worlds seized by Mahābali, His divine foot extended to Brahmalōka, after gracing the heads of all beings without discrimination, expanding in size. Āḻvār illustrates that the protector's [emperumāṉ's] excitement surpassed the magnitude of what He protected. The Puruṣa Sūktam 1 proclaims, "sahasra śīrṣā puruṣa: sahasrākṣa: sahasrapādh | sa bhūmim viśvathō vruthvā athyathiṣṭadhdhaśāṅgulam ||" (Nārāyaṇa, known as Puruṣa, possesses countless heads, eyes, and legs; He encompassed the earth on all sides and pervaded countless yōjanas beyond).

Āḻvār addresses emperumāṉ thus, recognizing that His divine feet, described by Thirumangai Āḻvār in Thirukkuṟundhāṇḍagam 6 as "amarar seṉṉippūviṉai" (the divine feet borne by nityasūris on their heads), had also graced his own head on that day. The Āḻvār reflects that it is due to the merit of that encounter that he has attained enlightenment today. He declares, "Having realized Your simplicity, I shall not depart from You hereafter, nor cling to anything else." He affirms that he will neither seek independence like a king nor become a servitor to another, echoing the essence of the Thirumanthram [aṣṭākṣaram]. Āḻvār assures emperumāṉ that his determination will last eternally, until his ātmā ceases to exist. Like Nammāḻvār in Thiruvāimoḻi 2.6.1, he offers solace to emperumāṉ, who grieves at the thought of the Āḻvār's departure. This epithet reflects not just the natural redness of emperumāṉ's eyes but the unique radiance acquired upon hearing the Āḻvār's declaration of eternal devotion. The Āḻvār, like Hanumān in the Rāmāyaṇa, offers refuge to periya perumāḷ in His archāvatāram, assuring Him of his unwavering devotion

english_scripts:
mazaikkanṟu varai mun ēndum
maindanē ! madura āṟē
uzaikkanṟē pōla
nōkkam uḍaiyavar valaiyuḻ paṭṭu
uzaikkinṟēṟku
ennai nōkkādozivadē
unnai anṟē azaikkinṟēn ādi mūrtti !
araṅga mā nagaruḻānē !
meaning: Oh! primeval supreme Being! Lord of the great city, Śrirangam! Oh sweet flow of bountiful compassion! Oh Lord of fresh youth (Śrī Kṛṣṇa) in which you lifted aloft on your little finger the mount Govardhana, for the Make of protecting the cowherds and Gokula (Āyarpāḍi) from the fury of Indra's torrential stony rain! Why are you going away without looking at me who am bound in the net of the doe eyed damsels? I do call You, Oh! supreme Lord!
purport:
Among the Āḻvārs, whenever they employ the term "maḻai" [rain], it invariably alludes to the hailstones that Indra [lord of celestial entities] showered when Kṛṣṇa lifted the Gōvardhan mountain, just as the word "āṉai" [elephant] always refers to Gajēndrāḻvāṉ [the elephant caught by the crocodile when it entered the pond to pluck a flower for emperumāṉ]. The Āḻvār now invokes the prevention of hailstones by lifting Gōvardhana mountain to illustrate his yearning to attain Him and overcome the sorrows of saṃsāra (materialistic realm). He recalls how the cowherds overcame the dangers posed by Indra by seeking refuge in Him. Just as the hungry call out to the wealthy, "Oh Lord! Please remove our hunger," the Āḻvār beseeches emperumāṉ, "Oh One who rids people of dangers! Please remove my peril."

The Śrīviṣṇu Purāṇam 5.11.13 states, "thathasthath gōkulam sarvam gōgōpījanasaṅkulam | athīvārththam harir dhṛṣṭvā maithrēyāchinthayath thadhā ||" (Oh Maitreya! Upon seeing the entire Gōkulam, full of cows and gōpīkās, in sorrow, [Kṛṣṇa] immediately began to ponder). Aṉṟu refers to the day when the calves, cows, and cowherds trembled at the sight of Indra's hailstones. The Āḻvār equates his present danger to that faced by the inhabitants of Gōkulam, beseeching emperumāṉ for protection from his shower of sorrow. When Indra commanded all clouds to open, they poured with such intensity that it resembled the great deluge. Seeing Indra's wrath for being denied food by Āyppādi, Kṛṣṇa, without time to summon His Sudarśana Chakra, lifted the nearest mountain. The Āḻvār infers that emperumāṉ cannot claim lack of suitable means to offer protection.

Having already used "aṉṟu" to denote a specific time, "muṉ" here signifies "before harm befell the cows." The Āḻvār emphasizes that emperumāṉ did not wait for harm to come to the cows and cowherds but protected them preemptively, as they had no other refuge. Āḷavandhār, in his Stōtra Ratnam 49, similarly beseeches, "avivēkaghanāndhathingmukhē bahudhā santhathadhu:kha varṣiṇi | bhagavan! bhavadhurthdhinē padha: skalitham māmavalōkayāchutha! ||"
The Āḻvār marvels at how Kṛṣṇa effortlessly lifted the mountain at merely seven years of age, as if it were a garland of flowers. He questions whether emperumāṉ's reluctance to protect him stems from a fear of fatigue.

Oh One of immense strength to lift a mountain! Alternatively, maindhaṉ indicates youthfulness, suggesting One who becomes young in spirit upon protecting His devotees. The Āḻvār laments that while protecting him benefits emperumāṉ, he must still call out for protection. Oh One who is like a river of sweetness! Even if You were not the protector but one who might chastise the devotee, Your beauty is such that none would forsake You. The Āḻvār likens emperumāṉ to a river rather than a sea, for river water proves useful for bathing on a hot day, washing one's face, or quenching thirst. Like a flowing river during floods, this loving river [emperumāṉ] gushes in, breaking the dam of unworthiness the Āḻvār had built around himself.

The Āḻvār, trapped in the net of women's fawn-like eyes, laments his suffering. These women, though devoid of genuine affection, feign devotion, ensnaring him with their deceptive gazes. He pleads, "ennai nōkkādhu oḻivadhē" – why do You not look upon me (protect me)? The Āḻvār's closeness to emperumāṉ and the latter's affability allow him to express such sadness. The Āḻvār reminds emperumāṉ of His responsibility as the creator, citing the Chāndōgya Upaniṣad 6.2.9, "thadhaikṣatha bahu syām prajāyēyēthi thath thējō'sṛjatha" (That Brahman took a vow "I will multiply myself" and created radiance).

The Āḻvār questions the need to seek protection at the origin of creation when emperumāṉ has already descended to Śrīraṅgam. He implores, "After You came to Śrīraṅgam to cultivate a taste for righteousness, and after I acquired that taste, should I lose it?" Even as the Āḻvār calls out, emperumāṉ remains silent, savoring the long-awaited sincere devotion. The efforts He had taken since time immemorial are now bearing fruit, and He wishes to hear the Āḻvār's earnest plea a while longer before responding.

english_scripts:
teḻivilā kkalaṅgal nīr śūz
tiruvaraṅgattuḻ ōṅgum
oḻi uḻār tāmē anṟē
tandaiyum tāyum āvār
eḻiyadōr aruḻum anṟē
en tiṟattem pirānār
aḻiyan nam paiyal ennār
ammavō ! koḍiyavāṟē !
meaning: The supreme Lord of great splendour dwelling in the lofty shrine of Srirangam which is surrounded by the agitated muddy waters (of the holy river Kāvēri), indeed, is our father and mother. Would He not ward off my anguish, by showering His ineffable grace on me, after saying "This pitiable fellow is, indeed, my boy worthy of my blessings"? But, He has not yet blessed me. Alas! what a cruelty of fate!
purport:
As the flow of water in Kāvēri eases, it gains clarity. Yet, with increasing floods, it remains perpetually muddied. Similarly, this Āḻvār, like Kāvēri, is in constant agitation. Before attaining emperumāṉ, he frets, "I have not attained Him." Upon attainment, he becomes agitated due to his love for Him. This river too, flowing westward towards the temple, grows agitated in anticipation of seeing periya perumāḷ, and eastward, in sorrow at departing from Him. Thus, without distinction between chētana (Āḻvār) and achētana (river) entities, even those who walk near the temple experience this agitation.

Just as Nammāḻvār says in Thiruvāimoḻi 10.10.10 "adhaṉil periya eṉ avāvarach chūḻndhāy", periya perumāḷ envelops the Āḻvārs with His love. Likewise, Kāvēri envelops periya perumāḷ out of her love for Him. Parāśara Bhaṭṭar's Śrīraṅgarāja Stavam 1.21 eloquently describes Kāvēri's devotion: "dhugdhābdhir janakō jananīyahamiyam śrīrēva puthri vā śrīraṅgēśvara ēthadharhamiha kim kuryāmithvākulā | sañjaccāmara chandra chandana mahāmāṇikya mukthōthkarān kāvērī laharēekarairvidhadhathī paryēthi sā sēvyathām ||"

Just as it is challenging to navigate Kāvēri's floods, it is equally difficult to penetrate periya perumāḷ's resplendent radiance and admire His divine form. After entering Thiruvaraṅgam (Śrīraṅgam), even the brightness in Paramapadham diminished, like daylight. The radiance at Śrīraṅgam aids lowly saṃsārīs like night-time illumination. Emperumāṉ, amidst nityasūris, is like a sun among suns. But standing amidst saṃsārīs, who suffer from worldly sorrows, His radiance acquires dominance.

The Subālōpaniṣad 16 states: "māthā pithā bhrāthā nivāsaś śaraṇam suhruth gathir nārāyaṇa:" (Nārāyaṇa is mother, father, brother, dwelling place, means for attaining mōkṣa, friend, and the one attained in mōkṣa). The Āḻvār declares that for him, it is not Paramapadhanāthan, common to all; not Vyūha or Vibhava forms of perumāḷ, common to a few; not other Archāvatāra vigrahas common to other Āḻvārs; but only periya perumāḷ who is his father and mother. This exclusivity is emphasized by the term thāmē (He Himself). The Mahābhāratam Vana Parvam 192.56 ślōka reinforces this: "sarvēṣāmēva lōkānām pithā māthā cha mādhava: | gacchadhvamēnam śaraṇam śaraṇyam puruṣarṣabhā: ||"  Unlike the cowherds, there is no need for difficult tasks like mountain-lifting to protect me. The Āḻvār pleads, "Is it not enough if You glance at me with Your comforting eyes?" Bestowing favors upon me. Even when emperumāṉ is not glancing at him, the Āḻvār acknowledges past favors, beseeching Him for this one. The Āḻvār yearns for emperumāṉ to say, "He has something good in him to be shown my mercy. He is my little fellow." The Āḻvār feels that only if emperumāṉ, the master, addresses him thus, confirming their master-servitor relationship, will his servitorship endure. This echoes incidents in the lives of pūrvāchāryas, such as Maṇakkāl Nambi addressing Thirumagizhmārban as "my son" and Piḷḷaippiḷḷai Āḻvāṉ referring to Appiḷḷai Āḻvāṉ as "little brother" and "my little fellow." The Āḻvār exclaims in deep anguish, "When I cry out to Him in sorrow, should He not rise? How can He sleep even after hearing my voice? Has His divine heart become so hardened?" The word amma indicates profound distress.

tamil_scripts:
மேம்‌ பொருள்‌ போக விட்டு,
மெய்ம்மையை மிக உணர்ந்து.
ஆம்பரிசறிந்து கொண்டு
ஐம்‌ புலன்‌ அகத்தடக்கி.
காம்பறத்‌ தலை சிரைத்த
உன்‌ கடைத்தலை இருந்து வாழும்‌.
சோம்பரை உகத்தி போலும்‌,
சூழ்‌ புனல்‌ அரங்கத்தானே !
english_scripts:
mēm poruḻ pōga viṭṭu
meymmaiyai miga uṇarndu
āmbariśaṟindu koṇḍu
aim pulan agattaḍakki
kāmbaṟa ttalai śiraittu
un kaḍaittalai irundu vāzum
śōmbarai ugatti pōlum
śūz punal araṅgattānē !
meaning: Oh supreme Lord dwelling in the holy city of Srirangam made fertile by the surround- ing, flowing waters of Kāvēri! it seems You are pleased with those who refrain from leading prākṛtic (materialistic) way of life, and then, properly understand the nature of souls, and further, decide that the divine service done to You alone is the supreme end of one's life, and hence, who after restraining all their senses, withdraw themselves from all other pursuits and paths, and thus, who once for all, reject all unrighteous paths and stay at your threshold in order to do your divine service alone.
purport:
Alvār speaks about the nature of a true prapanna, a true bhāgavata. mēmpōrul refers to this body which can decay and is bound to perish once born. When a jīvātman realizes the essence of this life and understands that this body is perishable, while service to bhagavān is eternal, that jīvātman feels this body to be superficial. Only those who have surrendered to the lotus feet of Rañganātha can receive this beautiful knowledge; else, by māyā, the intertwined body makes the jīvātman feel "I am this dēha" which gives rise to ignorance. Refraining from such ignorance, a prapanna serves bhagavān. Until the jīvātman leaves material desire and the ignorance of "I am the body," he is destined to grow the tree called saṃsāra, as stated in Viṣṇu Purāṇa 7.11 as follows: "anāthmanyāthmā buddhir yā asve svam iti yā mati | saṃsāra-taru-sambhūti bījam ētat dvidhā sthitham ||" Hence, Alvār states to give up such traces completely. To give up such traces, the body must realize the divine nature of the ātman and īśvara. Once it realizes it is not the body, the tree called saṃsāra slowly withers away. When that ātman realizes its true nature, it realizes its svarūpam.

Even after realizing "I am not the body," the jīvātman must fully realize its true svarūpa—that it is the servant of bhagavān—and only then is liberation possible. When this knowledge is gifted to that jīvātman by bhagavān himself, it desires to serve the Lord eternally and strives to liberate itself from saṃsāra. In the attempt to liberate itself, it gives up the wealth, that is, the ignorance called "I am the body" and attaches itself to service to bhagavān. Realizing that removal of bondage through its own attempts is not possible, that jīvātman surrenders to bhagavān, keeping the Lord himself as the means to attain him. This is the essence of prapatti or śaraṇāgati, which was narrated to Arjuna by Kṛṣṇa in Bhagavad Gītā 18.66. 

Alvār compares the means to attain bhagavān to hair. Just as hair brings a sense of prestige to a person, these means can bring the essence of pride—"I am my own protector" or "It is by my efforts that I am attaining bhagavān or achieving liberation". One must forget this thought and realize that it is not the means (Karma Yoga, Bhakthi Yoga and others) but the compassion of bhagavān which brings us closer to Him. He alone can get us out of saṃsāra; indeed, He is the means itself. This itself becomes a prosperity to the jīvātman.

Alvār goes to the extreme of saying "aimpulan agathtadakki"—that is, while a jīvātman performs kaiṅkarya (divine service) to bhagavān, it experiences happiness due to the divine nature of the service. But a true prapanna should renounce this happiness too. He must perform the service for the happiness of bhagavān and not for himself.

Looking at Thiruvāraṅga's face, Alvār states that He is smiling happily while observing such great devotees who have left everything and are performing their rituals and duties assigned by the śāstras for the happiness of bhagavān alone, because bhagavān has ordered them to do so. Such souls are the foremost among His devotees. Due to the disappearance of grey clouds called ignorance, the love and compassion of the Lord, known as dayā, eternally falls upon them like sunlight.

tamil_scripts:
அடிமையில்‌ குடிமை இல்லா,
அயல்‌ சதுப்பேதி மாரில்‌,
குடிமையில்‌ கடைமை பட்ட.
குக்கரில்‌ பிறப்பர்‌ ஏலும்‌,
முடியினில்‌ துளபம்‌ வைத்தாய்‌ !
மொய்‌ கழற்கன்பு செய்யும்‌,
அடியரை உகத்தி போலும்‌.
அரங்க மா நகருளானே !
english_scripts:
aḍimaiyil kuḍimai illā
ayal śaduppēdi māril
kuḍimaiyil kaḍaimai paṭṭa
kukkaril piṟappar ēlum
muḍiyinil tuḻabam vaittāy !
moy kazaṟkanbu śeyyum
aḍiyarai ugatti pōlum
araṅga mā nagaruḻānē !
meaning: Oh Lord of the great city, Śrirangam! O supreme God with Tulasi leaves adorning your crown! it seems, You are more pleased with these who, though born in the lowest castes, seek the divine service under your pair of feet, and are highly devoted to You alone, than those who recite all the four Vedas, but do not seek the divine service under You, as the supreme goal.
purport:
Even those who do not recognize that performing kaiṅkaryam is inherent to their nature. It is fitting to think, "Kaiṅkaryam is natural to us. Just as we cannot live without food and water, we cannot exist without performing kaiṅkaryam." The Āḻvār refers to those who lack this understanding.

Those who differ from the chaturvēdhis who are not immersed in kaiṅkaryam. Sadhuppēdhimāril refers to those who study the four Vēdas. The benefit of Vēdic study is to realize that emperumāṉ is the master of all worlds, that we are His possessions, and that performing kaiṅkaryam to emperumāṉ and His devotees is our appropriate goal. Ayal signifies not knowing that the purpose of learning Vēdas is to obtain this knowledge. The Pādhmōttaram states: "viṣṇubhaktivihīnō yas sarvaśāstrārtha vēdhyapi | brāhmaṇyam tasya na bhavēt tasyōtpattir nirūpyatām ||" (Even if one knows the meanings of all śāstras, without devotion to Viṣṇu, one lacks the qualities of a brāhmaṇa, and their birth is questionable).

Kuḍimaiyil kaḍaimaippaṭṭa kukkaril piṟapparēlum - Those who, after many births of not following Vēdic injunctions and engaging in forbidden acts, are born into very low castes due to accumulated sins. Kukkar (kuṣka) refers to a class lower than chaṇḍāḷas. The Āḻvār's use of piṟapparēlum (even if they are born) indicates that birth status is not a determinant of understanding the meanings mentioned in the previous pāsuram. In Śrī Rāmāyaṇa Āraṇya Kāṇḍam 68.24, Śrī Rāma tells Lakṣmaṇa: "sarvatra khalu dṛśyante sādhavō dharmacāriṇa: | śūrā: śaraṇyās saumitrē tiryak yōni gatēṣvapi ||" (O Lakṣmaṇa! Those who are like sages, following the path of righteousness, fit to be surrendered to, are seen even among those born as animals and other species!). Just as emperumāṉ adorns tuḷasi on His head, these devotees are also fit to be kept on His head like tuḷasi. This adornment indicates His quality of being sarvēśvaran (lord of all).

These devotees cast aside their own happiness to serve only for His happiness, with affection, similar to sēvaḍi sevvi thirukkāppu (Thirupallāṇḍu 1). To them, this is the only purposeful way to spend time, and they consider this their goal. They consider His compassionate divine feet as the means. As mentioned in pāsuram 38 as sōmbar, they know that their ātma svarūpam (nature of the ātmā) is being eternally subservient to emperumāṉ and will not engage in self-protection. You delight in these followers who possess this knowledge, regardless of their lowly birth, rather than the chaturvēdhis who lack this understanding. The purpose of coming to Śrīraṅgam and reclining here is to hear these people who have affection towards You, even if they are of lowly birth. If You desired to hear only from the exalted, You would have remained in Śrīvaikuṇṭam.

tamil_scripts:
திருமறு மார்வ ! நின்னைச்‌.
சிந்தையுள்‌ திகழ வைத்து .
மருவிய மனத்தர்‌ ஆகில்‌.
மா நிலத்துயிர்கள்‌ எல்லாம்‌.
வெருவறக்கொன்று சுட்டிட்டு ,
ஈட்டிய வினையர்‌ ஏலும்‌,
அரு வினைப்‌ பயன்‌ அதுய்யார்‌.
அரங்க மா நகருளானே !
english_scripts:
tirumaṟu mārva ! ninnai
śindaiyuḻ tigaza vaittu
maruviya manattar āgil
mā nilattuyirgaḻ ellām
veruvaṟakkonṟu śuṭṭiṭṭu
īṭṭiya vinaiyar ēlum
aru vinai ppayan aduyyār
araṅga mā nagaruḻānē !
meaning: Oh Lord Ranganatha residing at Srirangam! O supreme Lord with God- dess Laksmi and the Śrivatsa mark adorning your broad chest! all the people on this earth should ever contemplate upon You and your consort, Goddess Sridevi, and then, they should install only both of You in their heart. If they do so, then even if they have committed the most heinous crimes, and so acquired such sins, they will not suffer from the fruits of those sins.
purport:
Hearken, gentle souls, to the wisdom of the Alvar, who once more doth proclaim the ineffable nature of the Divine Lord. He standeth beyond the confines of prakriti's elements, His essence a mystery that mortal minds can scarce comprehend. Verily, His virtues and qualities be infinite, stretching far beyond the reach of our humble understanding.

The Alvar, in his profound insight, declareth that only the Lord Himself knoweth the full measure of His divine play, His wondrous Leelas that unfold across the tapestry of creation. The sacred Taittiriya Upanishad, in its venerable verses, doth proclaim "aprāpya manasā saha" - even as the mind striveth to grasp His nature, it returneth baffled, unable to fathom the depths of His glory.

Yet, take heart, for though He be beyond the reach of common thought, He deigns to reside within the sanctum of pure hearts. As the hallowed Vishnu Sahasranama doth attest, He is "yōgihṛddhyānagamyaṃ" - accessible through the meditations of yogis whose minds are unburdened by impure thoughts. Thus, the Lord maketh His abode in the hearts of His true devotees.
The Alvar, in his boundless wisdom, counseleth us to acknowledge our limitations. How can we, mere mortals, hope to sing the praises of He whom even Brahma and Rudra, mighty deities themselves, find beyond their capacity to laud? Nay, our mortal tongues and finite minds fall short in this endeavor.

Therefore, the Alvar guideth us toward a path most true and efficacious. Let us, in our devotion, turn to the chanting of His divine names and the constant remembrance of His glory. For in this sacred practice lies the key to accessing His divine presence. What sweeter pursuit can there be, what nobler endeavor, than to invoke the Supreme Lord through the utterance of His holy appellations?

Indeed, the Alvar assureth us, there existeth no higher or more potent means to draw near to the Divine than through the sincere and devoted chanting of His names. In this simple yet profound practice, we find the essence of bhakti, the purest form of devotion that bridgeth the gulf between the mortal and the Divine.

tamil_scripts:
வான்‌ உளார்‌ அறியல்‌ ஆகா,
வானவா ! என்பர்‌ ஆகில்‌.

ஊனம்‌ ஆயினகள்‌ செய்யும்‌,
ஊனகாரகர்களேலும்‌
போனகம்‌ செய்த சேடம்‌.
தருவரேல்‌ புனிதம்‌ அன்றே
english_scripts:
vān uḻār aṟiyal āgā
vānavā ! enbar āgil
tēn ulām tuḻaba mālai
śenniyāy ! enbar āgil
ūnam āyinagaḻ śeyyum
ūnagāragargaḻēlum
pōnagam śeyda śēḍam
taruvarēl punidam anṟē
meaning: If the devotees call You, as "Oh the supreme Lord dwelling in the Paramapada whom even the celestial beings cannot realise! O Lord with your head adorned by honey-laden garlands of Tulasi!" even if it be that they are of vile deeds, and they cause others commit crimes - nevertheless, if they could offer to us, the remnant of their food, it is, indeed, sacred and holy for us.
purport:
Verily, hearken to the words of the Alvar, who speaketh of the Lord who dwelleth eternally in Paramapadham, that celestial abode beyond the ken of even Brahma and the heavenly host. As those perched upon lofty balconies cannot discern the stars above, so too are the denizens of Satyaloka and other celestial realms unable to perceive the Lord of Paramapadham.

Though these celestial beings possess great knowledge and power, 'tis not sufficient to breach the gates of Paramapadham. The word "AgA" herein signifieth both impossibility and prohibition - as a lowly Chandala may not enter sacred grounds, so too are these celestial entities barred from Paramapadham's hallowed realm.

Yet, lo! The Alvars, those blessed souls, have glimpsed the Lord of Paramapadham. This cometh not from their own merit, but through His divine grace. As the Bhagavad Gita doth proclaim, those who fancy themselves as gods cannot perceive Him. The Alvars, like seafarers who cross vast oceans by ship, traverse the tumultuous sea of Samsara with Vishnu as their vessel. The celestial beings, in their pride, are as those who would attempt to swim across unaided.

The Alvars, in their wisdom, have surrendered fully to the Lord, recognizing Him as both the means and the end. They chant, "O Thou adorned with a honey dripping Tulasi garland upon Thy crown!" - proclaiming His supremacy among the gods and His sweetness that surpasseth all earthly delights.

Even those who once committed grievous sins - binding and slaughtering creatures for base sustenance - if they should come to know the Lord and take refuge in Him, they too may be redeemed. For the knowledge of the Divine transformeth the heart, turning even the most cruel to compassion. Alvar speaketh of the sanctifying power of the food remnants of the truly wise. As Parasara Bhattar once gifted his disciple Nanjiyer with such blessed morsels, so too can these remnants purify the partaker instantly, like a philosopher's stone transmuting base metal to gold. Thus doth the Alvar extol the greatness of the Lord and His devotees, showing that the path to salvation lieth not in celestial power, but in humble devotion and the grace of the Divine.

tamil_scripts:
பழுதிலா ஒழுகல்‌ ஆற்றுப்‌,
பல சதுப்பேதி மார்கள்‌,
இழி குலத்தவர்களேலும்‌ .

தொழுமினீர்‌ கொடுமின்‌ கொண்மின்‌ ! என்று.
நின்னோடும்‌ ஒக்க.

மதிள்‌ திருவரங்கத்தானே!
english_scripts:
pazudilā ozugal āṭru
pala śaduppēdi mārgaḻ
izi kulattavargaḻēlum
em aḍiyārgaḻ āgil
tozuminīr koḍumin koṇmin ! enṟu
ninnōḍum okka
vazi paḍa aruḻināy pōl
madiḻ tiruvaraṅgattānē !
meaning: Oh the Lord of Śrirangam girt by seven Prakāras (ramparts)! I surmise that You have instructed the followers of Vedic lore as "O the reciters of the Vedas! O you who follow the age-old customs of your lineage faultlessly! even though the devotees of my feet have been born in the lowliest class (of the society), you have to bow to them; you offer to them whatever you know and whatever you can; you learn from them; treat them on par with me."
purport:
Álvár calls upon the learned scholars, the Brāhmaṇas who have studied the four Vedas, to transcend the ego associated with being born into an upper caste and to eliminate the pride of possessing greater knowledge than others. He explains that discrimination based on appearance and birth is meaningless and should be abandoned, as such prejudices stem from the belief that materialistic goals are the ultimate pursuits. When the jīvātmā is eternal and born into this world through karma, assigned to a specific gender and clan, how could this matter to a mumukṣhu who has realized their true nature as śeṣa of Bhagavān? This is the essence of Álvár's teaching. Every jīvātmā has Bhagavān as the inner witness. Consequently, a prappanna will perceive Bhagavān everywhere. Why would such a person harm another simply due to their birth? A person with wealth, knowledge, or prestigious lineage may easily develop ego, as illustrated in the traditional saying: vidhyāmadho dhanamadhaḥ tṛtīyo'bhijano madhaḥ: ēthē madhāvaliptānām ētha ēva satām damaḥ. Therefore, Álvár advises against taking pride in one's language or acquired wisdom, recognizing that such knowledge is ultimately a gift from Bhagavān. 

He further elaborates that speaking ill of others is unbecoming of a true Bhāgavata, and criticizing devotees of Bhagavān—particularly regarding their birth or background—is a grave transgression. Bhagavān himself teaches us to engage with his devotees: to share spiritual wisdom, show respect, and treat them as equivalent to the divine. Every devotee encountered should be honored as a manifestation of Bhagavān, for the divine resides within these devoted souls. Nammálvár's words in Thiruvāymoḻi 7.10 beautifully capture this sentiment: tīrththaṅgaḷē eṉṟu pūsiththu nalgiyuraippar tham dēviyarkē, even Nitya sūris speak about such great devotees! The teaching continues, niṉṉōdum okka vaḻipada aruḷiṉāy, suggesting that the devotees of Raṅganātha should be revered equally. These spiritual seekers must be respected as Ācāryas, regardless of their background or learning. Their sacred presence should be welcomed with utmost reverence and joy. This pasurama glorifies sripada teertham of Bhagavatas which have to taken with devotion and respect.

tamil_scripts:
அமர ஓர்‌ அங்கம்‌ ஆறும்‌.
வேதம்‌ ஓர்‌ நான்கும்‌ ஓதித்‌.
தமர்களில்‌ தலைவராய.ஃ
சாதி அந்தணர்களேலும்‌ ,
நுமர்களைப்‌ பழிப்பர்‌ ஆகில்‌,
நொடிப்பதோர்‌ அளவில்‌,
ஆங்கே அவர்கள்‌ தாம்‌ புலையர்‌ போலும்‌,
அரங்க மா நகருளானே!
english_scripts:
amara ōr aṅgam āṟum
vēdam ōr nāngum ōdi
tamargaḻil talaivarāya
śādi andaṇargaḻēlum
numargaḻai ppazippar āgil
noḍippadōr aḻavil
āṅgē avargaḻ tām pulaiyar pōlum
araṅga mā nagaruḻānē !
meaning: Oh Lord of the sacred temple city, Srirangam! among your devotees, if a section of devotees though born in higher classes of society, though taking a leading part in all activities, though well- versed in all holy scriptures, viz. the four Vedas and the six Vedāngas speak ill of other devotees belonging to lower classes of society, then, at that very moment, they are deemed to be.
purport:
Re-iterating the essence of the previous pasuram, Álvár speaks again to the learned ones that, though they might be well-read and versed in Vedas, if one speaks ill about the devotees of Bhagavān's devotees, they do not stand as learned ones; indeed, these are the lowest of all! The Vedas are considered to have six aṅgas: śikṣā (articulation or pronunciation of words), vyākaraṇa (grammar), chandhas (poetic metrics), niruktha (etymology), jyotiṣa (astrology), and kalpa. Parāśara Bhaṭṭar states in his Śrī Raṅgarāja Stavam that the Vedas with their aṅgas are speaking about none other than Śrī Raṅganātha! The ones who have studied these aṅgas and mastered them are worthy of celebration, as stated in the Purāṇas.  This celebration arises from the nature of Vedas as apauruṣeya - not created by humans. 

But Álvár provides an exception in celebrating such learned ones. If these learned ones end up speaking ill about a devotee, such people haven't learned the Vedas in their true sense. If a sense of hatred, especially towards the Bhāgavatas, arises even in those who have read the Vedas, how can they be considered learned? The Upaniṣads and Bhagavad Gītā, which are said to be the essence of the Vedas, state that devotees of īśvara are great and should be respected. Bhagavān goes to a greater extent, stating in Bhagavad Gītā 7.18: ātmaiva me matam āsthitaḥ sa hi yuktātmā mām evānuttamāṁ gatim - meaning the devotees who are ever devoted to Bhagavān and have considered him as the supreme goal, whose service to him is the supreme state, are very self of Bhagavān himself! Such jīvātmas are indeed rare. Hence, if Bhagavān has gone to such great lengths to praise his devotees and show the unbounded prema he has towards his dear devotees, how can the so-called learned ones speak ill of such great souls? Indeed, they haven't learned anything from the Vedas, which at their core speak about Bhagavān! Being a mumukṣhu is far from their sight when they do not have the maturity to look at the great devotees of Bhagavān.

meaning: When Lord Siva with his matted locks of hair in which the girl makes a stroll (i.e. flows the holy river Gangā), and the four-faced Lord Brahmā are not able to perceive your true form - even though both of them (Siva and Brahmā) took to severe austerities (penance) for innumerable aeons and aeons and so both of them become dejected, Oh Lord Ranganatha! You have run swiftly towards the great devotee, Gajendra (the lordly elephant), and protected him by showering your grace on him. Oh Lord! are you without sympathy towards me? Why is it that I do not consider You as the only succour for me?
purport:
Bhagavān is the Creator of Jagat, the creator of Brahmā and Śiva. The Mahānārāyaṇopaniṣad states: "eko ha vai nārāyaṇa āseet, na brahma, nēśāna" - meaning at the beginning, only Nārāyaṇa existed, neither Brahmā nor Īśa (Śiva) were present. Hence, without a second doubt, Nārāyaṇa is considered the Paramātma. The Vedas state this with multiple pramāṇas. At the same time, he is the final Puruṣārtha to attain Mokṣa, for all jīvātmas from Brahmā to animals. Poygai Álvár states similarly in Mudalai Thiruvandadi: "kadikkamalam thannuḷ irundhum kāṇkilān kaṇṇan adikkamalam thannai ayan" - even the lotus-born Brahmā, though born from Bhagavān's navel, is unable to see the lotus feet of Para Vasudeva (Kṛṣṇa).

The fact that Rudra provides a seat to Gaṅgā, which is the śrīpāda tīrtha of none other than Trivikrama avatāra of Bhagavān, speaks to the fact that even he is devoted to Nārāyaṇa. As the Taittirīya Upaniṣad states, "yatho vācho nivarthanthe" - words cannot describe Brahman. Brahmā performed the thiruvārdhana of Śrī Raṅganātha in Satya loka. Rudra performed penance near Chandrapuṣkaraṇi to remove the doṣa attained by removing Brahmā's 5th head. The same Śiva glorifies Śrīraṅgam and Raṅganātha while describing it to Nārada in Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa. To access you and your divine form, even such great Sarva Jñānis have to perform severe austerities. How great is your compassion that you listened to the calls of Gajendra! The elephant finally understood its helplessness and called you with all love and devotion, surrendering to your lotus feet, praying to you as Ādimūla.

Indeed, as Bhagavān states in Bhagavad Gītā 11.48: "na veda-yajñādhyayanair na dānair na cha kriyābhir na tapobhir ugraiḥ evaṁ-rūpaḥ śhakya ahaṁ nṛi-loke draṣhṭuṁ tvad anyena kuru-pravīra" - neither by performing austerities nor by reading the Vedas can anyone see his divine form.
But when questioned about what will give us his protection, especially from the tiger called Saṁsāra, Bhagavān assures in Bhagavad Gītā 18.66: "sarva-dharmān parityajya mām ekaṁ śharaṇaṁ vraja ahaṁ tvāṁ sarva-pāpebhyo mokṣhayiṣhyāmi mā śhuchaḥ" - the famous Charma śloka stating us to surrender to the divine feet of the Lord and perform all activities of Dharma for the sake of the Lord, abandoning its result. Bhagavān himself assures protection to these Prapannas. These are indeed the highest among all! Gajendra performing total surrender to Bhagavān at that moment, the Lord jumps from his seat to save his devotee without a moment's delay.

Álvár quotes two important points here: first, the surrendered ones need not fear anything when Sathya Saṅkalpa Mahā Viṣṇu has assured their protection. Secondly, when Bhagavān himself accepts the devotion of devatas as well as an elephant equally, and even aided the elephant much faster, it states that there is no sense in discriminating people. Any jīvātma which desires Bhagavān alone is worthy to be celebrated.

Completing the divine Tirumalai, Álvār surrenders this set of 45 poems to Bhagavān's lotus feet. Thoṇḍaraḍippoḍi sol – in line with his service orientation towards bhāgavathas, he has Thoṇḍaraḍippoḍi as his name. It is clear from this that his identity is not jñānam, ānandham, or bhagavat śeṣatvam [our sacred texts say that ātmā is full of jñānam (knowledge), ānandham (happiness), and is śeṣabhūthan (carrying service to Emperumān)], but bhāgavatha śeṣatvam (service to followers of Emperumān). Just as Nammālvār in his Thiruvāimozhi 7.1.11 said "thoṇḍar thoṇḍar thoṇḍar thoṇḍan Śatakōpan" (Śatakōpan, another name of Nammālvār, is Emperumān's follower's follower's follower's follower), this Álvār called himself Thoṇḍaraḍippoḍi (the dust sticking to the feet of a follower of Emperumān). By following naichyānusandhānam, Álvār states these poems to be lowly (but in reality are gold of bhakti extracted from Vedānta).

Álvār sees Namperumal smile at him with happiness, which makes him exclaim that his gibberish words have pleased Bhagavān, who defeated the elephant in his Kṛṣṇa avatāra, just as a child's words please the father.

The sun has arrived at the peak of the eastern side, dispelling the heavy darkness of the night. As the beautiful morning time has arrived, honey is oozing out of the most exquisite flowers.\
The dēvās and kings are arriving quickly in groups, pushing each other to the south side of the sannidhi (temple) where your divine vision will reach. They stand there, filling the entire place. Along with them, large groups of male and female elephants (which are the vehicles of the dēvās, kings, etc.) and persons playing musical instruments have arrived.\

purport:
The Sun (kadiravan) has arrived at the peak of Udaya Giri in the east. His rays, blazing everywhere, remove the darkness of the night. All the dēvās and kings have assembled to seek your grace as morning has arrived. The Sun is able to remove the darkness of light, but not the ignorance within us. This ignorance of ours leads us to be stuck in saṃsāra, ever captive by the things of this world. But you, the Supreme Being, by your grace alone, can destroy this ignorance. The knowledge granted by your compassion can destroy all our false assumptions. As Nammālvār states in the first paśuram of Thiruvāymōḻi, "mayarvu aṟa mati nalam aruḷiṉaṉ evaṉ avaṉ" - by His grace itself, the ignorance can be destroyed. He himself would grant us the supreme knowledge. 

Kings and dēvatās have assembled in front of you, ready to serve you and seek your grace. To grant them grace, Alvār requests Rañganātha to wake up. Bhagavān is indeed the Master of all, just as Thiruppāṇ Alvār states in his Amalanādhipirān, which directly translates to Him being the blemish-free Lord who is the ruler of dēvatās. Just as humans and animals like Gajendra seek to serve bhagavān, even the dēvatās seek to serve the Supreme Being. Pratividhi Bhayaṅkara Svāmi states in Veṅkaṭēśvara Suprabhātam: "sevāparāḥ śiva sureśa kṛśānudharma rakṣo'mbunātha pavamāna dhanādināthāḥ | baddhāñjali pravilasan nijaśīrṣa deśāḥ śrīveṅkaṭācalapate tava suprabhātam" That is, Śiva (Īśāna), Sureśa (Indra, the Lord of the Dēvās), Kṛśānu (Agni, God of Fire), Dharma (Dharmārāja or Yama), Rakṣa (Nirṛti), Ambunātha (Varuṇa, the Lord of Water), Pavamāna (God of Air), and Kubera (the Lord of Wealth)—who are themselves shining with a Divine Glow—are standing with their palms joined in devotion, asking: "Wake, Oh Lord of Veṅkaṭādri to shower grace on us!" Similarly, Alvār states that the kings and dēvatās have assembled to serve you. Wake up to shower your grace upon them! 

Flowers have been arranged here to shower upon your lotus feet, to serve you, my Lord! These flowers have blossomed in the rays of the Sun and are oozing honey from their buds. As they reach your feet, they are indeed blessed! Thoṇḍaripperumal Alvār feels just like Kulaśēkhara, who in Periya Thiruvāymōḻi wanted to be a Champaka tree on Tirumala. Elephants and drummers have assembled, playing the sounds of drums. Oh Lord of Śrīraṅgam, these sounds are like the waves of the ocean. Alvārs call Rañganātha "Karuṇā Sāgara," the ocean of compassion. Hence, to shower your compassion upon us, please wake up!

meaning: Oh Lord Rañganātha! Now the gentle morning breeze from the eastern direction blows, bringing with it the sweet fragrance of flowers from the jasmine (mullai) creepers. The swans have risen from their bed of lotus flowers, shaking off the dew drops from their wide wings. Oh, the Lord of Śrīraṅgam, You have protected the great elephant, Gajēndran, which was in distress after being caught within the massive teeth of the crocodile. Oh Lord! Please wake up and bless us!
purport:
When the Sun rises in the east, the jasmine blossoms growing on creepers intermingle their fragrance with the gentle, blowing wind. The Āḷvār poetically narrates that the wind has penetrated the inner sanctum of Śrīraṅgam, as if the very flowers are offering their prayers at the lotus feet of the Lord. In the early morning, the swans awaken with utmost diligence. The Āḷvār beautifully describes how the male swan rises, delicately removing the morning dew clinging to its wings. Tenderly, this swan then assists its mate, wiping the dew from her wings. The Āḷvār interprets this specific moment of the swan rising and spreading its wings as a herald of morning. Significantly, Bhagavān once appeared as Haṁsa, a swan, to impart divine knowledge to Brahma and Śaṅka Munis. Therefore, just as other swans stir from their slumber, our beloved swan (Raṅganātha) should also awaken. Just as the male swan removes the dew from its wings, Oh Lord, please remove the ignorance from our hearts by bestowing Your divine grace.

The Āḷvār then transitions to the profound narrative of Gajendra, the blessed elephant. A Pāṇḍya king who disregarded Sage Agastya was cursed to become an elephant. The sage, recognizing that the king's momentary lapse stemmed from his deep remembrance of Nārāyaṇa, blessed him with a profound boon: that same divine recollection would ultimately liberate him from his elephantine existence in the hills of Tirukkuṭa. This king was reborn as Gajendra. Concurrently, a Gandharva had been transformed into a crocodile, dwelling in Varuṇa's lotus-filled pond. A sage had previously decreed that the Gandharva would be released from his crocodile birth only upon seizing the leg of the devoted Gajendra. A ferocious struggle ensued for several years, with the crocodile relentlessly attempting to drag the elephant king into the watery depths, while Gajendra desperately tried to free himself from the creature's powerful jaws and sharp teeth. Drawing upon wisdom from his previous birth, Gajendra gathered lotus flowers and began to pray to the eternal protector, Śrīman Nārāyaṇa. Initially, he believed in his own physical prowess to overcome the challenge. However, when he finally realized that no one except the Supreme Lord could save him, his ego and sense of individual identity completely dissolved. At that profound moment of absolute surrender, Gajendra prepared to eulogize the Lord with the sacred verse from Srimad Bhagavatham 8.3.24: "sa vai na devāsura-martya-tiryaṅ na strī na ṣaṇḍho na pumān na jantuḥ nāyaṁ guṇaḥ karma na san na cāsan niṣedha-śeṣo jayatād aśeṣaḥ". This prayer of prapatti translates as: "You are neither deity, demon, nor mortal; neither woman, man, nor creature. You transcend all attributes, actions, and states of being. May that supreme, all-encompassing being appear to protect me!"

As soon as Bhagavān heard Gajendra's prayers, He rushed to protect him without hesitation, hurling His Sudarśana disc at the crocodile, thereby liberating Gajendra. The Āḷvār emphasizes that Gajendra ultimately realized his true spiritual state and jīvātma svarūpa. He understood that liberation and attaining the Divine is not achieved through personal efforts or bhakti yoga, but through the compassionate grace of Bhagavān itself. This profound knowledge liberated him from the cycle of saṁsāra. The Āḷvār implores that Lord of boundless compassion to awaken!

meaning:
Oh Lord of Śrīraṅgam! The Sun's lustrous rays have now pervaded all sides. The lightning-like lustre of the stars has diminished, and the bright moon has grown pale. The darkness that enveloped everything has now dispersed.
A gentle morning breeze now blows over the gardens, cleaving through the branches of areca nut trees, carrying their sweet fragrance. Oh Lord Rañganātha, holding the mighty and bright discus-weapon (cakrāyudha) on Your glorious and long hand! Please arise and bless us!
purport:
The Āḷvār declares that the night has waned, and the stars have gradually faded from the celestial canvas. The moon is losing its luminescence as the Sun ascends, and thus he implores: "Awaken, Raṅganātha!" The Sun radiates with such brilliant intensity that its rays disperse everywhere, causing the lustrous moon and stars to vanish entirely. This magnificent solar nature emerges from the presence of Nārāyaṇa within, who infuses such extraordinary radiance into the Sun. Consequently, He is revered as Āditya-Hṛdayam (the one who resides at the heart of Āditya). Raṅganātha bears a profound connection to the illustrious Ikṣvāku dynasty, the Solar clan. When Brahmā presented Vivasvān with the archa mūrti of Raṅga, the twelve Ādityas worshipped Him, as proclaimed in the Ṛg Veda: "dhyeyaḥ sadā savṛtr-maṇḍala-madhya-varti nārāyaṇaḥ sarasijāsana-sanniveśitaḥ" - signifying that Nārāyaṇa eternally resides at the very center of the Solar mandala. Therefore, as the Sun ascends, Oh Raṅganātha - worshipped by the solar deity himself - please awaken! Rise to reveal a radiance unparalleled, as the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (1.9.67) declares: "tejasām rāśim ūrjitam" - His effulgence glows incomparably. Just as the Sun dispels darkness, similar to how Asuras flee from Your Sudarśana Chakra in its ready-to-launch position, illuminate our world with Your divine presence. 

The lotuses have blossomed, and the fragrance of the areca nut tree has intermingled with the gentle morning breeze. This exquisite aroma heralds the arrival of dawn. The Āḷvār beckons Raṅganātha to awaken to these fragrances and deploy His Chakra to defend all deities and devotees assembled before Him. The Āḷvār's emphasis on Raṅganātha's prayoga chakra subtly entreats the Lord for comprehensive protection and grace upon all bhāgavatas. Moreover, it represents a profound request to dispel our ignorance and bestow divine wisdom.

Please awaken from your divine slumber and bless us!
purport:
Cattle gather enchantingly at the melodious call of the cowherd's flute. The commentator Periyavāccān Piḷḷai delightfully highlights the Āḷvār's subtle sense of humor. In the Purāṇas, humans are considered superior in intelligence compared to beings like cattle, as stated in the Narasiṁha Purāṇa (16.13): "āhāra nidrā bhaya maithunāni tulyāni kalvatra samasta-jantoḥ, jñānāt viśiṣṭo hi naraḥ parebhyo jñānena hīnaḥ paśubhiḥ samānaḥ" - suggesting that while eating, sleeping, fear, and procreation are common across all creatures, humans are distinguished by their capacity for higher knowledge, and those devoid of such wisdom are equivalent to animals. The Āḷvār provocatively notes that even the cattle have awakened, yet You - the Supreme Being proclaimed as Brahman by the Vedas - continue to slumber. Awaken, Raṅganātha! 

Next, the Āḷvār experiences the mūla mūrti (primary form) of Raṅganātha as Kṛṣṇa, and the utsava mūrti, Namperumāḷ, as Rāma. He contemplates  Rāma's vīra-tattva (heroic essence) during the protection of Viśvāmitra's yajña. Viśvāmitra's sacred ritual was being disrupted by rākṣasas and asuras like Mārīci, Tāḍakā, and others. Thus, he requested Daśaratha to send Rāma to defend the yajña. Though Viśvāmitra was himself capable of protecting the ritual, and Daśaratha equally powerful, the sage's deeper desire was to facilitate the meeting of Rāma and Sītā, ultimately leading to their divine marriage while simultaneously revealing Rāma's heroic nature. Rāma, wielding his legendary kōdaṇḍa bow, decimated these asuras with such extraordinary might that when he directed an arrow at Mārīci-son of Tāḍakā - the rākṣasa was hurled multiple times across the ocean. Eventually, Mārīci was compelled to recognize Rāma's divine supremacy. Such was the magnificent power of our great Lord! He who destroys enemies called asuras (and ignorance), he who ruled Ayodhya, remains asleep while the cows have awakened. Rāma ruled for a millennium, while You - existing beyond time - have been, are, and will be eternally present to bless us. Therefore, Raṅganātha, awaken!

amarargaḻ pugundanar ādalil ammā

emberumān ! paḻḻi ezundaruḻāyē
meaning: Oh Lord! The birds in the flower garden have awakened. The night has passed away, and the morning has arrived. The sounds of ocean waves are emerging from the east. The celestials have arrived with beautiful garlands made of manifold flowers, humming with honey bees, ready to offer them at Thy holy feet. Therefore, my Master, Oh Lord of the temple where the ruler of Laṅkā (Vibhīṣaṇa) worships Thee! Wake up from Thy divine slumber and bless us!
purport:
The melodious chirping of birds heralds the morning, signaling the sacred time to serve the Lord. Night induces the tāmasic guṇa, compelling us into slumber, whereas the morning sun bestows sāttvika guṇa, making brahma muhūrta the most auspicious moment for divine worship. Śrīraṅgam is renowned for its ethereal natural beauty. Gardens brim with blossoming flowers, while bees voraciously drink their nectar. These bees' melodious hum seems to chant "Raṅga! Raṅga!" and the peacocks dance in sublime rhythm. The Āḷvār poignantly asks: "Despite all these vibrant activities and sounds, why do You still slumber, Oh Raṅga?"

The ocean's waves crash thunderously, creating a mysterious backdrop. One might wonder why the Āḷvār speaks of the ocean when Raṅganātha resides near the Kāvēri River. Periyavāccān Piḷḷai provides a profound interpretation. From across the ocean, from Laṅkā, came Vibhīṣaṇa - the very being who transported Raṅganātha from Ayodhyā to Śrīraṅgam. Facing eastward, it appears as though Raṅganātha awaits Vibhīṣaṇa's arrival. Thus, the Āḷvār provocatively questions: "Until Vibhīṣaṇa comes to awaken You, will You not rise?" Nañjīyar provides a complementary commentary. Vibhīṣaṇa, born as Rāvaṇa's younger brother - the same Rāvaṇa whose lustful gaze fell upon Sītā - was nonetheless wholly accepted by Rāma. Despite his lineage, Vibhīṣaṇa possessed profound bhakti towards Nārāyaṇa, ultimately surrendering to Rāma for divine protection.
Rāma, our Raṅganātha, embodying the Prapanna Parijāta (wish-fulfilling divine tree for those who surrender), embraced Vibhīṣaṇa's śaraṇāgati (complete surrender) and offered him unequivocal protection. The Āḷvār's rhetorical question resonates: "With celestial deities standing before You, are You, out of compassion for prapannas, waiting specifically for Vibhīṣaṇa?"

araṅgattammā ! paḻḻi ezundaruḻāyē
meaning: Oh Lord of Śrīraṅgam! The following dēvās have assembled near the gates of Your holy shrine, which resembles a great mountain, to receive Your first and foremost merciful and matchless glances: Here are the twelve Ādityas with their lofty chariots bedecked with jewels; the eleven Rudras riding their bulls, who rule over the worlds; the six-faced Subrahmaṇya riding the peacock; the Maruts and the eight Vasus. They have all arrived with their retinues, singing and dancing, accompanied by their horses and chariots. Oh Lord! Please awaken from Your divine slumber and bless us all!
purport:
This pāsuram bears striking similarities to the first pāsuram and Veṅkateśvara Suprabhātam. All the devatās seeking Bhagavān's protection have assembled before Raṅganātha. The Āḷvārs reference the Ekādaśa Rudras as controllers of mortal beings. The Yajur Saṁhitā (6.2.8) elucidates how these Rudras obtained their power to control mortals: "sa abravīt varam vṛṇa aham eva | paśūnām adhipatiḥ asāṇīti tasmāt rudraḥ paśūnām adhipatiḥ ||" - essentially praying to become the leader of saṁsāris (worldly beings) who are likened to paśus (animals). 

Even these Rudras have arrived, riding their bulls, to serve the Lord. The twelve Ādityas have also assembled to offer their reverence. These Ādityas symbolically represent the twelve months of the cosmic cycle. The Āḷvār emphasizes that celestial deities seeking protection and bhāgavatas yearning for divine grace and kaiṅkarya (sacred service) have congregated to serve the Lord. "Awaken, Raṅganātha, and accept our service!" The Āḷvār invokes the concept of kumāra-dhaṇḍa, which carries two profound interpretations: First, Śanmukha (Kārttikeya), the son of Rudra, has assembled here. Second, these deities stand like dhaṇḍa (thick sticks), representing their unwavering devotion. The term kumāra often signifies youthfulness, suggesting these devatās - eternally young - stand densely packed, eagerly awaiting divine blessings. To these devatās and prapannas, the Āḷvār implores: "Oh Raṅganātha, awaken! Rise to accept our sacred service!"

meaning: Oh Lord of Śrīraṅgam! Many deities have arrived with magnificent treasures, offering them reverentially to receive Your benevolent glances. They have brought the vāyurai (arugam grass); the sacred cow Kapilā; mirrors and other sacred implements like padimakkalam for Your morning ārādhana. The illustrious sages, Tumburu and Nārada, have descended to glorify You with their divine vīṇās. Dawn has already broken, with the radiant Sun ascending and dispersing his luminous rays across the celestial expanse. Darkness has retreated, even from the ethereal realms. Oh Lord of Śrīraṅgam! Awaken and bestow Your divine blessings upon us!
purport:
As the Sun has ascended, its radiant rays have illuminated everywhere, dispelling the darkness bestowed by night. This luminescence extends not only to the human realm but to the celestial domains of the devatās as well. This profound imagery suggests that Bhagavān removes ignorance not just for humanity, but for the exalted celestial beings praised across countless traditions. To shower divine grace upon all the assembled beings, the Āḷvār implores: "Awaken, Raṅganātha!"

The Āḷvār beautifully explicates the sacred process of awakening Raṅganātha in Śrīraṅgam. The devatās and yogis assembled before Him have brought auspicious objects to present upon His awakening. According to Āgamas like the Pāñcarātra's Parameśvara Saṁhitā, specific objects must be ceremonially presented: mirrors, vessels containing milk, and collyrium (the sacred black substance used to adorn divine eyelids). Accompanying these ritual objects, an elephant and a cow with its calf are brought before the sanctum, for His beloved consort Mahālakṣmī is believed to reside within these sacred animals. These objects originated during the Kṣīra Manthana (churning of the cosmic ocean) and were subsequently gifted to the devatās. The profound theological principle dictates that before these sacred objects are enjoyed by devatās or humans, they must first be reverentially offered to the Supreme Being.

The archakas of Śrīraṅgam, meticulously adhering to ancient Āgamic traditions, simultaneously bring waters from the river Kāvēri. In the morning light, the river shimmers magnificently, reflecting the Sun's rays like liquid gold. These consecrated waters are gathered for Raṅganātha's daily ritual ablutions. Divine music becomes the final element of this sacred awakening. Tumburu and Nārada have assembled to play their vīṇās and tambūris, creating a melodious invocation. Sama Gāna, the most sublime of musical offerings, is especially beloved by Bhagavān. "Oh Raṅga," the Āḷvār entreats, "Awaken and bless us!"

purport:
Alvār concludes waking up Rañganātha by asking him to provide bhāgavata kaiṅkaryam. The sun has grown away from the ocean to the sky and magnificently shining. Ladies following their daily routine and rituals, having bathed in Kāveri and are returning home to dry their clothes. Adorning fresh garments, they are preparing themselves to serve you.

Alvār says to Bhagavān that, with great compassion he has accepted him as his devotee and now requests him to grant him to serve his devotees. This pattern is well observed in Divya Prabandham and every grantha-stotra-prabandham written by any Śrī Vaiṣṇava ācārya. The concepts of bhāgavata śeṣattvam, i.e., the acceptance to serve the devotees of the Lord with great respect, is the character of a prapanna. Hence Alvār, who was originally called Vipranarayana, has the name Toṇḍaraṭṭupuṭi, which literally translates to "the one who holds the dust emerged out of the feet of the devotees on his forehead." Rāmānujācārya in his Śrīraṅga Gadhyam repeats the same as "prītikāritāśēṣāvasthōcitāśēṣaśēṣataikaratirūpa nityakaiṅkarya prāptyupāyabhūtabhakti" where the Ācārya asks Namperumāḷ seated along with Rañganāyaki Nācchiyār to bless him the opportunity to serve their devotees. Hence Alvār calls himself Toṇḍaraṭṭupuṭi, who is holding the garland of Tulasī ready to be worn by Rañganātha, who is raising his head up from Ananta!

mārgazi ttiṅgaḻ madi niṟainda nannāḻāl
nīrāḍa ppōduvīr pōduminō nēr izaiyīr
śīr malgum āyppāḍi ccelva cciṟumīrgāḻ
kūr vēl koḍun tozilan nandagōban kumaran
ērārnda kaṇṇi yaśōdai iḻam śiṅgam
kārmēni cceṅgaṇ kadirmadiyam pōl mugattān
nārāyaṇanē namakkē paṟai taruvān
pārōr pugaza ppaḍindēlōr em pāvāy
meaning:
Now has arrived the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. The days are auspicious and the nights are filled with moonlight. You, the beautiful young women, enjoying all the comforts of the prosperous village Vrepalle and wearing strange and attractive ornaments! Listen, all those who wish to participate in the morning bath, join us and move ahead. Kṛṣṇa is the son of Nandagopa, who in his solicitude for his son, ever keeps alert, with his sharp Velāyudha always poised, to punish severely those who intend harm to him.

Kṛṣṇa is the beloved lion-cub of Yaśodā who contemplates him with her large beaming eyes; Kṛṣṇa with his body shining with the colour of a dark cloud, with his eyes bright as red lotus-petals, with his divine face radiating the mingled beams of the bright sun and the mellow moon,—this Kṛṣṇa is no other than Nārāyaṇa Himself. He is ready to give, only to us (people who never seek anything from any but him) what we badly need, namely, the instrument "parai" which is required for the fulfilment of this ritual. Therefore, join us in all your numbers in this ceremonial rite and make the world of onlookers happy.
purport:
The Mārgaśīrṣa month is considered to be very auspicious as per the śāstras. Kṛṣṇa declares in Bhagavad Gītā 10.35 "māsānāṃ mārgaśīrṣo 'ham" that among the months of the year, He is Mārgaśīrṣa. Often, the star which appears on the full moon day of that month defines the name of the month. Just as the star Citrā appears on full moon day and the month becomes Caitra, similarly Mārgaśīrṣa month is presided over by Mṛgaśīrṣa star on the full moon day. These twelve stars are visualized as an antelope, and the star on its head is called Mṛgaśīrṣa. This month is also considered as the time of Brāhma-muhūrta for devatās, as a human year is a day for them.

Āṇḍāḷ says let's start this nombu on this auspicious month and on a full moon day. This month is also compared to the lotus of the Lord because it is soft, cold, and warm. She calls the day to be auspicious as she and those who desire Kṛṣṇa alone have assembled to perform the nombu. She calls upon everyone who resides in and desires to reach Kṛṣṇa. He is dark as a cloud and she refers to Him as the son of Nanda Gopa. Gopa, who used to be very delicate while walking before Kṛṣṇa being his son, now always holds a spear which used to defeat all those who try to harm Kṛṣṇa. That's the fatherly love he had towards Bhagavān. The reference to Him being called a young lion cub is more of Āṇḍāḷ's desire to marry Him as her age is similar to His.

The core essence of this pāsuram comes from the sentence "nārāyaṇanē namakkē paṟai taruvān". Externally, the inference is she is asking Kṛṣṇa, who is none other than Nārāyaṇa, to provide the musical instrument used in this ritual. But the inner meaning of paṟai refers to kaiṅkaryam. Āṇḍāḷ refers that it's not by her efforts she is going to attain Kṛṣṇa and serve Him, but Nārāyaṇa Himself will give the grace to attain Him and serve Him. This is the core essence of prapatti. Hence she calls all to assemble to celebrate the divine attributes of Nārāyaṇa.

english_scripts:
vaiyattu vāzvīrgāḻ ! nāmum nam pāvaikku
śeyyum kiriśaigaḻ kēḻīrō
pāṟkaḍaluḻ paiya ttuyinṟa paraman aḍi pāḍi
ney uṇṇōm pāl uṇṇōm nāṭkālē nīr āḍi
maiyiṭṭezudōm malariṭṭu nām muḍiyōm
śeyyādana śeyyōm tīkkuṟaḻai śenṟōdōm
aiyamum piccaiyum āndanaiyum kai kāṭṭi
uyyumāṟeṇṇi ugandēlōr em pāvāy
meaning: All, who though born in this world of sorrow, yet enjoy bliss as contemporaries of Kṛṣṇa, listen to the manner of our performing this ritual. We shall gently sing benediction to the feet of the Supreme Person, who has been resting quietly on the Kṣīra Sāgara (sea of milk). During the period of this ritual, we shall take our bath before dawn. We shall not partake of milk or ghee. We shall not adorn our eyes with collyrium nor shall we deck our hair with flowers. We shall avoid actions not sanctioned by our elders; nor shall we ever utter anywhere falsehoods or words that might hurt others. We shall honor the wise with liberal gifts of grain and money. We shall bestow charity on the brahmacārīs (celibates) and the sannyāsīs (ascetics). We shall always reflect upon the way of higher life. May you witness this and feel happy!
purport:
After calling all the gopīs to perform the nombu, Āṇḍāḷ speaks to them saying that we are fortunate to live in this divine place, much glorified compared to Śrī Vaikuṇṭha itself! "Vaiyattu vāzvīrgā" here refers to this essence. Why is Āṇḍāḷ saying this? Compared to the Supreme Abode, we can enjoy the infinite divine and auspicious qualities of Bhagavān here, in the Līlā Vibhūti. The Nitya Vibhūti, i.e., Śrī Vaikuṇṭha, is ever-shining as there is no scent of karma or vāsanā there. Though Bhagavān has so many auspicious qualities, they cannot be expressed fully in the Supreme Abode compared to the Līlā Vibhūti, i.e., the universe. The comparison can be given as: the importance of light and its beauty can be experienced to its fullest when it is brought to a place which is dark. Bhagavān, who is called parama jyoti by Nārāyaṇa Sūktam of Taittirīya, His divine qualities can be experienced beautifully and their importance known well here in this Līlā Vibhūti where we are stuck in the cycle of saṃsāra by ignorance, which is darkness personified.

She again refers to "mamum nam pavaiku," which refers to the same essence that we, who have left all desires and only want Kṛṣṇa, have come here to participate in this nombu. Āṇḍāḷ refers to Kṛṣṇa as Kṣīrābdhi-nātha. The reference here is of the Kṣīra Sāgara, which is as large and plentiful as His divine qualities which are supreme and incomparable, hence she calls them param. Also, the sleeping posture of Nārāyaṇa is always seen to be much more beautiful compared to others. Viśvāmitra, seeing Rāma in yoga-nidrā, is so mesmerized and sings to awaken Him. Sītā too is mesmerized by Rāma who is laying on her lap. Āṇḍāḷ, remembering Raṅganātha, who is none other than Kṛṣṇa, is mesmerized. Though He remains in this yogic posture, He is always alert to protect the surrendered ones. Then she, with the participants of the nombu, decides to follow certain disciplined rituals for the nombu.

She states to avoid eating milk and ghee. By remaining immersed in devotion and love towards beloved Kṛṣṇa, she is not ready to partake of food like milk and butter which are considered royal, rich, and 'elixir on earth'. After enjoying and in the process of enjoying the divine elixir called Kṛṣṇa-prema, how can these worldly things sound fitting to the mind? Leaving these, she also calls upon them to take bath early in the morning. Referring to this, the pain of separation always triggers heat. To cool down the body, often devotees take early bath. Bharata, separated from Rāma, used to take morning baths. This is an expression of pain of separation towards Kṛṣṇa by Āṇḍāḷ and all who have joined her group.

Next, she repeats to give up adorning collyrium for her eyes and she states to not wear flowers. In the pain of separation, the wife doesn't desire to decorate herself. All she waits for is her husband to return. Āṇḍāḷ here says the same, that Kṛṣṇa Himself has to provide the collyrium and flowers to them. The inner meaning of what Āṇḍāḷ tries to infer here is: collyrium which decorates the eye and makes it look bright refers to jñāna, and the flowers which are pleasurable to look at, smell, and wear, which shows bhoga, represents bhakti. Āṇḍāḷ repeats the same - she doesn't want to use jñāna yoga and bhakti yoga to attain Bhagavān. He Himself is the means and He Himself will make them attain Him. If He desires to bestow knowledge and devotion to the prapanna, i.e., those who have helplessly and totally surrendered to Him without any expectation, then she is ready to accept it.

Āṇḍāḷ further continues by referring to "śeyyādana śeyyōm" where she tries to emphasize following the regulations laid down by Ācārya Puruṣas. Vedas sometimes provide certain flexibility in ways to lead life, such as kṣatriyas having the eligibility to hunt. Though such flexibility is given, they are said to be optional, and Ācāryas recommend highly to avoid them. In our example, though kings were allowed to hunt, often these ended up in bad outcomes and mostly became the causes of death in the long term. Daśaratha, Pāṇḍu, Parīkṣit are some examples of this reasoning. Hence, Āṇḍāḷ states even if Vedas provide that optional flexibility, we still follow the Ācāryas and won't perform such activity. This is the same stated by Bhagavān in Gītā 4.34 - "tad viddhi praṇipātena paripraśnena sevayā | upadekṣyanti te jñānaṃ jñāninas tattva-darśinaḥ", i.e., Bhagavān tells Arjuna to gain this knowledge from Ācāryas who have the knowledge about Brahman. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad states the same in Śikṣā Vallī 1.11.4 - "atha yadi te karmavicikitsā vā vṛttavicikitsā vā syāt . ye tatra brāhmaṇāḥ saṃmarśinaḥ . yuktā āyuktāḥ . alūkṣā dharmakāmāḥ syuḥ . yathā te tatra varteran tathā tatra vartethāḥ", i.e., it states "If there should arise any doubt regarding your acts, or any uncertainty in respect of your conduct in life, you should act in those matters exactly as those Brāhmaṇas who are present there, who are thoughtful, religious (experienced), not set on by others, not cruel (i.e., gentle) and are devoted to Dharma." Hence following the directions of Ācārya, she is performing the nombu. She says she will donate to the needy and the Brāhmaṇas until they are satisfied (and feel sorry to give no more). It also infers that she is donating the knowledge about the kalyāṇa guṇas of Bhagavān to the people who are ready to ask. Āṇḍāḻ expressed her pain of sepearation and intends to perform nombu for the quickness to attain.

meaning: As we chant the sacred name of the Supreme Person, Trivikrama (who, upon receiving the gift from Emperor Bali, grew in stature up to the sky and measured the three worlds with His feet) and take our bath under the auspices of this ritual, may the world be refreshed with three good showers a month and be free from all physical ills and feel happy! While the paddy plants shoot up to the sky and fish leap about in the waters of the corn-fields, and the charming bees slumber in lotus flowers, may the land smile with rich harvests! May the cattle sheds abound with cows whose udders, on a mere touch of the steady milkman (gopāla), release potfuls of milk! May the whole land be filled with prosperity that never wanes nor comes to an end! May the whole land ever flow with milk and honey!
purport:
Contuning to praise Bhagavan, Andal now praises hsi Vibhava rupa as Vamana and Trivikrama.  When aditi the mother of Indra was in grief that her son has lost his postion. She prays to Narayana who bestwos her to be his mother and hence he is born as Upendra or Vamana. Bail who defeated Indra and had conqured the three world was noble by nature. At the same time he belonged to the linague of Prahalada who had the boon from Narasimha that his generations will never be destoyed by Lord. But Bail had ego that all these were his possesion and his efforts lead to the gains. He had fail to relaises that it was bestwoed by someone who own all the worlds. Unable to bare the pain of his devotee, Aditi, Lord who rests on Ksheera sagar jumps up and takes the form of Trivikrama assuring protection. He decides to beg the worlds from Bali as a drawf. Drawfness and begging aren't something desired by people. But when Vishnu takes these, it becomes something beautifu and noble. such is the nature of Lord. The litreall assoctaion with him leads to gain in Sattvic nature. When we take birth, we are born with sorrow and Samsric attachment. But Bhagavan on the other hand is born with his own will and his yoga maya. His compassion is so great for the sake of devotees he is ready to beg, wash the feets of horses though he is the supreme being. Vamana seeks for 3 foot of land even when insted he persists to ask for the 3 foot of Land. The 3 foot of land repsents 3 aspects which Krishna states to arjuna to surrenders; Offer to Bhagavan whatever we do and whatever we eat; Consecrate to Bhagavan whatever we sacrifice in the sacred fire and whatever we gift in charity; Dedicate to Bhagavan all the austerities and penances. By doing these three we will be devoid of ego and accpte He as the means to attain him. The essence here is that the jiavatma has to relaise that it is not the Bhoktha or the Kratha but Bhagavan alone is as antaryami. When Bali is betwosed the lands, Lord removed his ego and granted him the knowldge of surrendce. The same Vama was born to Aditi when she was Kausalya as Rama, born as Krishna when she was Devaki. The Vishnu Suktam glorifies this form of Trivikrama. Singing the names of Bhagavan who protect the enitire univers Trivrikaram bestown libreation itself!

Andal says we perform this nombu for the happiness of the whole world. She feels for all those who are unabelt o perform the nombu and hence says she perform for the bliss of the word not for herself. The ritual of the gopikās is described as bringing prosperity to the land in multiple ways. She explains how their worship ensures three showers of rain every month, making the fields abundant with tall paddy crops where fish leap about. The imagery extends to bees sleeping in lotus flowers and cows yielding endless pots of milk, symbolizing the material abundance that flows from proper devotion. This prosperity is described as being permanent and extending beyond their immediate region to benefit the entire world, similar to how during Śrī Rāma's reign, all people experienced happiness (hṛṣṭam), contentment (tuṣṭam), and freedom from disease (ārogam) and fear (bhayam).

The deeper spiritual significance of these images is then elaborated. The three showers of rain represent three kinds of spiritual knowledge: ananyaśeṣatvam (belonging solely to the Supreme), ananyaśaraṇatvam (taking refuge in none but the Supreme), and ananyabhogyatvam (finding relish only in being enjoyed by the Lord). The paddy fields filled with water represent consciousness filled with thoughts of God, while the fish jumping in the water symbolize sages reveling in divine consciousness. The lotus flowers represent the hearts of sages where Śrīmannārāyaṇa resides with Lakṣmī.

Andal explains the significance of milk abundance as representing spiritual knowledge flowing from preceptors (Ācāryas) to disciples. The cows represent the Ācāryas who, like the cows nourished by Kṛṣṇa's touch and flute music, are sustained by divine grace and God-consciousness. The four teats of the cows correspond to four reasons why preceptors bestow knowledge: divine ordinance, answering disciples' prayers, compassion for suffering souls, and their natural inability to contain wisdom. This Ācārya sampada (abundance of spiritual teachers) is described as being inexhaustible and constantly available for the benefit of all seekers.
