meaning: Oh Parjanya, the majestic celestial being presiding over rain! Do not diminish your customary liberality in giving. Plunge deep into the midst of the majestic ocean, drink all its waters to the full, rise with a roar and spread yourself across the sky, with your dark form resembling the divine image of Śrīman Nārāyaṇa, who is the Cause of the whole universe. Flash forth in lightning, like the Sudarśana-cakra held in the handsome right hand of the lotus-naveled (Padmanābha), broad-shouldered Lord; startle the world with thunder, resembling that which emanates from the Pāñcajanya śaṅkha in His left hand; shoot forth showers, like the arrows that rain from His bow (Śārṅga), in such abundance and continuity that the whole world feels refreshed; and that we feel happy to have our bath in Mārgaśīrṣa.
purport:
Āṇḍāḷ gives the comparison of Varuṇa, who bestows rain, to the Ācāryas who bestow knowledge of the Supreme like the rain. By the blessing of Kṛṣṇa (referred here as Kaṇṇa), the clouds shower rain. By stating "onṟu nī kai karavēl," Āṇḍāḷ requests the clouds to shower rain without holding back. When such rain is experienced, it brings flourishment to the land and hence brings prosperity to us. This is similar to the preceptor or the Ācārya. When the knowledge about the divine attributes of the Lord is being showered upon us by the preceptor, she requests to do so without holding back, hence the disciples can experience Bhagavān with full bliss as per their capacity. Bhagavān has assigned different tasks to different devatās who oversee specific elements or tasks: Yama for death, Agni for heat and burning, and several others. But Varuṇa, on the other hand, unless provoked, is large-hearted. He bestows rain everywhere with large-heartedness. Similarly, Ācārya is large-hearted; irrespective of good or bad, he bestows the knowledge of Nārāyaṇa.

Āṇḍāḷ calls the clouds and says "āzi uḻ" which refers to her saying the clouds to go to the mid-sea and drain the salt water, later to be rained as sweet rain. The clouds follow the cycle of nature to drain the water from the salty sea to be showered upon as beautiful rain. The Ācāryas are similar too. The Vedas are like the ocean, magnanimous in nature and difficult to be understood even by the intelligent ones, hence similar to the salty water. The Ācāryas are clouds which extract the required Vedānta from the Vedas which speaks about the Brahma-tattvam and shower the knowledge upon the disciple, hence converting the hard and difficult to understand Vedas to sweet teachings. The specific need to go to the sea, not to reservoirs like ponds or lakes, indicates from where the knowledge has to be extracted by the Ācārya. Vedas are the most authoritative as they are called apauruṣeya. But these are huge and contain all knowledge similar to an encyclopedia. But for a surrendered ātmā, it only requires the knowledge about Brahman which is hidden in corners of Vedānta. Bhagavad Gītā 2.46 states "yāvān artha udapāne sarvataḥ samplutodake | tāvān sarveṣu vedeṣu brāhmaṇasya vijānataḥ" i.e., a thirsty man will only take what is required from the reservoir; he won't drink the entire water body. Similarly, the one who desires to know Brahman (Brāhmaṇa), only fetches the knowledge about the Brahman from the Vedas which provide all kinds of rituals to attain spiritual and materialistic desires. The Ācārya has to fetch this knowledge alone and shower upon us.

Next, Āṇḍāḷ requests the clouds to turn like the color of the all-controller Nārāyaṇa and shower rain upon us with lightning like the Sudarśana-cakra! The simile which she brings here itself is beautiful as it describes the divine divya-maṅgala-rūpa of Nārāyaṇa. The Vedas like Nārāyaṇa Sūktam state that the inner soul of all, Śrīman Nārāyaṇa, has the divine color of kṛṣṇa-piṅgala which is similar to dark grey of clouds with a mix of sapphire dark blue and emerald green (ṛtaṃ satyam paraṃ brahma puruṣaṃ kṛṣṇapiṅgalam). Āṇḍāḷ now calls upon the clouds to turn into the color of that Brahma-tattvam and shower rain upon us. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad 5.8.1 states "brahmopāpnavānīti" i.e., attains and becomes like the Brahman (Sarūpya Mokṣa) to the one who performs the upāsana of the Praṇava mantra. When an Ācārya is immersed in such knowledge, he too experiences this and overflows with knowledge and bhakti. Like the Supreme's dark color which represents coolness, he too provides knowledge about Bhagavān with whole-hearted coolness. Sages who have such identity are fit to preach about Bhagavān.

She further expresses that the rain should show lightning like the Sudarśana-cakra of Bhagavān. The auspicious disc which dispels all ignorance and darkness, that which represents time, that which represents the Saṅkalpa Śakti (will-power) of the Supreme Controller is called as the Sudarśana. Viṣṇu, the all-preserver with His broad beautiful shoulders, protects one and all! His disc glows with such great effulgence even though He is still. Similarly, Ācāryas might be immersed in bhakti towards Nārāyaṇa and remain still, but their effulgence through their knowledge (Jñāna Śakti) and activities performed as per śāstras which please Kṛṣṇa (Kriyā Śakti) glow like the disc. It too provides protection to all the disciples who are stuck in the ignorance of this saṃsāra.

Āṇḍāḷ further elaborates that the cloud also needs to thunder loud and clear, saying "valamburi pōl ninṟadirndu." The comparison she gives for the sound is that of the divine Pāñcajanya conch of Bhagavān. The gopīs keep the divine conch dear to them. Unlike the disc which leaves the divine hands of the Lord for performing duties of killing demons and asuras, the conch, on the other hand, always stays with Nārāyaṇa, and in fact, the sound it vibrates is when it associates itself with the divine mouth of the Supreme. The sound itself is enough to destroy enemies with fear. Just like the sound of the conch which symbolizes the sacred Praṇava, the Ācārya too opens his divine mouth to chant Praṇava and then showers the knowledge of the divine attributes of the Lord. She calls upon the clouds to shower rain in such an unstoppable manner similar to the Śārṅga bow of Viṣṇu. Until the enemy falls defeated, the bow keeps striking arrows, such is its power. The Ācārya who is immersed and is overflowing with divine knowledge about the attributes of Bhagavān, like a cow which showers milk when its udders are filled to unbearable extent, he too showers grace and knowledge upon us like the arrows of Śārṅga. May the rains shower to their full extent and make all the elders and gopīs happy. Seeing their happiness without envy, we rejoice as our Ācāryas have showered grace upon us to gain this divine knowledge.

meaning: Bhagavān Śrī Kṛṣṇa's miraculous deeds evoke reverent wonder everywhere. He is the outstanding Leader of Northern Mathurā, which is ever closely associated with godliness. The ferry of the pure and deep waters of the Yamunā, being His favorite haunt, has become His distinguishing mark of identification. He is the auspicious radiating light of the gopa family; and eager to bring effulgence to Yaśodā's womb, He has allowed Himself to be bound by her and thus has become Dāmodara. Let us purify ourselves as we approach Him; let us worship Him with fresh flowers; let us join our hands in reverence; let us sing His praises; and let us, with all our hearts, meditate on Him. Should we do so, all our accumulated sins of the past and the entire pile of sins which is to accrue to us in the future will be burnt to ashes like cotton in fire. Let us therefore join in glorifying His name.
purport:
Āṇḍāḷ now starts beautifully describing the divine līlās and attributes of the beloved Lord. She calls Him as the one who has the power of māyā and hence, using it, was born in Mathurā as its Lord. Kṛṣṇa, who appears as a cowherd of Gokula, is indeed the Supreme, unimaginable Brahman. The Taittirīya describes Him as unimaginable by the mind, and the mouth cannot sing all His glories! He is beyond the capacity to be perceived. Even though He is inaccessible, He is very accessible to His devotees. To Devakī and Vasudeva, He was born as Kṛṣṇa. Unlike us who are born out of karma and vāsanās, Bhagavān incarnates with His own will and through His yogamāyā He takes incarnation. Kṛṣṇa Himself states this to Arjuna in Bhagavad Gītā 4.6 as "ajo 'pi sannavyayātmā bhūtānām īśvaro 'pi san | prakṛtiṁ svām adhiṣṭhāya sambhavāmyātma-māyayā" - i.e., though He is imperishable, unborn, He appears through His divine power of yogamāyā. When He appeared to Devakī and Vasudeva, Śrīmad Bhāgavatam 10.3.9 glorifies His divine form as: "tam adbhutaṁ bālakam ambujekṣaṇaṁ catur-bhujaṁ śaṅkha-gadādy-udāyudham śrīvatsa-lakṣmaṁ gala-śobhi-kaustubhaṁ pītāmbaraṁ sāndra-payoda-saubhagam" - i.e., He was born with divine attributes of the Supreme: disc, conch, mace, Śrīvatsa mark and the auspicious jewel Kaustubha. This speaks about how accessible He is to His dear devotees, which is termed as saulabhyam.

Āṇḍāḷ calls Him as "vaḍamadurai maindanai" - i.e., the Lord of the Northern Mathurā (specifically calls northern as the famous city called Madurai in Tamil Nadu is the Tamil term for the Sanskrit word Mathurā). This divine city always has association with Bhagavān. The appearance of Vāmana or the rule of Śatrughna with the divine worship of Lord Varāha is always associated with Mathurā. She calls Kṛṣṇa as the Lord of Mathurā due to His courageous activities which left everyone stunned and mesmerized. She continues to sing Kṛṣṇa's glory, calling Him "tūya perunīr yamunai ttuṟaivanai". Kṛṣṇa spent most of His childhood at the banks of Yamunā. The river Yamunā is glorified to be equivalent to the river Virajā, and Mathurā being the goal to attain like Vaikuṇṭha. The river always had association with Kṛṣṇa. He used to play with gopīs in the river, perform līlās too. When Vasudeva carried Kṛṣṇa, Yamunā reduced the level of water so that Bhagavān could reach without any obstacles. Similarly, if we provide a seat to Kṛṣṇa in our hearts, we too can cross the ocean called saṃsāra.

Next, she describes the Dāmodara līlā in the same pāsuram. She describes the one who is called as māyā, the Īśvara, the ruler of universe, comes down as son of Yaśodā. He who liberates jīvātmā from knots of saṃsāra is tied by Yaśodā as Dāmodara. This shows the saulabhyam guṇa of Bhagavān that to His devotees, He Himself will serve them and listen to them. By remembering Śrīman Nārāyaṇa as Dāmodara, one is liberated from all sins. Gopīs move forward remembering Kṛṣṇa, that there is no ultimate motive other than attaining Kṛṣṇa and serving Him. By doing so, they are sure Kṛṣṇa would be unable to bear their strain and at least then He would fly to reach them, thereby burning their sins. The purpose to meditate upon Kṛṣṇa is not liberation, which is secondary, but to attain Him and serve Him alone. As one meditates upon Kṛṣṇa, involuntarily the sañcita karma of that jīvātmā burns down like cotton on fire. Hence, Āṇḍāḷ calls upon gopīs to assemble and shed their sins to start this vrata by remembering Kṛṣṇa.

meaning: The birds have risen from their nests and they make noisesas they poise for flight in search of food. From the temple of Viṣṇu, who is the Lord of their master Garuḍa, emerges the loud booming sound of the white conch summoning the devotees to worship. Haven't you, O girl, heard that sound? You might wonder how we have got up and who has awakened us. The munis and yogis have securely installed in their hearts the Lord who, as child Kṛṣṇa, has sucked poison from the breasts of Pūtanā (and her life with it), and who, crying for a feed, has stretched his leg, and with one kick smashed to smithereens the cart, whose shape was assumed by a demon with intent to kill him. They have their minds occupied with the Lord, the Creator of the universe, who in deep concern for its protection has lain in yogic sleep, stretched on the cool, soft and delicate snake-bed in the ocean of milk. As these munis and yogis slowly awaken themselves, they constantly repeat the name of Hari; and the loud sound caused by this repetition has penetrated into and refreshed our hearts and roused us from sleep. Bestir yourself and join us.
purport:
From this pāsuram to the next nine, Āṇḍāḷ tries to wake up ten gopikās to gather together and perform the nombu. Metaphorically, these ten gopikās indicate the indriyas - five being karmendriya and the next five being jñānendriya. As the pāsurams of Āḷvārs echo about śeṣattvam of the jīvātmā to Nārāyaṇa, i.e., we are all devoted servants of Bhagavān and it is our svarūpam. Āṇḍāḷ wakes up the indriyas so that they can be used to perform service to Bhagavān. Now, she starts by waking up a gopī who is novice to Bhāgavata śāstram and the devotional path. While doing so, the gopikā questions Āṇḍāḷ and the gathered bhāgavatas, "What is the sign that dawn has occurred?" A beautiful and sweet conversation unfolds in this pāsuram.

When Āṇḍāḷ wakes her up, the gopī questions, "How do you know dawn has occurred?" The reason she asks is because the previous night she did not sleep, being immersed in devotion towards Kṛṣṇa. Now she doesn't want to share her experience with other bhāgavatas, and she doesn't want to move out of that experience. Such behavior is novice in nature. Envy should be completely absent in the devotional path. There should be a process of sharing knowledge with each other. She fears she might lose that experience by sharing it. This stage is called childhood spiritual experience. Bhagavān Himself says to Arjuna in Gītā 10.9 that the great prapannas who have surrendered to the lotus feet of the divine couple discuss their experience of devotional service with other bhāgavatas (mac-cittā mad-gata-prāṇā bodhayantaḥ parasparam).

Hence, Āṇḍāḷ tries to educate her to transcend such a novice mindset and enjoy serving Bhagavān with other devotees. She states that birds are chirping and going in search of food. These birds represent the great preceptors who are ready to share knowledge and have assembled near temples. Such ācāryas have vairāgya, bhakti, jñāna, and karma as their wings. They not only possess great knowledge but also perform actions according to that knowledge. Those with just knowledge are like birds with no wings, and those who perform actions without understanding the essence behind them are like birds which are blind. Clinging to such people is of no use. But the ācāryas who have knowledge and perform actions accordingly are like great birds who can help us cross the ocean of saṃsāra if we cling to them.

Now the gopī disagrees, stating that in Gokula (as Āṇḍāḷ perceives she is in Gokula), even birds don't sleep, thinking about Kṛṣṇa, immersed in Kṛṣṇa-prema. Hence, they too have gone in search of food without sleeping, thinking it's dawn. Āṇḍāḷ further justifies that it's time for sunrise by saying that these bhāgavatas have assembled near the temple of the Lord of Garuḍa. The term often used for temple in Tamil is kōyil. Interestingly, 'kō' refers to the King of birds, Garuḍa, and kōyil refers to the residence of the Lord of Garuḍa. Hence, devotees have assembled near the sanctum of Garuḍa to move towards the inner main sanctorum.

She further continues by saying that the conch appears white (as dawn has appeared and there is better lighting). We can hear the loud booming sound of the conch in the temple. The gopī argues, saying that such sounds can be heard every hour; this doesn't indicate dawn. The spiritual essence of calling Nārāyaṇa as the Lord of Garuḍa refers to the fact that He is praised by the Vedas, as Garuḍa represents Veda. Hence, by following the Vedas, we reach Bhagavān. The sound from the conch is praṇava, which at its core essence reminds us we are śeṣa, i.e., servants of the Supreme, Kṛṣṇa.

Āṇḍāḷ calls the gopī piḷḷai, i.e., a novice and ignorant child. She calls upon the gopī to come and enjoy the Bhagavat-kaiṅkaryam, i.e., experience serving the Lord in this group of devotees. That is indeed the right way to show devotion towards the Lord. The gopī questions further, asking who woke up the group which has arrived to wake her up. At this time, Āṇḍāḷ provides a beautiful explanation.

Kṛṣṇa sucked the breasts of the demon Pūtanā who foolishly disguised herself as Yaśodā. Another time, He destroyed the false cart Śakaṭāsura, when Yaśodā laid Him under the cart for protection. These two incidents indicate how a jīvātmā can be liberated from saṃsāra. Pūtanā represents prakṛti with her two breasts representing ego and possessiveness (ahaṅkāra and mamakāra). Bhagavān Himself sucked the breasts and caused her death, i.e., He Himself will remove the essence of ego and possessiveness from the devotees who have surrendered to Him. Śakaṭa represents the body. Unless we are liberated from the body, we cannot completely enjoy Kṛṣṇa. By breaking Śakaṭa using His foot, it indicates that by surrendering to the lotus feet of the Lord, we indeed can be liberated from this body. Āṇḍāḷ says that yogis have assembled in the temple chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa as Hari. The divine name Hari refers to one who destroys or tears down all sins. These chants entered our ears, made us remember Kṛṣṇa and His pastimes, increasing the heat of agony and awakened us. Hence she calls upon the gopi to wake up! The pasuram emphasise on the aspect that once we have Bhagavatha Sambhandam .i.e company with great devotees, our mind is set on Bhagavan and try to protect him (out of love) but until then we are immersed fear to protect ourselves.

meaning: Knowing they must remain separated throughout the day, the bhāradvāja birds gather at dawn from all directions, conferring in groups. Have you not heard their melodious discourse? O maddened one! As the gopikās engage in churning curds, their hair-bands loosen, and their flowing tresses, adorned with flowers, suffuse the air with fragrance. The movement of their hands causes their bangles to tinkle, and this sound, merging with the resonance of their neck ornaments, ascends to the heavens. Have you not heard this surging, rhythmic symphony? O Leader! How can You remain still, even after hearing the voices praising the Lord who, though pervading all creation through divine love, chose to incarnate as Kṛṣṇa specifically for our vision, and vanquished our enemies like Keśi? We behold Your radiance. Open the door and allow us to experience Your splendor without any impediment.
purport:
Āṇḍāḷ tries to wake the gopī again who was immersed in Kṛṣṇa-prema. She speaks about chirping birds, specifically calling them bharadvāja birds who are discoursing with each other before moving apart to gather food. The reference to 'bharadvāja' indicates these birds to be brāhmaṇas. Those who possess the knowledge about Brahman are called brāhmaṇas. These people are well-versed in Vedas and are mumukṣus. These brāhmiṇs, also called śrotriyas, recite Vedic verses in the morning. Having understood the meaning behind the verses, they don't merely recite them but also put them into practice. As seen in the previous pāsuram, birds represent the preceptors, and Āṇḍāḷ continues that analogy here. She emphasizes that both knowledge and its practical application are crucial. These great brāhmaṇas or ṛṣis, when they sleep, immerse themselves in spiritual experience, then wake up to impart knowledge to us. These great devotees engage in all their daily actions as service to Bhagavān, hence Āṇḍāḷ questions the gopī, "Haven't you heard the conversations of these great sages?" But the gopī argues that these birds (sages) have been conversing throughout the night about Kṛṣṇa, hence they continue their discourse even now, not realizing dawn has broken.

Āṇḍāḷ provides another justification for daybreak. She describes married women churning curd, their golden bangles colliding and creating sounds. The fragrance of fresh flowers in their hair spreads everywhere, indicating morning's arrival. These gopikās who churn curd are immersed in remembering Kṛṣṇa. While churning, they chant His name in hymns. When selling dairy products, they don't shout "Butter, Curd, Milk" but joyfully sing "Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava." They are in such an exalted state that they hardly comprehend what they're selling. Such women are married in all sense to Kṛṣṇa. The surrender of a jīvātmā to the paramātmā is akin to a divine marriage. Jīvātmās represent femininity, with Bhagavān being the puruṣārtha (ultimate goal). When jīvātmā surrenders to the Lord, it takes three vows, like the three knots of the sacred maṅgala sūtra: ananya śeṣatva, ananya bhogyatva, and ananya śaraṇatva. Ananya means 'exclusive'. These three vows represent: eternally serving the Lord, desiring to be enjoyed by Him alone, and surrendering to Him exclusively.
Āṇḍāḷ addresses the gopī as a leader, encouraging her to guide the assembled devotees. She calls them to join in remembering the divine names Nārāyaṇa and Keśava. She elaborates on Kṛṣṇa's grace and magnificence. He is called Nārāyaṇa as He pervades everything, including the jīva-tattvas. His love is boundless - during pralaya, He absorbs all jīvātmās, providing protection. He safeguards devotees by vanquishing demons and ill-wishers, as evidenced by His destruction of the asura Keśī when gopālas and gopīs feared for Kṛṣṇa's safety. Though unbounded by form, He manifests for His devotees. Though capable of accomplishing everything through mere will, He incarnates and plays among us. In Vaikuṇṭha, He shines like infinite suns, eternally praised by the nitya-sūris, yet desires all jīvātmās trapped in saṃsāra to reach Him, hence engaging in creation. Āṇḍāḷ questions the gopī why she hesitates to join them in chanting such beautiful names of Kṛṣṇa, who loves us more than anyone.

meaning: Day is breaking in the east. The buffaloes are released for feed; they are freely making their way to the small meadow. The other girls are proceeding to the place of the ritual, as though their whole purpose lies in reaching there. We have stopped them, and we come here to invite you; we stand in your courtyard. O woman of intense longing! Wake up and join us. Let us praise Kṛṣṇa's attributes and launch upon our ritual; let us obtain 'paṟai' which is the essential implement required for our rite. Let us adore Kṛṣṇa. He has killed the demon Keśī by splitting him into two; He has destroyed the wrestlers Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika; He is the God of all gods, God of all the celestials. When we go to Him and render Him worship, He will feel concerned that we have taken the trouble of going to Him, and will hasten to consider all the aspects of our situation and grant us what we want.
purport:
Āṇḍāḷ continues to wake the gopī who is not agreeing that dawn has arisen. She quotes that the day has broken and requests her to wake up; the sun is rising from the east, spreading its rays everywhere. These rays are similar to the gopī's face. As soon as night occurs, these gopīs run to meet Kṛṣṇa and enjoy listening to His veṇugāna. But while immersed in the experience, there is slight worry in them; they keep looking east, checking if dawn breaks. Each time they rotate their heads, their faces glow like the moon, emitting rays of spiritual love. But here, the gopī was unable to participate in the act and is waiting to meet the Gopāla of Vṛndāvana.

Āṇḍāḷ awakens her by saying the buffaloes have been let out to graze in the small meadows, similar to how Toṇḍaraḍippoḍi Āḷvār tries to wake Raṅganātha. Unlike cows, buffaloes are left to graze twice - near dawn and later morning. At dawn, they graze in nearby meadows and later are sent far off. Hence, by saying the buffaloes are grazing near the small meadows and will soon return to their sheds, Āṇḍāḷ indicates the risen dawn. On the level of spiritual knowledge, these buffaloes represent the guṇas rajas and tamas. Rajas induces passion for material pleasures, and tamas brings ignorance which forces one away from spiritual knowledge. Internally, even if we reduce such guṇas' impact, due to vāsanās carried from several previous births, we are forced to act upon them. Only after dawn are buffaloes sent far off; similarly, only when we cling to Bhagavān can we ward off such guṇas and adopt sattva alone, which brings desire for spiritual knowledge and peace of mind. If buffaloes wake at dawn to graze upon mere grass, then devotees of Kṛṣṇa like the gopī too need to wake at dawn, going towards the objective of enjoying the Supreme Self. Now the gopī wants reassurance that such people have gathered here to meet this objective.

To assure the gopī, Āṇḍāḷ beautifully quotes that other devotees and gopīs have assembled here waiting for her. She particularly addresses why devotees try to meet Kṛṣṇa even when attainment may be uncertain. Her justification is wonderful - she emphasizes that though we may or may not attain Kṛṣṇa, the journey itself provides immense bliss. Moreover, we don't desire such great bliss but only to serve Bhagavān. That itself is part of the journey, hence we are happy irrespective of the result. When Akrūra was ordered by Kaṃsa to fetch the two gopālas of Vraja - Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma - he was in bliss thinking that merely going to Vṛndāvana itself was the goal. When Vibhīṣaṇa was banished from Laṅkā, he went to the northern shore where Rāma stayed. Vālmīki specifically quotes "Uttaram tīra māsādya khasthaḥ eva vyatiṣṭhata" - he stood in the sky above the shore. Using a continuous word for the verb 'stand', Vālmīki seems to indicate that he stood watching Rāma, merely happy about that fact. Similarly, Āṇḍāḷ says "vandu ninṟōm." The gopī questions Āṇḍāḷ about why they have gathered to call her. Āṇḍāḷ responds that she knows well the gopī desires Kṛṣṇa more than life itself, as does Kṛṣṇa desire her. After knowing this, how could they not call her? She speaks similar to Sītā Devī showing sympathy for those under Rāvaṇa's cruel regime. Hence, Āṇḍāḷ calls upon the gopī to participate in the nombu and receive Kṛṣṇa's blessings to obtain the paṟai (which also refers to divine service).

When the gopī asks why Kṛṣṇa would deign them paṟai, Āṇḍāḷ responds by narrating His līlās. She describes how He split the mouth of the demon Keśī, who took the form of a horse, to protect the gopīs. Spiritually, Keśī represents ego, which stands between us and Bhagavān. Ego arises when the self identifies with the body, yielding attachment to material desires and preventing us from realizing Kṛṣṇa, serving whom provides much greater fulfillment. Next, she narrates the killing of Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika, the two wrestlers at Kaṃsa's command. These represent kāma and krodha - desire and anger. These twins cause all issues and are the source of qualities obstructing us from realizing Bhagavān. The Gītā repeatedly instructs us to control these two. Desire is the seed of anger, as Bhagavān states in Gītā 2.62-63: "saṅgāt sañjāyate kāmaḥ kāmāt krodho 'bhijāyate krodhād bhavati sammohaḥ sammohāt smṛti-vibhramaḥ smṛti-bhraṃśād buddhi-nāśho buddhi-nāśhāt praṇaśhyati."
Such Kṛṣṇa is also called devādi deva. Śrīmad Bhāgavatam 7.8.37-39 beautifully describes how devas assembled to calm Nṛsiṃha: "Devas headed by Lord Brahmā, King Indra and Lord Śiva, including great saintly persons and residents of Pitṛloka, Siddhaloka, Vidyādhara-loka, and the planet of snakes. The Manus approached, as did chiefs of various planets. The angelic dancers, Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Yakṣas, inhabitants of Kinnaraloka, Vetālas, inhabitants of Kimpuruṣa-loka, and personal servants of Viṣṇu like Sunanda and Kumuda. All approached the Lord, who glowed with intense light, offering individual obeisances and prayers." Hence, Yaśodā's darling Kṛṣṇa is truly the Supreme. When He sees devotees striving to reach Him, these surrendered souls, He feels their distress and surely comes to them, bringing fruits to their spiritual aspirations.

meaning: O daughter of aunt, who sleeps soundly on the comfortable couch, surrounded by flaming wicks and pervaded with the aroma of scented sticks, in your mansion made of pure gems of all nine varieties! Lift the latch of your gem-studded door. O aunt, at least you may awaken her. Is your daughter mute or deaf or ill? Or are guards preventing her movement? Or is she under a spell of deep slumber? Sing and glorify His names: 'Mahāmāyāvi' (the great mystic), 'Mādhava' (consort of Mahālakṣmī), 'Vaikuṇṭhavāsa' (resident of Vaikuṇṭha), and other such names, and see that she wakes up.
purport:
Waking up the gopī, Āṇḍāḷ describes her sleeping in a room decorated with different types of gems, of nine varieties. Along with gems, the room has several lamps lit everywhere with their aroma spreading around. Āṇḍāḷ calls the gems pure. Bhagavān is pure and stainless. He is beyond the prakṛti guṇas. Unlike us, He creates with His sheer will alone. The Nārāyaṇopaniṣad calls Him as "niṣkalo nirañjano nirvilkalpo nirākhyātaḥ śuddho deva eko nārāyaṇaḥ" - that is, He is pure, stainless, not subject to change; such characteristics are His alone and second to none. The gopikā who is immersed in Bhagavad-dhyānam also attains a similar character. The mukta, when attaining liberation, obtains similar characteristics as that of Bhagavān. Here too, the mumukṣu who is the gopī is immersed in Kṛṣṇa-prema and hence remains pure like gems. The nine gems decorating the mansion represent nine types of relationship (navavidha-bhāva) with Bhagavān. They are: Pitṛputra Bhāva (Father-son relationship), Rakṣyarakṣaka Bhāva (Protected-protector relationship), Śeṣa-Śeṣī Bhāva (Master-servant relationship), Bhartṛbhāryā bhāva (Husband-wife relationship), Jñātṛ-Jñeya Bhāva (Knower-known relationship), Sva-svāmī Bhāva (Owner-object owned relationship), Ādhāra-ādheya Bhāva (Sustainer-sustained relationship), Śarīrātma Bhāva (Body-soul relationship), and finally Bhoktṛ-Bhogya bhāva (Enjoyer-object enjoyed relationship). Bhagavān is the father, husband, savior, protector, master, owner, the ātmā, object to be known, the enjoyer, and sustainer. The gopī immersed in this navavidha bhāva is not waking up.

The mansion is lit with several lamps. The light emitting from the lamp represents knowledge. Like how light dispels darkness, so does knowledge dispel ignorance. The gopikā who is immersed in Kṛṣṇa-bhakti has such immense knowledge, and her ignorance is destroyed. Āṇḍāḷ also mentions that the wicks emit scented aroma. If light represents knowledge, then the scented aroma represents practice or anuṣṭhānam. A true devotee will be like the lamp with light and aroma - knowledge and anuṣṭhānam.

Āṇḍāḷ requests the gopikā to open the door studded with gems. This gem-studded door represents ignorance. The gopikā who plays the role of the ācārya needs to wake up and help the gathered group by removing ignorance, thereby bringing them closer to Kṛṣṇa. Irritated by the gopikā not waking up, Āṇḍāḷ asks her mother who is seated nearby to wake her up. She questions, "Is your daughter deaf? Dumb? Tired and in fatigue lying on the bed?" The gopikā, well knowing Kṛṣṇa alone is the means to attain Him, is immersed in love towards Him. Hence Āṇḍāḷ asks her, "Are you dumb? Have you stopped speaking because you are in a state immersed in Kṛṣṇa-anubhava? But this doesn't suit your character! Though you have sacrificed all means to attain Him but accept He alone is the means to attain Him, you need to engage yourself in service to Him along with us. Hence respond to our calls and wake up!" She calls her dumb, stating, "Are you dumb because you are listening only to the music of Kṛṣṇa's flute? Have you isolated yourself only to listen to Kṛṣṇa's words? Won't you wake up and grant us the knowledge of spiritual experience?" She further continues, "Spending time with Kṛṣṇa all night, are you in fatigue and unable to get up? O mother of hers, please wake her up. Let her at least respond to us!"

The gathered group of gopikās question the gopikā inside the room, asking her, "Are you in deep sleep because of Kṛṣṇa? Has He put any kind of spell on you? Sure He would have! Isn't He māyān, the Lord of Māyā!" Losing the sense of ahaṅkāra and mamakāra, the gopikā is immersed in Kṛṣṇa-anubhava and not ready to wake up. Surely it has to be Kṛṣṇa who is not letting her wake up. Āṇḍāḷ beautifully calls that Kṛṣṇa as māyān, Mādhava, Vaikuṇṭha and puts it in a wonderful order. He is called māyān because He controls māyā. He plays with this creation which is His potency called māyā. He incarnates with His saṅkalpa with His yoga-māyā. He has mesmerized the gopikā indeed with His beautiful form like māyā. Māyā is the wonderful power of Bhagavān as stated by Rāmānujācārya as 'adbhutam'. Then she calls Him as Mādhava, the dear of Mahālakṣmī. Then she calls Him as Vaikuṇṭha. The beauty of this order is, when the jīvātmā loses ignorance and gains the knowledge that it is the servant of Bhagavān, it surrenders. Mahālakṣmī, His divine consort and our divine mother, shows compassion on us, acting as means to attain Him. By her compassion, we attain Him who is the supreme goal (Vaikuṇṭha) and attain paramapadam (Vaikuṇṭha). This starts with the realization of His power, i.e., māyā. We realize He is beyond birth and death. He is the creator, sustainer, and destroyer. He has pervaded everywhere and inside as antaryāmī. But how do we know this controller of māyā is Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme? It is because Śrī has housed herself on His chest forming the mark of Śrīvatsa. The Puruṣa Sūktam glorifies Him as the Supreme Puruṣa and ends by saying He who is the divine consort of Lakṣmī and Bhūdevī, indeed He is the Supreme Puruṣa described who shines like the stars in night. Now that we know we are jīvātmās and there is a Supreme Lord who is the controller of this creation using māyā, and Kṛṣṇa is that Supreme Lord, we follow the śāstras to attain Him, His abode Vaikuṇṭha. Hence finally she calls Kṛṣṇa as Vaikuṇṭha-vāsa where He shines as Para-Vāsudeva served by nitya-muktas. By calling these names, she tries to wake up the gopikā.

meaning: O fortunate girl, you who have completed the rite before our arrival and experienced happiness! Won't you speak to us, even if you do not open the door? Nārāyaṇa, whose crown is adorned with garlands of fragrant tulasī, is so generous a benefactor that He bestows upon us, who have nothing of our own, the desired objective of 'paṟai,' merely for singing His benediction. He once cast Kumbhakarṇa into death's jaws. Could it be that demon has been defeated by you in a contest of sleep and has surrendered his rich possession of sound sleep to you? O dear one, whom dense drowsiness never seems to leave, you, who are the śirobhūṣaṇa (crown-jewel) of us all, arise from sleep, shake off your drowsiness and come to open the door. Open your mouth and speak. Remove the veil and reveal yourself to us.
purport:
Waking up the Gopikā, Āṇḍāl asks her, "Have you already performed the Nombu? Is that why you have already attained Kṛṣṇa? Is it right for you to remain in your nature and not allow us to attain the same state? Hence, please wake up!" The Gopikās address the sleeping lady, who appears to have attained the state of one who has completed all spiritual rites (kṛta-kṛtya). They observe that while they intended to perform rites to attain Kṛṣṇa, she has achieved the fruit of these rites through her profound realization that Kṛṣṇa Himself is both the means (upāya) and the end (upeya).  This profound understanding aligns with the declarations of Vedic scholars and spiritual masters, who proclaim Kṛṣṇa as the eternal dharma. While karma (works), jñāna (knowledge), and bhakti (devotion) are means to attain God, they are not always accessible. However, God Himself remains ever available as the ultimate means. The Gopikā, understanding this tattva (truth), has surrendered completely, making no independent effort, similar to what is described in the Bhagavad-gītā's Puruṣottama-prāpti Yoga. Her state reflects one who has truly understood the nature of Prakṛti (material nature), Jīva (individual self), and Īśvara (Supreme Lord). 

The Gopikās address her as "Ammā" (Mother) and as one who has reached Svarga (heaven). Here, Svarga represents the eternal bliss (ānanda) of being with Kṛṣṇa, as exemplified in Sītā’s words to Śrī Rāma: that being with Him is heaven, and separation is hell. They recognize her as their potential savior, capable of securing divine union for the entire group, as she perpetually dwells in God-consciousness without intermission. The Gopikās ask her, "If you are not waking up, won’t you at least speak to us? Reply to us!" This shows how desperate they are to hear from her. The Gopikā, as we know, represents the Āchārya. Āchāryas have experienced Bhagavān and are therefore capable of sharing their experiences with us. They do so for those disciples who have surrendered to them by narrating their divine experiences. Here too, the Gopikās eagerly wait for the narration of the Gopikā, who is immersed in Kṛṣṇa-bhāva. She is called upon to open the door—to break the doors of ignorance standing between them and Bhagavān. The Āchārya is the one who destroys our ego and imparts knowledge to help us attain Bhagavān.

Seeing the Gopikā not waking up, the gathered Gopikās ask her, "Has that Kumbhakarṇa, defeated by Rāvaṇa, left his sleepiness to you? Why aren’t you waking up? We are waiting for you!" This statement seems out of the ordinary and may appear as a strange comparison. The Gopikā, who is said to be immersed in Kṛṣṇa-prema, is being compared to a Rākṣasa like Kumbhakarṇa. How is this possible? The comparison is sāttvic. The Gopikās only speak about sleep, not other qualities. Additionally, the term "Kumbhakarṇa" refers to two personalities: Rāvaṇa’s brother and one born from a Kubha (jar), i.e., Agastya. 

Here, the Gopikās question why she is sleeping like Rāvaṇa’s brother. Kumbhakarṇa, due to his tāmasic nature, slept for half the year, only to wake up and eat during the other half. But the Gopikā, on the other hand, does not possess such a tāmasic quality. Her sleep is sāttvic, immersed in Kṛṣṇa-bhakti. Hence, how appropriate is it for her to wake from that slumber to perform service to Kṛṣṇa along with them? How can she deny them such pleasure? Like Kumbhakarṇa stood between Sītā and Rāma, if she does not join them, Kṛṣṇa will not reveal Himself to them. He has promised to grant them Parai (the opportunity to serve). Thus, the context of Kumbhakarṇa must be understood in this Pāsuram. Additionally, she is compared to Agastya. Agastya, the great Ṛṣi belonging to the spectacular seven sages, is known for three important deeds: destroying Vindhya’s ego, drinking the entire ocean, and vanquishing Vātāpi, the cunning demon. Similarly, the Gopikā possesses three important qualities: conquering her ego, gaining spiritual knowledge as vast as the ocean, and maintaining unbroken meditation on Bhagavān.

The sleeping Gopikā is then compared to a crown jewel. This signifies that even in her state of inaction, she is as precious as a jewel. Unlike other objects of decoration, jewels remain intact yet add beauty to those who wear them. Such is the presence of the Gopikā. Her mere presence makes the place beautiful and filled with bliss. How so? Kṛṣṇa has spent the night with her! Āṇḍāl is able to smell the fragrance of Tulasi, which confirms that Kṛṣṇa has indeed visited her! The devotion of the Gopikā is like the fragrance of Tulasi. Even if hidden, the fragrance is perceived by those nearby. Similarly, the divine qualities of the Gopikā can be identified even if she remains asleep. The gathered group, along with Āṇḍāl, urges her to carefully wake up and open the door.

meaning: O golden creeper, sprouted in the community of blameless gopālas, who excel in milking herds of cows (which, though having mothered calves, are still young themselves) and who possess great strength and valor in facing and fighting enemies! O maiden, with hips resembling the hood of a serpent in its hole! O girl with beautiful tresses shining like the peacock in the forest! Come! Your kith and kin and companions have all arrived. They are assembled in the courtyard of your house. They are glorifying the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose body shines with the hue of the dark cloud. How is it that you still remain dull and mute? O wealthy maiden! Explain to us the meaning of your sleep.
purport:
Āṇḍāḷ describes how the gopālas are milking the cows, which are countless in number. The clan of cowherds possessed cows in the lakhs (hundreds of thousands). Indeed, Āṇḍāḷ emphasizes their vast numbers, drawing a parallel to how the number of births we jīvātmas have taken, the attributes of Bhagavān, and the incarnations He has taken are all beyond counting. These divine cows maintain their beauty and youthfulness, yielding abundant milk due to their association with Kṛṣṇa, His graceful touch, and the divine melody of His flute. They remain eternally twenty-five years old due to Bhagavān's constant presence.

These cows symbolize the mukta jīvātmas (liberated souls). Having been freed from the cycle of saṃsāra and devoid of all karma and vāsanās, they remain in eternal association with the Supreme Being in Vaikuṇṭha. The presence of Bhagavān invariably brings ānanda (bliss and happiness). This is illustrated in the Rāmāyaṇa when Daśaratha cried in anguish as Rāma departed for fourteen years of exile – it was as if his very happiness was being sent away. The significance of twenty-five years holds deep meaning. In the Rāmāyaṇa, when Sītā Devī converses with Anasūyā about dharma, she mentions her age as eighteen while her husband Rāma is twenty-five. The world comprises twenty-four tattvas of prakṛti, with the twenty-fifth tattva being the jīvātma. When a jīvātma correctly identifies itself and doesn't conflate itself with prakṛti tattva, it gains clarity about all tattvas and its own nature. This enables it to recognize itself as the śarīra (body) of Īśvara, that is, Kṛṣṇa.

The gopālas milk these numerous divine cows, a task that distinguishes them from other gopālas of different regions. This is analogous to a brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary texts, earning respect beyond their prescribed duties. These gopālas represent ācāryas. They perform their duties knowing well that it is not the duties themselves but Kṛṣṇa alone who grants liberation. Yet, they perform their duties out of pure love for Kṛṣṇa, finding satisfaction in His happiness. Just as the gopālas protect the cows from enemies, the ācāryas defeat internal enemies like desire (kāma) and anger (krodha) that obstruct their daily spiritual practices. The gopālas and gopikās possess courage similar to the Lord's and show great mercy to those who repent their mistakes.

Continuing to praise her attributes, Āṇḍāḷ offers a beautiful comparison, describing the gopī as a golden creeper. Creepers grow dependent on support, lest they fall and break. Similarly, we jīvātmas are not independent – our dependence is on Bhagavān, who alone is independent. Whether we realize this truth or not, it remains unchangeable. When we do realize our dependence on Īśvara, as the gopī has, such jīvātmas become mumukṣus or liberated souls. They shine like gold, hence Āṇḍāḷ's metaphor of the golden creeper.

Āṇḍāḷ further draws a unique comparison of the gopī, likening her waist to a coiled snake in a hole, followed by the image of a peacock unfurling its feathers. This progression from the coiled snake to the spreading peacock feathers represents the evolution of devotion. Referencing Rāmānujācārya's Śaraṇāgati Gadyam, where he prays to Mahālakṣmī for blessings of devotion: "parabhakti parājñāna paramabhaktikṛta." Beautifully, the same Mahālakṣmī, here as Āṇḍāḷ, explains these stages of devotion in a prapanna. Parabhakti is the stage where separation from Bhagavān becomes unbearable, inducing viraha. Parajñāna leads to seeing Him everywhere, and finally, Paramabhakti is the state where serving Bhagavān becomes the devotee's sole desire.\
Āṇḍāḷ continues by describing her immense wealth – the greatest wealth of kaiṅkarya (service to the Lord). In the Rāmāyaṇa, none was as wealthy as Lakṣmaṇa, who possessed kaiṅkarya lakṣmī, enabling him to serve the Lord eternally. Āṇḍāḷ beseeches the gopī to share this kaiṅkarya experience with them, asking her to awaken from sleep. This presents the contrast between kaivalya and mokṣa. Kaivalya is a state where the jīvātma immerses itself in self-bliss. Though this appears like liberation, it remains incomplete and imperfect. True mokṣa is attained only when the jīvātma realizes its nature as a servant of the Lord and completely surrenders. Similarly, sharing spiritual experiences with fellow devotees surpasses solitary practice. Hence, Āṇḍāḷ calls upon the gopī to awaken and praise the dark-complexioned Kṛṣṇa.

meaning: Fondly thinking of their young calves and imagining they have stretched their mouths to their udders, herds of mahiṣīs (she-buffaloes) spontaneously rain milk through their teats. There are no gopālas at hand to milk them, yet the entire gośālā (cow shed) becomes drenched and miry with their flowing milk. "O sister of the wealthy owner of such magnificent herds! We stand here at your dvāra (door), holding the threshold, while the prabhāta's dew falls upon our heads. We are singing the glory of Śrī Rāma, the hṛdayeśa (charmer of hearts), who in righteous anger vanquished Rāvaṇa, the King of Laṅkā in the dakṣiṇa (south). Hearing our devotional singing, how is it that you do not deign to open your mukha (mouth)? Will you not take care of us? Why this deep nidrā (slumber)? The entire grāma (village) has come to know of your secret. Rise now from your sleep!
purport:
Āṇḍāḷ describes the young buffaloes whose udders overflow with milk as they think lovingly of their hungry calves. Though burdened by the pain of excess milk, their concern is not for themselves but for the calves separated from them. Their affection mirrors the compassion of Bhagavān, who cannot bear the suffering of the jīvātmas separated from Him. The milk begins to flow spontaneously, without the touch of the milkman or the calf itself, simply through remembrance born of love. Unlike clouds that release rain only at intervals, these buffaloes pour forth milk continuously, illustrating how true affection knows neither measure nor restraint. Āṇḍāḷ subtly asks the sleeping gopī why she remains unmoved by the distress of the devotees waiting outside when even animals express sorrow at separation.

The overflowing milk symbolizes the boundless grace of the ācāryas. Just as the buffaloes pour forth milk without being asked, great preceptors freely bestow the divine meanings of Bhagavān upon worthy seekers. Arjuna did not request the profound teachings of the Upaniṣads, yet Kṛṣṇa, out of compassion, revealed the wisdom of the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā*. This truth is celebrated in the verse *sarvopaniṣado gāvo dogdhā gopālanandanaḥ*, where the Upaniṣads are compared to cows, Kṛṣṇa to the milkman, Arjuna to the calf, and the Gītā to the milk produced for the benefit of all devotees. Thus, if even the buffaloes of this household display such generosity, Āṇḍāḷ wonders why the gopī herself withholds the blessing of her company.

The abundance of milk drenches the entire courtyard, raising the question of why the milkman has neglected his task. The answer reveals his greatness. Like Lakṣmaṇa, who set aside even prescribed duties in order to accompany and serve Śrī Rāma and Sītā Devī in exile, this gopāla has become wholly immersed in service to Kṛṣṇa. Such abandonment of duty is not born of laziness or disregard for śāstra, but of complete dedication to Bhagavān. Therefore Āṇḍāḷ calls him *naṛ celvan*, one who possesses true wealth. Real wealth is not worldly prosperity but *Kṛṣṇa-kaiṅkarya*. Lakṣmaṇa, Gajendra, and Vibhīṣaṇa were all celebrated as truly wealthy because they placed service to the Lord above all else. Moreover, this wealth is contagious, inspiring devotion in all who come into contact with it.

Addressing the gopī as the sister of this blessed devotee, Āṇḍāḷ gently teases her. Her brother has abandoned the buffaloes under his care due to absorption in Kṛṣṇa-kaiṅkarya, while she has abandoned the devotees eagerly waiting at her doorstep. Yet this comparison ultimately glorifies her rather than criticizes her. Just as Vibhīṣaṇa dedicated himself to Śrī Rāma and his daughter Tṛjaṭā served Sītā Devī, the sister of such a devotee ought naturally to join the company of devotees undertaking the sacred vow. Standing amidst rain from above and streams of milk beneath their feet, the gopīs patiently wait outside her door, hoping she will emerge and join them.

When the gopī remains silent, the gopīs turn to singing the glories of Śrī Rāma. Though renowned for patience equal to that of Bhūdevī, Rāma became enraged whenever His devotees were harmed. Rāvaṇa had tormented the sages, abducted Sītā Devī, slain Jaṭāyu, opposed Vibhīṣaṇa, and insulted Hanumān. Therefore Rāma destroyed not merely Rāvaṇa himself but also his armies, weapons, power, and pride before finally ending his life. Unlike Kṛṣṇa, whose playful pranks often bewildered the women of Gokula, Rāma stands as the ideal protector who endured immense suffering for the sake of His consort and devotees. The remembrance of such a Lord naturally cools the hearts of those afflicted by separation.

For this reason Āṇḍāḷ calls Him *manattukkiniyān*, the One who delights the heart. The gopīs sing not of Kṛṣṇa's playful mischief but of Rāma's compassion and selfless protection. His divine name is capable of restoring life, hope, and comfort to those overwhelmed by sorrow. They urge the gopī to awaken and join their singing, not merely for their sake but for her own, since the remembrance of the Lord alone can relieve the pain of separation. Even Bhagavān rushed instantly to rescue Gajendra when called upon, yet this gopī remains asleep despite repeated appeals.

Finally, Āṇḍāḷ marvels at the depth of her slumber. The entire village now knows that the gopīs stand outside her house pleading for her to awaken. Her greatness is known to all, as is the devotion and helplessness of those waiting for her. Nothing remains hidden. Having praised her virtues, her family, her devotion, and the compassion of both Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, the gopīs make one final appeal: she should arise, join the assembly of devotees, and participate in the collective experience of praising the Lord, for such shared devotion is far superior to remaining alone, however exalted one's spiritual state may be.

meaning: O perfect one in worship! The red lotuses in the well situated in the garden to the rear of the house are blooming; and the black tulips are folding up. Arise! The ascetics who have fine sets of white teeth and who are filled with a spirit of renunciation have put on their ochre robes and are going to their temples for worship. Arise! You have pledged your word that you will yourself come and wake us up. Have you forgotten it, O shameless girl! Get up! O adroit talker! Come out to sing the glory of the Lord of the lotus-eyes and long arms, who holds the śaṅkha and the cakra in His hands.
purport:
Trying to wake up the gopī, Āṇḍāl states that the tulips have shrunk, and lotuses are blooming. Tulips are nocturnal plants, and lotuses bloom during the day. This symbolizes that the night has broken. But the gopī is not ready to accept this. She argues, saying, "You are seeing my eyes, which are slowly opening up, and in happiness, you call them lotuses, but the dawn has not broken." Āṇḍāl continues to emphasize the blossoming of the lotus by saying they have bloomed in "your garden." The purpose of using "your" is to give a swift shock to the gopī. Being a mumukṣu, the gopī has given up mamakāra and ahaṅkāra—the sense of "mine" and "I." She knows everything, including herself, belongs to Kṛṣṇa alone. But when Āṇḍāl says "your," she fears mamakāra. Mṛtyu, i.e., death, which leads to rebirth, truly occurs as long as this jīvātma holds the egotistic sense of "mine," as expressed in Dvyākṣarastu bhaven mṛtyuḥ, i.e., the death in the two-letter word "mama." Eternal life or liberation is in the three-letter word "na mama." One who realizes that he is not the bhoktā (enjoyer) but Bhagavān is, and that he is not the kartā (doer) but Bhagavān is, becomes merely an agency for the Supreme to act. Such a person has liberated himself from the results of his actions. Karma yogis who reach this state finally surrender to the Supreme as they realize that they themselves are His and are meant to be enjoyed by the Supreme. One who attains such a stage finds his lotus blooming under the sunlight of knowledge of Bhagavān. The lotus here refers to the blossoming of the suṣumṇā-nāḍī. From here, the jīvātma travels via the Arcirādi mārga, attaining Vaikuṇṭha—the place without return—where the muktātma enjoys bliss equal to that of Īśvara, who is omnipresent. The shrinking of the tulip represents the removal of the knowledge of self-independence. We are all asvatantra (dependent) and depend entirely on Īśvara. Realizing this, the lotus blooms.

The gopī argues, saying, "The lotuses are just blooming, and the tulip is just shrinking. It is still too early for the sun to rise." Āṇḍāl provides another justification, stating that ascetics dressed in red robes have gathered here, walking towards the temple, their teeth shining white. They wear the sacred mṛttikā (white clay) and have śrīchūrṇa on their foreheads. She says, "Wake up! Dawn has arrived!" The ascetics have broken the ochre stone to form the mṛttikā. The ochre stone represents the manas (mind), which distracts us, and red represents attachment. By grinding and wearing it, the ascetics have controlled their manas to show love only to Bhagavān. They are ācāryas who carry the kuñcikola to open the temple doors. This kuñcikola represents the upadeśa-mudrā. The upadeśa-mudrā, where the forefinger touches the thumb and the three fingers stand apart, symbolizes that the forefinger and thumb represent jīvātma and Īśvara, respectively, while the three fingers represent the three guṇas—sattva, rajas, and tamas. Renouncing these guṇas and adopting śuddha-sattva, the jīvātma attains sāyujya with Bhagavān.

The gopī still argues, saying, "Ascetics always sing and serve the Lord at all times. How does this represent the arrival of dawn?" Āṇḍāl now says, "You promised to wake us up, and now we are waking you!" It must be understood that Āṇḍāl asks the gopī to wake up and attain complete fullness. The gopī promised to wake up, i.e., to see Bhagavān beyond Māyā. Now, she must help others too, like the ācāryas. It is only through the association of other devotees that one can attain fullness. Āṇḍāl scolds her lovingly, saying, "You are of divine knowledge. O shameless girl! O adroit talker! Get up. Are you feeling ashamed that you could not come early and wake us up? No, do not feel that way. By your constant association with Śrī Rāma, you may have developed a feeling of bashful embarrassment. When the ṛṣis came to Śrī Rāma in Daṇḍakāraṇya and sought His protection, Śrī Rāma felt embarrassed and apologized to them: 'Alas, I should have come to you venerable ones myself and given you protection. Instead, I have unwittingly allowed time to slip until you came to me and told me of your troubles. I feel deeply ashamed of my lapse.'" Similarly, Āṇḍāl suggests that the gopī might feel ashamed for making others come to her. However, she reminds her that it is her nature to help those who depend on her. 

Āṇḍāl then asks her to sing about the lotus-eyed Lord, the holder of the conch and discus. The divine implements—the conch and discus—serve distinct spiritual purposes. The conch represents the praṇava (Oṃkāra) and serves to summon both straying cows and wandering souls back to the divine fold. The gopikas particularly envied the conch's fortune of constant contact with Kṛṣṇa. The discus, known as Sudarśana, helps devotees achieve a clear vision of the Supreme Self and acts independently to execute Kṛṣṇa's will, protecting devotees while keeping enemies at bay. Both implements work in harmony to protect supplicants and instill fear in enemies. Kṛṣṇa's lotus eyes hold special significance in this divine imagery, displaying various aspects, from humility to authority, depending on the context. To the gopikas, these eyes could appear meek, clever, authoritative, or charming, while also serving to protect and enthrall the residents of the Heavenly Abode.

meaning: The Gopikās standing outside called out sweetly to their friend inside, addressing her with the tenderness of a parrot's tone and asking why she was still asleep. From within, the Gopikā responded with mild irritation, calling them perfect gopikās but requesting them not to summon her with their shrill, annoying voices, assuring them she would come presently. The Gopikās outside then teased her, calling her clever and acknowledging they were already familiar with her harsh and adroit way of speaking. The Gopikā inside retorted sarcastically, saying they alone were clever and harsh, questioning their argument before conceding with irony that she alone was harsh. The Gopikās outside then questioned what made her so special and why she insisted on staying alone, urging her to come out quickly. The Gopikā inside inquired if all the gopikās were present, to which they confirmed and invited her to count them herself. She then asked what they wanted her to do, and the Gopikās outside requested her to come out and sing the glory of Kṛṣṇa, specifically praising Him who had killed the mighty elephant Kuvalayāpīḍam, routed the arrogance of enemies, and wielded mysterious power.
purport:
After waking up nine gopīs, Āṇḍāḷ is waking up the last gopī who is partially awake. Āṇḍāḷ calls the gopī a parrot. While everyone sings, she too joins in chorus and melody as they sing together. Her voice is so mellow and soft like the tune of the parrot, and her youth looks like that of the parrot too. Immersed in Kṛṣṇa anubhavam, the face of the gopikā has turned red just like the beak of the parrot. Āṇḍāḷ requests the gopī to wake up and share the experience of Kṛṣṇa she has had. While the gopikā listens to this, she gets annoyed. She was immersed in experiencing Kṛṣṇa, and these voices are not letting her continue, thereby making her irritated. The call 'tender parrot' irritates her. She who has vanquished all ego and mamakāra feels she doesn't deserve such a title. She states, "You are, indeed, the perfect ones. How can I have the fullness which you have? Those only are perfect who, on hearing the voices of devotees, enjoy bliss and bestow praise on them. I am not fortunate to have such opportunity. Do not trouble me further. You are all gathered together; and you are enjoying together one another's experiences; and that makes for fullness. Since you have that ripeness, you could call me 'the tender parrot.' Those who are really suffering from the misery of separation from Kṛṣṇa will have fainted on hearing his name; and felt annoyed with, and not praised, those who uttered it. You should have, like me, forgotten yourselves if you are yearning for him. But you hear my singing of his praises, feel happy and compliment me on my song. This is proof of your fullness. So please, I shall be with you in a moment."

The to and fro conversation which goes between Āṇḍāḷ and the gopikā represents humility. When the gopikā calls the gathered group perfect ones, they argue they are not. They call her harsh for using such great words to them, though they feel incompatible with it. These words could bring mamakāra and ahaṅkāra which would lead them away from Kṛṣṇa. Humility is one of the important qualities of a Vaiṣṇava. With humility, a true Śrīvaiṣṇava sacrifices mamakāra, ahaṅkāra; sorrow and joy look the same to him as Kṛṣṇa states in Bhagavad Gītā 12.13 as "adveṣṭā sarva-bhūtānāṃ maitraḥ karuṇa eva ca, nirmamo nirahaṅkāraḥ sama-duḥkha-sukhaḥ kṣamī." A true devotee looks at everyone as a friend, sacrifices all sense of difference in happiness and sorrow. In such a state, he remains as sthitaprajña and thereby lives in humility. Āṇḍāḷ and the gathered groups of gopikās continue asking her to wake up fast and join them. Spiritual experience should always be shared and enjoyed together. She asks if all have come, Āṇḍāḷ replying yes, all have! If you want to make sure, you can count them too. Calling upon the gopikā, Āṇḍāḷ asks her to join them to sing about Kṛṣṇa who killed Kuvalayāpīḍa, the elephant which represents ahaṅkāra.

meaning: O Guard protecting the mansion of Nandagōpa, the Commander of all! Let us in. O Keeper of the gate, which shines bright with its wreathed decorative arches and flag aloft! Lift the latch of the doors studded with gems. Lord Kṛṣṇa of sapphire-hue and mysterious power gave us his word yesterday that he would give us the musical instrument called 'pārai.' We, the gopikās, have not come here seeking any other benefit. We have come here with pure minds. We have come to awaken Kṛṣṇa with our song. Good Sirs! Do not say 'nay' to us. We pray that you yourselves will open the doors which, drawn by mutual love, stand close and tight. Open them and let us in.
purport:
Āṇḍāḷ with all awakened gopikās gather in front of the mansion of Nandagōpa where Kṛṣṇa lies sleeping on a couch with Nappinnai (Nīladēvī). She requests the guard of the mansion to open the doors. Now she is requesting the guard and Nandagōpa to open the doors. Āṇḍāḷ specifically calls Nandagōpa as commander of all, including Kṛṣṇa. How so? Isn't Kṛṣṇa Īśvara, which literally translates to the supreme controller? Yes, indeed he is Īśvara, yet he is Bhakta parādhīna. Though he is independent of all, yet he voluntarily decides to serve his devotees. Rāma calls himself as Dāśarathi, similarly Kṛṣṇa calls himself as Nandagōpa Kumāran. Āṇḍāḷ knows He loves it when we call him with devotees' names such as Devakinandana, hence she calls the mansion as belonging to Nandagōpa. In Nityavibhūti Śrī Vaikuṇṭha or līlā vibhūti, he always shows himself to be dependent on devotees. Ananta, Garuḍa, Viśvaksena do not leave him and keep him in their control in the supreme abode. Here, he listens to Prahlāda, Balarāma, Nanda, Yaśodā, Arjuna and all those who have surrendered to him. His love for his devotees has no bounds so much so that he is ready to be a messenger, a charioteer, sevaka, dvārapālaka to his devotees. The guard is the ācārya, kōyil referring to the mantra. Nandagōpa translates to 'the one who enjoys ānanda and protects' i.e., ācārya. They are jñānis who enjoy Nārāyaṇa and protect the mantra. The mantra, which is the residence of Lord, helps us to reach him. Without permit of Nanda, we can't see Kṛṣṇa; without the permit of ācārya we cannot receive the mantra and without which we cannot reach the supreme abode to enjoy Bhagavān.

Āṇḍāḷ requests the guard to open doors of the mansion which are embedded with gems. She calls the guard as kōyil kāppāne i.e., one who protects the residence of temple where Bhagavān resides. Though calling him as guard might sound rude due to the discriminative mindset of ours, in reality devotees love when they are associated with Bhagavān and ācāryas. People call themselves as dāsan of ācāryas and Bhagavān indicating they always love it when they are called as servants of Lord. The gate studded with jewels has made all the onlookers stand there stunned. This is very similar to the Vaikuṇṭha. Rāmānujācārya in Vaikuṇṭha Gadyam states that the supreme place desired by mumukṣus is shining with all types of jewels, calling it as maṇi maṇṭapam. When the liberated jīvas see the door, they get stunned and stuck there, unable to move on. The door represents prakṛti, which attracts us. Beyond the door lies the loved by all, Vāsudeva. By his wish alone the door opens, thereby unstunning the liberated ones to immerse them again in much greater ānanda i.e., himself. Similarly here, the dark cloud, emerald and sapphire-hued Kṛṣṇa rests beyond the doors; to see him we need to go beyond the three guṇas. That mansion has a red flag waving indicating indeed this is the place of Kṛṣṇa. The flag represents Praṇava. Kṛṣṇa is called as Karuṇā sāgara hence he is the ocean. The Praṇava mantra acts as the pointer to this ocean or lake. That flag has Garuḍa on it who represents the Vedas, the Vedas which lead us to Bhagavān.

The pāsuram stands as a beautiful conversation between the gopikās and gate keeper. The gate keeper is on duty to protect Kṛṣṇa at all cost. As said, devotees know that he is Īśvara yet they always have vātsalya bhāva towards Kṛṣṇa which makes them always keep an eye on him and protect him at all cost, even if it costs their lives. The guard is not ready to let them in as he fears they could be people with not the right mindset. Āṇḍāḷ urges saying that who can threaten the lord of Ananta? How can there be fear there? Guard argues that asuras keep threatening him. Pūtanā, Śakaṭāsura, Ṛṣabhāsura and so many have tried to kill him, hence he can't let them in so easily. Gopikās argue saying they are women, how can they do that, for which the keeper protests saying wasn't Tāṭakā, Pūtanā demons too? Now Āṇḍāḷ states that they have come here with pure mind to serve him alone. Kṛṣṇa himself had called them and promised to give the parai instrument. The guard laughs asking isn't it contradicting to say you came here to serve him alone but you ask for the instrument too? Gopikās correct it by saying they have asked for the instrument to sing the glories of Kṛṣṇa. The guard is not ready to listen; he states that by doing so you can awaken him. They say in chorus, they will just sing and watch him from the doorsteps, so please open the door. The guard knows they are indeed here to serve but yet wants to listen to how they glorify Kṛṣṇa. Now the gopikās, tired, plea to the keeper, "If you do not help us who can help us? You are the protector, the keeper of the treasure like Kṛṣṇa. You have to listen to our plea and pain. Good Sir, please open the door!" The words of Āṇḍāḷ clearly show the guard is none other than ācārya. He is the one who mediates and protects the jīvātmās who have surrendered to him. On behalf of us, he requests Lord to accept us and grants us liberation.

meaning: O Nandagōpa! How great is your munificence! You clothe the naked; you quench the thirsty; you feed the hungry—and all this you do with rectitude and without expecting return. O our revered master! Arise! O Yaśodā! You who are like a tender shoot among women with delicate bodies resembling the prabhālī trees! You, the auspicious light of our community! Our dear mistress! Awake! O Trivikrama! You who have grown in stature splitting the mid-sky, and measuring all the worlds with your feet! Wake up! You, Lord of the Nityasūris, the Ever-wise! You should not sleep. Get up. O Balarāma! You who wear an anklet of pure shining gold on your foot! You and your brother, pray, wake up!
purport:
Requesting the guard to open the doors, the guard argues let Kṛṣṇa himself come and open the door. Here Āṇḍāḷ along with all gopikās try to awaken Nandagōpa, Yaśodā, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma in respective order. Nanda stays awake and alert. He remains always in alert state, trying to protect Kṛṣṇa from all harms. Not just that, he is a man of kindness. He always helps the needy by donating what they seek for; clothing, food, cows, land and so much more. Nandagōpa is none other than the ācārya, or more of communities of all ācāryas. The gopikās request him to wake up and open the door, to serve Kṛṣṇa they are here. Nanda being the ācārya is always prepared to preach the mantra to the disciple letting them reach Bhagavān. Similar to Nandagōpa's character, ācāryas too have several auspicious qualities which the Taittirīya Upaniṣad speaks about in Prathama praśna that righteousness, control of senses, truthfulness, forgiveness, tapas, agnihotra all are characters of an ācārya. An ācārya who has such divine nature is eligible to teach the mantra. Like Rāma was pleased to be with Sītā because his father had approved it, Bhagavān too will be pleased with the jīvātma because of the permit given by ācārya. Hence, Āṇḍāḷ wakes up ācārya first.

Next she wakes up Yaśodā, who represents the Thirumantra. Yaśodā with complete love towards him lays peacefully thinking about her child. It is only after the permission of the mother, we can access Bhagavān. By waking up the parents, she asks for their permission to awaken Kṛṣṇa. Yaśodā represents the divine aṣṭākṣara mantra. In Vaiṣṇava theology there are many bījākṣara mantras among them three are important; ṣaḍakṣarī (Viṣṇu mantra), dvādaśākṣarī (Vāsudeva mantra) and aṣṭākṣarī (Nārāyaṇa mantra). Due to these mantras speaking about the all-pervasiveness of Bhagavān, they stand apart. Among these three, the aṣṭākṣarī is highly glorified by the Taittirīya Upaniṣad and Pāñcarātra Āgamas. It explains the all-pervasiveness of Bhagavān in complete sense along with the svarūpa of jīvātma. Yaśodā represents this mantra. By waking her up and then Kṛṣṇa, it shows the right process of upāsana. First it is to obtain the mantra from ācārya and then to meditate upon it thereby attaining Bhagavān.

Āṇḍāḷ now wakes up Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Nitya Muktas. As the Viṣṇu Sūktam states ""tadviṣṇōḥ paramam-padagṃ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ"" i.e., there in Paramapadham, the Supreme abode, Viṣṇu is being glorified by the Nitya Sūris. The Nityas like Ananta, Garuḍa, Viśvaksena eternally serve Him, never touched by karma and this saṃsāra. When he incarnates, they too incarnate. The Lord of these Nityas is our Kṛṣṇa. Nammāḷvār starts Tiruvāymoḻi with this point of view calling him as the Lord of immortals i.e., the Nityas. That Bhagavān is now fast asleep laying on the bed with his divine consort, hence Āṇḍāḷ asks how right is it for you to sleep being the Lord of these Nitya sūris. Similar to the third pāsuram, here too Āṇḍāḷ describes about Trivikrama avatāra. When Aditi and Indra were in distress, He decided to help Indra and with begging as nimitta kāraṇa, he sprung to a massive form as Trivikrama and measured the whole world. That person who measured the whole world is sleeping now. Hence request the Supreme Lord to wake up and open the doors for them so that they can come and serve him.

Now seeing Kṛṣṇa still laying on the bed, Āṇḍāḷ tries to awaken his elder brother Balarāma. She realizes that only after waking up Balarāma will the mischievous Kṛṣṇa wake up! Balarāma is none other than Lakṣmaṇa. In Dvāpara he was conceived in the womb of Devakī later to be transported to Rohiṇī with the yogamāyā of Bhagavān who is also called as Durgā. In Rāmāyaṇa, fight between Vāli and Sugrīva took place with Rāma's task to slay Vāli. Though Rāma could easily distinguish both, the first try he enacted as if he couldn't. This was because Sugrīva paid respect to Rāma alone and not to Lakṣmaṇa. Only after Lakṣmaṇa put the garland on Sugrīva thereby blessing him that Rāma slayed Vāli. Hence here too Āṇḍāḷ asks Balarāma to wake up and wake up Kṛṣṇa too. Kṛṣṇa always listens to his elder brother. Hence Balarāma is capable of waking up Kṛṣṇa on command. It was Balarāma who consoled the gopikās when they left to Mathurā. Hence here they knew Balarāma will help them for sure. Rāma could live away from Sītā for 10 months in sorrow but for sure he cannot live without Lakṣmaṇa for a minute, that's how attached he was to him. Similarly Kṛṣṇa is closely attached to Balarāma. Balarāma being Ādiśeṣa eternally serves Bhagavān. If Kṛṣṇa sits, he becomes his chair; he stands, becomes umbrella; walks, he becomes pāduka; sleeps, he becomes the couch. Such is the service of Ādiśeṣa. Now laying down in the bliss due to the touch of Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma should wake up and help them listen to them. Isn't Balarāma the ācārya Rāmānuja who helped prapannas to reach Vaikuṇṭha? How so can he now stay asleep? Thereby she requests him to get up

meaning: Nanda has the strength of a tusker with dripping fat; he takes delight in fighting the elephants, of which he has a herd; and his might of arms knows no rebuff from the enemy! O you, daughter-in-law of Nandagōpa, arise! Nīladēvī, radiant with tresses wafting fragrance! Open the latch of the doors. The cocks have been crowing everywhere. The kokils, perching in groups on the lattice supported by mādhavī-creeper, have begun singing. Note, it is dawn. You who hold a ball in your hand! We tell you that we have come to glorify the qualities of our brother-in-law. Please wake up and walk to the threshold in joy and open the door, with the beautiful bracelets on your red-lotus hand making a loud jingling sound.
purport:
Kṛṣṇa still asleep, the gopikās realize that they have to approach someone who is inseparable to him, under whose influence he lives, without whom he can't stay away even for a moment. She is Mahālakṣmī called as Śrīdēvī. She manifests herself as Bhūdēvī and Nīladēvī. Here, Nīladēvī incarnates as Nappinnai, the daughter of a Yādava chieftain Kumbha who was a close friend of Nandagōpa. The chieftain is worried by few bulls causing issues to his subjects and speaks about it to Nandagōpa. Kṛṣṇa hearing this, defeats these bulls and immersed by this act, Nappinnai agrees to marry him. It is Nappinnai whom Āṇḍāḷ prays to wake up and thereby waking Kṛṣṇa too. The Pāñcarātra texts from which the Lakṣmī Tantra originates speaks about the divine relationship between the Supreme controller Nārāyaṇa and Śrī, his divine consort. Śrī represents the Kriyā Śakti of Bhagavān. Though she herself and Bhagavān are part and parcel i.e., different but can never be separated, as per the saṅkalpa of Bhagavān, she makes the prakṛti run. If he is sun, she is sun rays; if he is happiness, she is satisfaction. If we all are the jīva tattvas and the prakṛti is acetana tattva, Śrī and Nārāyaṇa who are inseparable together form the Īśvara tattva. She also represents the Dayā śakti or compassion of Bhagavān. She is the one who induces the will to grant liberation in him. Hence, Āṇḍāḷ and gopikās pray to her. The word Śrī represents 6 divine qualities of her. They are: One who solicits support, One whose support is sought, One who listens, One who communicates what one hears, One who helps ripening and the One who causes infliction of pain. It is she who acts as mediator called as Puruṣakāra when we have to be liberated. It is practically impossible to please Him without her support. It is her words which mesmerized Him to accept our surrender. Gopikās pray to her to wake up Kṛṣṇa and grant the opportunity to not just serve Kṛṣṇa but both of them together as a couple.

Nandagōpa here is said to hold tusks of defeated elephants. Though this might sound questionable, it is here Āṇḍāḷ referring to Nandagōpa as ācārya. Ācāryas should have the power to destroy all kinds of obstacles which come between disciples and the supreme such as ignorance, arrogance and others. Ācāryas are powerful like the mahouts who control strong elephants. Purandaradāsa calls Kṛṣṇa as māri aṇṇe i.e., baby elephant. He is powerful like an elephant but for sure yields to the mahout i.e., ācārya. The elephant listens to the small poking spear which is devotion. The elephant bends its leg for the mahout to climb similarly the Supreme does when he has to grant mokṣa to ācāryas. Once permission given by mahout, the elephant grants permission for others to climb upon just like the Supreme does for the disciples. Throughout the past eleven pāsurams, Āṇḍāḷ prays to different gopīs who are compared to ācāryas and calls upon them to shower their divine knowledge and experience. Now the ācārya too doesn't approach Bhagavān directly, he too approaches via Śrī i.e., here Nīladēvī. It is by her mediation we attain the compassion of Kṛṣṇa. In the Praṇava, A-kāra represents Bhagavān and m-kāra represents us. The u-kāra is the mediation which is Śrī who helps us connect to Bhagavān. So gopikās approach the divine mother now calling her daughter-in-law of Nandagōpa.

While Bhagavān is angered by our ill-actions which are against the śāstras and Vedas, he is disappointed we are not approaching him and if we do, we are doing it after eternity. He is unable to bear this but is mellowed down by the divine mother. She touches him and hugs him thereby letting the soft flowers press his chest softening him. Her compassion, beauty, her qualities make Bhagavān go insane for her. He listens to her without a question, and by her referral to forgive us, he burns our sins. Hence gopikās call her to be wearing the flowers. The divine mother holds prakṛti as a ball in one hand of hers and Bhagavān's hand in another. He listens to her words. Sustaining, protecting this universe like a ball for a long time, her hand has turned red like lotus. Like the lotus she has beauty, like its fragrance she has knowledge which she grants to jīvātmās like us. It is by her grace we climb the stairs of bhakti from viveka, vairāgya, bhakti, parā bhakti, parā jñāna and finally a state where we have lost ourselves and only in service to Bhagavān called parama bhakti. Āṇḍāḷ calls upon a creeper on which kokils are singing. Here the creeper is the divine mother and the kokils are the ācāryas and āḷvārs. She supports our devotion and great ācāryas enable it to reach to larger mass. Gopikās want Nīladēvī to come and open the door by waking and walking towards the door. They too want to see her mesmerizing beauty which has mesmerized the Supreme being itself, see her bangles which jingle when trying to open the door. This pāsuram is nectarful and speaks about the essence of dvaya mantra. Rāmānujācārya used to recite Tiruppāvai everyday but used to love this pāsuram and the upcoming 29th one.
