meaning:
On a bed, distinguished for its comforts of height and width, coolness, whiteness and softness, spread on a cot with ivory leg-supports, and surrounded by clusters of wicks burning bright, lies Nīladēvī with bunches of blooming flowers decorating plaits of her tresses; and close to her sleeps, Kṛṣṇa with his broad bosom pressing her breasts.
O Kṛṣṇa! Won't you open your mouth and speak! O Nīladēvī! how impressive are your large eyes decorated with collyrium! How long will you prevent your lover from rising? Not to endure separation from him, even for a while, is inconsistent with your nature and your characteristic tendency!
purport:
After waking up the gopī, Āṇḍāḷ with all the gopikās try to wake up Kṛṣṇa with his divine consort Nīladēvī. In the supreme abode Vaikuṇṭha, Śrī, the divine consort who is inseparable from Lord expands herself as aṃśas in Bhū and Nīladēvī. The Vedas glorify her as Nīlā in Nīlā Sūktam, a part of Taittirīya Saṃhitā. Āṇḍāḷ prays to Nīladēvī to wake up Kṛṣṇa, who is mesmerized by the beautiful eyes of Nīlā and lays on the bed with his broad chest pressing against her blossoms. It is a common principle to always approach the provider who is of higher status through the referral of a mediator. Similarly, a mumukṣu approaches Nārāyaṇa for liberation and the fulfillment of serving him eternally through Lakṣmī, she being the mediator. The Pāñcarātra Āgamas beautifully glorify this as Lakṣmī being the will of mercy and Nārāyaṇa who acts upon. He is called as the protector because he acts on the will of mercy which is Mahālakṣmī. She indeed is called as Dayā Dēvī. To this Śrītattva, Āṇḍāḷ (who herself is incarnation of Lakṣmī) prays to wake up Kṛṣṇa and fulfill our desire to serve the eternal couple.

On the ivory-legged bed lay the divine couple immersed in love. Behind them there is a lamp burning with five wicks. The lamp represents Nīladēvī. A lamp has the unique nature to shower brightness thereby making itself visible and making the surroundings visible too. Bhagavān is difficult to be perceived by our own efforts. Our Karmas restrict us to see him. Immersed in Ānanda he stays. To us who are suffering in saṃsāra, his beloved showers compassion. Pity on us she develops the will in him to look at us and take us. Just like the lamp she decides to show herself and from her compassion leads us to Nārāyaṇa thereby becoming the mediator. Through providing us knowledge via the 5 lights from 5 wicks which are: Smṛti, Śruti, Purāṇa, Itihāsa and Āgama, she helps us reach him. This lamp can be moved anywhere. Unlike us, who are bonded to this Saṃsāra and hence the constant association with Kṛṣṇa is difficult, Nīlā on the other hand is independent and can always be with him. She doesn't have any restrictions of dawn and night. Through her own will she serves him with love and devotion. This Nīladēvī has mesmerized Kṛṣṇa with her lotus-like eyes which is not letting him be away from her. Āṇḍāḷ prays to provide us too the bliss of the divine couple. Both are immersed in ānanda, due to their very nature, similar to Rāma and Sītā in vanavāsa who enjoyed each other. Vālmīki quotes that Lakṣmaṇa too was in Ānanda, but why was he in bliss? For Lakṣmaṇa, serving the divine couple itself is great bliss and hence the three all together were in ānanda. Āṇḍāḷ prays to offer us too the same opportunity to serve them.

The ivory stand of the bed represents Kṛṣṇa being the great warrior, the one who defeated the elephant of Kaṃsa called Kuvalayāpīḍa by removing its huge tusks. Nīladēvī is the warrior consort of this Kṛṣṇa. The aspect here is similar to Nīladēvī, all the prapannas i.e. the surrendered ones fear nothing. They have completely surrendered to Lord and hence entire responsibility of theirs has been put upon him. Sītā didn't fear to walk in the forests, she had complete faith in Rāma, so too the prapannas. They, the Īśvara tattvas, lay on this bed immersed with love towards each other. When the jīvātma attains liberation, it climbs the couch of Ādiśeṣa to attain the lap of Bhagavān where questioning who it is, it says "Ahaṃ Brahmāsmi" i.e. I have realized the antaryāmī within me who I am subservient to. To attain the bed of Nārāyaṇa i.e. Mokṣa, it is one of the Brahma Vidyās called Paryaṅka Vidyā. He, the Para Vāsudeva, rests upon such a bed with jñāna, bhakti, vairāgya, aiśvarya as the supports, which here are compared to ivory ones. Thereby Āṇḍāḷ requests her wake up Kṛṣṇa. "How is it possible for a mother to rest well when her children are suffering? How are you able to rest with Kṛṣṇa O Divine mother, when we are screaming loud for your help to serve you and him! Please do let us also rest upon the bed where you two lay" Āṇḍāḷ states. The divine bed has five natures; Coolness and warmth according to surroundings, Fragrance, Whiteness, Softness, Spaciousness. These five represent the Arthapañcaka of Śāstras i.e. "The nature of Brahman to be attained, The nature of the individual self that is worthy to attain, The means to attain God, The result to be gained by the attainment of God, The impediments to the attainment of God." Thus who realizes this fivefold knowledge attains Vaikuṇṭha.

Nīladēvī adorns divine flowers which are blessed to touch Kṛṣṇa when he presses his divine chest. The gathered group with Āṇḍāḷ have vowed not to wear flowers until they meet Kṛṣṇa. Āṇḍāḷ asks the divine mother how right is it to wear flowers when your children cannot wear them as the flowers would fade with the heat of separation of these. Hence, she asks her to bestow the same pleasure of association with Kṛṣṇa to them. Now they peek to see that Nīladēvī wakes up to open the door on the other hand Kṛṣṇa pulls her and throws her on bed, letting her rest upon his broad shoulders. Now Āṇḍāḷ calls upon Kṛṣṇa "Kṛṣṇa, you are immersed towards her and her tresses touch you, that touch blossoms the flowers. But can't you spare one word for us? We desire your happiness alone, O Lord please open the door!". The Supreme is avikāra i.e. he doesn't change, neither does he expand or contract yet due to kinship with Śrī he blossoms like a flower. That blossom is his compassion. Āṇḍāḷ doesn't want to separate them which Rāvaṇa did, hence she just wants to hear the words of protection from Kṛṣṇa.

Resting below Lord, Nīladēvī wears the black collyrium. Her eyes have made Bhagavān go insane for her. Like a fish which protects its eggs just with its eyes, so does Bhagavān protect his children. But if his eyes are keeping us alive, it's her eyes which keep him alive. Looking at her encapsulating eyes Kṛṣṇa says "I cannot live without looking at this beauty even for a minute". It looks as if she is not letting him get up or speak. Āṇḍāḷ beautifully quotes "You are not ready to let your love wake up. You have entangled yourself with him, his will being yours and your will being his. You can never be away from him, always resting on his chest. Yet physically you still do not want to remain away from him, hence are you not letting him wake up O mother? Is it fair to your children like us who want him? You have monopolized him, he is yours. Please let us too near him. We are not here to separate you two like Rāvaṇa but here to serve you two as the divine supreme couple!" She further continues saying "This is not of your true nature. You are the divine mother filled with compassion alone. Ready to bestow anything asked for! You are known for your nature of easy accessibility, compassion and love. Please favor us and let us serve you two." Lakṣmī is personification of compassion. She will bestow anything to her children from material wealth to Bhagavān himself. After all he is her treasury! When asked by Hanumān who was ready to crush rākṣasīs of Laṅkā, she bestowed protection on them as they internally had surrendered to her. Even without any explicit call she assured protection. Now Āṇḍāḷ asks to bestow the similar oppurtunity serve Kṛṣṇa to them. She being the Queen and divinity of Lord as stated by Śrī Sūktam, bestows all kind of pleasures to her children. The reference to Āṇḍāḷ asking for opportunity to serve the divine couple to Nīladēvī is beautifully captured by Rāmānujācārya in his Śaraṇāgati Gadyam where he calls her as a reflection of Lord with all attributes same as his, qualities same as his to bestow the opportunity to serve them and their devotees, to bestow the referral for Mokṣa.

meaning: O Puissant Warrior! How graciously you advance into the battlefield long before danger threatens, and stand in the forefront if only to rescue thirty-three crores of celestials from fear of their enemies! Pray, wake up! Of immense strength and great uprightness and absolute purity, you are by nature inclined always to give protection; and regarding the foes of your suppliants as your own enemies, you strike them with terror. We request you to wake up. O Nīladēvī, how perfect you are in beauty with breasts like gold tumblers and ruby nether lip (resembling the fruit of coccinia indica—doṇḍa, kovai), and slender waist! Pray, wake up! Full of perfection, you are equal to Lakṣmī. Do give us the fan and the mirror; and help us to bathe together with your lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
purport:
Trying to wake up Kṛṣṇa now, the gopikās question him for lying down even after their call. They ask him, "Will you only wake up and answer calls to the 33 devatās who come and seek your protection from asuras, daityas, and rākṣasas?" Bhagavān exists in different states. The Pañcarātra texts split these states into 4 primary forms: Para, Vyūha, Vibhava, and Arcā. It is in the Vyūha rūpa that he stays as Kṣīrābdinātha, laying on the cosmic ocean. Here is where devatās come and seek his help. When Indra lost all wealth by the curse of Durvāsa, he and the 33 devatās—8 Vasus, 12 Ādityas, 11 Rudras, and the twins Aśvinī Kumāras—come and seek his help. From his advice, they churn the cosmic ocean yet face difficulty in taking Mount Meru from its position. It is Bhagavān with his Sudarśana cakra who removes the Meru and then carries it upon Garuḍa. Later, when the churning Meru is sinking without a base, again Bhagavān incarnates as Kūrma, letting the Meru churn. The devatās and asuras lose strength while churning, and it is Bhagavān who enters them and provides strength. Again, at the end, he is the one who brings the elixir, Amṛta, as Dhanvantari. When this Amṛta was stolen by asuras, he is the one who deludes them as Mohinī. In all instances, he protects the devatās. Hence, Āṇḍāl questions, "Will you only listen to their calls? Are you going to wait for them to join us and call you? Won't you listen to us who have come here to serve you? The devatās sought your help for their own purposes, but we seek you to serve you, for you alone, yet why don't you listen to us? Have you vowed not to help us? Please awaken, O protector of all!"

Kṛṣṇa is known for his uprightness and purity. As he himself states in Bhagavad Gītā 9.20: "samo'haṃ sarvabhūteṣu na me dveṣyo'sti na priyaḥ ye bhajanti tu māṃ bhaktyā mayi te teṣu cāpyaham," i.e., he doesn't hate anyone or hold anyone especially dear, yet those who have realized he is the source of all and surrendered to him, they reside in him and he resides in them. He is like the sun whose grace, in the form of sun rays, indiscriminately reaches everywhere. Due to our clouds of karma, we might sometimes be deprived of these rays, but when we remove the ignorance, his rays fall upon us. Hence, though he never discriminates and provides everyone what they deserve, he loves his devotees, especially the prapannas. Hence, he is pure and always protects his devotees. Āṇḍāl reminds Kṛṣṇa of his affection towards his devotees. When he entered the court of Hastināpura as a messenger from the Pāṇḍavas, the courtiers saw who he truly was! Later, when asked to stay in the palace, he replies by saying, "It is improper to eat in the house of enemies or to feed enemies. Though I am a friend to all, you have enmity towards the Pāṇḍavas, who are my life and breath; hence you have gained my enmity too." When Arjuna decides to kill Jayadratha for not letting Yudhiṣṭhira protect Abhimanyu, he vows that if he doesn't do so by sunset, he would enter the fires to perish. Kṛṣṇa, angered by Arjuna's impetuous action done in anger, advises him to be well prepared. The previous night, worried about Arjuna, he asks Sātyaki to prepare his chariot. He is ready to break his vow of not fighting to protect Arjuna. When Bhīṣma threatens Arjuna, an angered Kṛṣṇa picks up the chariot wheel, transforming it into Sudarśana, ready to slay Bhīṣma—he broke the vow for the sake of protecting Arjuna. Without a doubt, he loves his devotees incomparably. Now Āṇḍāl asks, "Such is your nature, and hence you need to protect us and listen to us; please wake up!"

Seeing Kṛṣṇa still sleeping, the gopikās continue to pray to Nīlādevī. They beautifully describe her beauty. Her waist is thin as she desires nothing and is immersed in Bhagavān. But Kṛṣṇa too is in deep love with her. He rests on her bosom. Her two breasts represent the two states of bhakti: parā bhakti and parama bhakti. He has been captivated by her and would not move an inch without her permission. Her bosom is soft and has captivated him. Only when she lets him move from her captivating bosom is when he can awaken and listen to their plea. Hence, please wake up and awaken Kṛṣṇa too!

The gopikās seek Nīlādevī to grant them fan and mirror and arrange a bath for them with Kṛṣṇa. The bath represents total immersion with Kṛṣṇa by serving him. The fan dries sweat and provides relief. The 'Namaḥ' mantra provides the jīvātmā relief from sorrows of ahaṅkāra and mamakāra. On the other hand, the mirror shows the reflection. Similarly, the Praṇava mantra shows the svarūpa of jīvātmā—that it is the subservient of the Lord. Only when these three are granted is the jīvātmā eligible for mokṣa; hence they seek Nīlādevī to grant them.

O glorious protector, valiant and unwavering in your promise to shelter all who seek refuge, awaken from your divine slumber! You, who shine as a radiant form of effulgence in this world, hear us now. Just as your foes, subdued by your boundless valour, fall humbly at your feet in surrender, so too have we come—drawn by love, unable to remain apart. At your threshold we stand, yearning to sing your praise and offer our heartfelt benedictions.
purport:
O son of Nandagopa, guardian of countless strong cows—those bountiful givers whose udders overflow with milk, filling every vessel to the brim—awake! O embodiment of the Supreme, whose might is upheld by the scriptures and whose radiance manifests even in the darkest corners of this world, arise! O valiant protector, ever ready to shelter the surrendered, wake from your divine rest. Just as your enemies, vanquished by your boundless valor, come humbly to your feet, so too have we—irresistibly drawn by love—gathered at your threshold to sing your praises and offer our benedictions.

Andal, in calling you the son of Nandagopa, presents more than a familial identity. She reveals a profound truth: Nanda represents the Acharya—the spiritual preceptor—through whom one gains access to the Divine. Without the Acharya’s grace, one cannot approach Bhagavan, let alone attain liberation. In likening Nanda to the owner of countless cows, Andal alludes to the boundless virtues of an Acharya—rooted in the Vedas—foremost among them being the eagerness to share spiritual knowledge the moment a disciple yearns for it, just as cows pour forth milk when pots are placed beneath them. Acharyas spiritual genius and influence are immense. Like Nanda’s cows—too numerous to count—their qualities are infinite, just as one cannot number the virtues of Sri Rama, the incarnations of the Lord, or the births of sentient beings. Even Krishna takes pride in this connection, preferring to be known as Nanda’s son, for the wealth of spiritual richness it represents. Though He is the Supreme, He chooses to descend among the cowherds, delighting in their simple devotion. The gopikas remind Him that His birthright and heritage are theirs too, and the abundance He has inherited should be for their protection—not to lull Him into slumber. Once He awakens, all sorrow dissolves; and if sorrow persists, the blame would be His alone. Thus, they call out to Him, urging Him to rise, that their longings may be fulfilled.

The five attributes of Nandagopa—his vigilant protection, noble leadership, generous charity, great strength, and possession of infinite cows—mirror the fivefold glories of an Acharya: his deep love for the Lord whom he blesses as if in need of protection; his inability to keep spiritual bliss to himself, sharing it freely; his transmission of mantras that lead to realization; his power to overcome spiritual obstacles; and his eloquence that lights the way for countless disciples. These disciples, in turn, become vessels of wisdom, just as the cows of Nanda nourish without end. The gopikas further affirm that this Divine Being, Krishna, is no ordinary child but the very Paratattva—the Supreme Reality—firmly established on the highest authority, the Vedas, which are not of human origin and hence immune to error. The strength of the Supreme lies in being supported by such flawless testimony. Inferential logic falters, but the Vedas remain unshakable, eternal, and pure—united in declaring Krishna to be none other than Srimannarayana. Though He transcends thought and speech, He reveals Himself by grace to those who seek Him, appearing in flesh and form for the benefit of the world.

So the gopikas exclaim: Ottamudaiyay! Periyay!—“O One founded on the strongest truth! O One of unmeasurable greatness!” The Vedas, trying to grasp His vast bliss, confess defeat: words and mind alike turn back. Yet, by His own will, this Effulgence emerges in the world—Ulaginil toṭṟamāy ninṛa sudarē!—taking human form, not due to karma but out of compassion. Though amidst the fallen world, He remains unsullied, shining even brighter. His greatness is such that even His partiality to devotees causes His enemies, like Śiśupāla and Duryodhana, to scorn Him. But for those who understand, this same favoritism becomes the gateway to grace. Even as a charioteer or envoy, Krishna embraces servitude for the sake of His devotees—showing that His compassion is His crowning glory. To ignore such excellence would diminish His own virtues, and so the gopikas urge Him to awaken, lest those qualities be defiled by inaction.

They declare: “Like your enemies, who surrender at your feet after defeat, we too come—overcome not by fear but by your beauty, mercy, and charm. Our sins are as grave as theirs; our distance from you as deep. But unlike them, we come not for gain, but to sing your greatness. We’ve tried all else, failed, and now stand surrendered, hearts broken by your attributes.” Just as Kāka Asura, unable to escape, returns to Rama for protection, so too do the gopikas confess: “We are no better than Rāvaṇa, filled with pride and blindness. Yet now, we relinquish all notions of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ and submit at your feet.” Though true surrender requires complete dependence and no initiative, the gopikas, like Sita awaiting Rama, break from protocol—drawn irresistibly to Krishna’s grace. They know their coming is forbidden, yet they come nonetheless, for their hearts have been captured by His virtues. They confess: “We, who should not have come, have come—like the enemies who surrender out of necessity, but we, out of love. Even if we perish, let your glory shine.” Like the Āḻvārs, they seek no return to their old lives of ego and bondage, but wish only to remain near Him, forever praising the One who was, is, and always will be their eternal refuge.

meaning:
Just as mighty kings, once rulers of vast and resplendent realms, abandon their pride—believing no force could surpass their own—and humbly gather before the throne of a conquering emperor, so too have we assembled in great numbers beneath your divine seat of glory, our ego utterly broken, our arrogance cast aside. We come not as subjects, but as surrendered souls, yearning for your mercy.

O Lord, gently part your eyes—those lotus-like eyes, half-open like the tender lips of a blossoming bell, blushed with the warmth of your compassion. Let them fall upon us with kindness. If those divine eyes, shining like the sun and the moon rising together in the firmament, were to glance our way, even the heaviest burdens of karma, once fastened to our fate like an unshakable curse, would dissolve and disappear—unable to withstand the brilliance of your gaze.
purport:
Just as kings who once ruled vast and splendid realms abandon their pride and kneel before the triumphant emperor, so too do we, stripped of ego and humbled, gather beneath your divine seat. Though rulers of their lands, those kings forget that the Supreme alone is the true possessor, while they are but dependent souls feigning dominion. So also are we—individual selves mistakenly believing in our own independence—now returning to your feet, realizing we are yours alone, like queens surrendering before the one true King.

From Brahma to the lowliest ant, all beings suffer from the same delusion: that what they see, feel, or command belongs to them. Yet their positions—earned by karma and gifted by grace—are but roles in a play designed by the Lord. The more one clings to ego, the deeper the sorrow becomes. Only when this conceit collapses can the soul draw near to the Supreme. Even Brahma, blessed by divine births, attains liberation only after long penance and divine mercy. But the humble, with no possessions to surrender, reach God with ease, for they have always believed all belongs to Him.

The gopikas mirror these humbled kings. They leave behind the pride of femininity and gather not before a throne, but beneath Krishna’s couch—seeking not restoration but refuge. They fear returning to worldly roles, lest others misread their silence as independence. Instead, they choose to remain together at His feet, proclaiming their belonging by their closeness. Like Bharata, who faints at being called a king, they refuse titles and roles that separate them from Him. Togetherness beneath the Lord’s gaze is their only desire.

They wonder how, after countless births and estrangement, they now find themselves near Him. Like the Emperor’s son raised by hunters who discovers his true heritage, they awaken to their natural kinship with Krishna. Karma had hidden it; now grace reveals it. Their long journey back to Him—slow, subtle, and blessed—unfolds like a miracle. Like Hanuman, a monkey entrusted with divine service, they marvel at the union of the lowly with the Lord.

Now, exhausted by separation, they beg for a tender, gradual glance. They compare His half-open eyes to the shy bloom of a lotus or the gentle lips of a bell, asking for His mercy to arrive like gentle rain after a drought. Sudden grace may overwhelm their fragile hearts—let it come slowly, nourishing them like starved souls fed with care. For in those eyes—half-open with mercy, glowing red with love—they find the healing of all sorrow, the end of all curses, and the dawn of bliss in union with the Supreme.

meaning: Like the lion who, after resting motionless in his mountain cave through the long monsoon, suddenly awakens—his eyes fierce and scanning the forest, his mane bristling, his limbs stretching wide—he shakes his mighty frame, roars aloud, and strides out, majestic and unstoppable— So too, O Lord, whose radiant form mirrors the deep blue hue of the ātasi flower, do arise from your divine repose. Step forth from your sacred abode, where time itself seems to pause in reverence, and ascend your peerless throne, the seat graced by endless celestial associations. Let your movements stir the very core of creation. Let your eyes fall upon us as the lion surveys his domain—not with wrath, but with the command of a guardian awakened. And then, we pray—listen. Lend your ear to our lowly yet earnest voices. We, who have waited, who have yearned, stand gathered at your gate, hoping that the King of kings might hear our call.
purport:
The lion, that has long lain asleep in his mountain-den during the rainy season, slowly begins to emerge. This monsoon season—chāturmāsya kāla—is not merely a meteorological period, but a sacred juncture for kings, poets, lovers, and ascetics. During these four months, wandering mendicants (yatis) stay in a fixed place and engage in deep meditation, undertaking the vow of chāturmāsya dīkṣā. Lovers separated by distance are tormented by longing, while poets, stirred by the cloud-filled skies, give birth to inspired verse. Kings suspend martial activities as roads vanish beneath rainwaters, and even enmities seem to dissolve.

It is said that during this time, Śrīmannārāyaṇa enters yogic slumber in His heavenly abode, Vaikuṇṭha. Lions, abandoning the hunt, retreat to their dens with their mates to rest. Śrī Rāma, though anguished by separation from Sītā, assists Sugrīva by slaying Vāli, only to spend the monsoon in the Malyavat mountains alongside Lakṣmaṇa, waiting for the season to pass. Sugrīva, reunited with his kingdom and his wife, loses himself in pleasure, forgetting his debt to Rāma. Rāma, beholding the rainclouds, is overcome with grief, thinking of His distant beloved.

The raincloud, symbolizing both hope and melancholy, has captivated sages like Vālmīki, Kālidāsa, and Śūdraka. In Kālidāsa’s Meghadūta, the cloud is animated as a loving messenger. This season signifies the transition from summer to winter, bringing inner and outer fertility—nourishing harvests and awakening the milk of cows. But alongside this physical rain lies another rain—an inner, spiritual shower. Śrī Yāmunācārya describes this as follows: “aviveka-ghaṇāndha digmukhe, bahudhā santata-duḥkha-darśini,
Bhagavan bhava-durdine pathitaṁ, mām avalokaya acyuta!” Ignorance, the thick cloud of aviveka, blinds the soul, causing it to drift in all directions, unable to discern its path. This ignorance rains down endless sorrow upon the jīva, binding it in saṁsāra. The gopikās, feeling like wanderers lost in torrential rain, plead for the Lord’s compassion to show them the path of liberation.

But there is another, redemptive rain: the downpour of divine grace (anugraha), rising from the waves of the ocean of His mercy, blown by the wind of compassion. This divine shower alone can save us. As sentient beings are tossed about on the sea of saṁsāra, it is God, out of sheer mercy, who rescues them. In both creation and dissolution, His grace operates—drawing the universe into Himself, filling all space, and entering into deep yogic sleep, like the lion in the mountain-cave. During pralaya, all beings—great or low—merge into Him. He shines silently in the cavern of the Vedas, veiled from manifest perception. In that undivided state, there is nothing distinct from Him. As the Upaniṣads declare: “sa devah asīd ekam eva advitīyam” – That Deva alone was, One without a second.

Just as the lion lies unseen in his den, the Supreme rests in a state far beyond comprehension. Yet, this state is not inert; it is alive with potential, with all of His auspicious attributes latent within. Dharma, the Supreme itself, is the means of abhyudaya (temporal progress) and niḥśreyasa (eternal beatitude). The Vedas declare that the essence of Dharma lies hidden in a cave: “dharmasya tattvaṁ nihitaṁ guhāyām.” This truth is subtle, elusive, and perceptible only through intense effort. As Sage Bharadvāja once saw the Vedas as towering mountains, so too is the Supreme veiled—its glory only revealed through persistent seeking.

meaning: Blessed be Thy divine feet, O Vāmana, with which Thou didst measure the three worlds—received as alms from King Mahābali, who, though possessing what was not his, caused distress to the amṛtas. Blessed be Thy strong and mighty arms, O Rāghava, with which Thou didst shatter the walls of Laṅkā, burn its splendid mansions, and destroy Rāvaṇa and his army for abducting Sītā Devī. Blessed be Thy wondrous glory, O Kṛṣṇa, when as a child, with an effortless stretch of Thy foot, Thou didst crush the demon lurking in the cart, which turned from protector to threat. Blessed be Thy sturdy legs, planted firm—one forward, one behind—when Thou hurled the demon-possessed calf upon the wood-apple tree, felling both in a single act. Blessed be Thy compassion, revealed in lifting Govardhana as a great umbrella to shield the gopas and cows from the thunderous storm Indra unleashed in his anger at being denied worship. Blessed be Thy divine discus, the Vēlāyudha, which in Thy hands whirls as the remover of obstacles and the vanquisher of foes. We have come to celebrate these valorous deeds and receive from Thee the parai, the sacred drum of our nōnpu. May Thou, O Lord, accept our devotion and grant our prayer.
purport:
This pāsuram opens with aṉṉiṟu—“then”—pointing to the time when Śrī Vāmana, the dwarf-incarnation, stretched his foot across the universe, humbling the pride of Mahābali. It concludes with iṉṟu—“now”—referring to the present moment when the gopikās lovingly impose strain upon the divine feet of Kaṇṇaṉ (Kṛṣṇa) by their service. These two instances—then and now—are equal in intimacy and reverence for the devotees. In three key pāsurams (3, 17, and 24), Āṇḍāḷ glorifies the Trivikrama avatāra, revealing its intimate relation to the accessible and enchanting avatāra of Kṛṣṇa. Vāmana’s act of laying claim to the universe without distinction, irrespective of people's desire or worthiness, mirrors the irresistible charm of Kṛṣṇa that pulls the gopikās to Him, shedding social norms, familial restraint, and personal pride (naṉṉeñjam, feminine propriety). The same divine feet that crushed the ego of Mahābali now trample upon the vanity of the gopikās' womanly pride.

Mahābali’s fall represents the human soul's (jīvātmā’s) egoistic bondage, forged through identification with prakṛti (primordial nature). He imagined himself the lord of the worlds, mistaking his transient ownership and actions as independent of Īśvara’s will. By placing His divine foot upon Bali, the Lord demonstrated that all possessions, power, and very selfhood (ahaṅkāra) are to be surrendered at His feet. In that act of subjugation, there were no contemporaries to celebrate or sing pōṟṟi (praise) for those divine feet. Now, as the gopikās see themselves freed from the grip of bodily pride and feminine hesitation by surrendering to Kṛṣṇa’s feet, they recall Trivikrama’s act and redeem that forgotten moment of glory by singing benediction. Pōṟṟi kaḷaḷaṭikaḷ!—Blessed are those tender yet all-encompassing feet!

Āṇḍāḷ, the daughter of Periyāḻvār, inherits his bhakti tradition of pallāṇḍu—auspicious benedictions. When Periyāḻvār was granted vision of the Lord during his royal court debate, he instinctively began to sing Pallāṇḍu pallāṇḍu! fearing an evil eye may fall upon the Lord. So too, Āṇḍāḷ begins this verse with pōṟṟi pōṟṟi—singing the auspiciousness of Kṛṣṇa’s limbs and deeds, especially His feet. She poetically feels that even when Vāmana sanctified the cosmos with His divine touch, no one was there to celebrate that act. Thus, the gopikās take it upon themselves to offer that missing maṅgalaśāsanam. Vāmana’s soft, lotus-like feet, so delicate that even Śrī and Bhū Devīs feared touching them lest they become sore, trod upon the rough, stone-laden earth with grace and compassion. Yet the very earth, dull and ungrateful, failed to rejoice or even recognize the sacred contact. Still, He claimed it all in silent, sovereign love.

This indifference did not bother Trivikrama; He stood above all, unshaken. Bali sulked, having lost his kingdom. Śukrācārya tried in vain to stop the offering. The devas, reclaiming their realms, departed without offering gratitude. No one offered even a simple pōṟṟi to those aching, divine feet. The gopikās, feeling anguished by this oversight, now amend it. Kaḷaḷ pōṟṟi!—let those divine feet be praised! Through this, Āṇḍāḷ not only praises the act but the Lord’s unfathomable saulabhya (accessibility), His readiness to endure for the sake of reclaiming the jīvātmā. His act of measuring the worlds was not just conquest—it was a reclamation, a gesture of affection, even when unrecognized. And yet, He did not pause for thanks; instead, He carried out the act for dharma, for re-establishing rightful order. The gopikās, unlike the others, understand this and sing with full heart.

In Trivikrama’s feet, the gopikās see the essence of śaraṇāgati—surrender. For them, it is not a historical act but a present, living experience. The pride that Mahābali bore is not unlike the pride they see subdued within themselves. The yearning they carry is not simply to praise, but to prevent harm—to guard those limbs from any evil, any fatigue, any oversight. And so they sing, not once, but again and again, in a mad repetition born out of love, fear, and devotion. They internalize pōṟṟi as not a formality but a sacred, essential act—protective, possessive, and devotional. It is their natural tongue, their nāma, their lifeline. As Periyāḻvār could not stop with a single pallāṇḍu, Āṇḍāḷ too cannot refrain from her cascade of pōṟṟi.

This is not literary; this is lived bhakti. The gopikās’ glorification of Trivikrama's feet is not just remembrance—it is re-experiencing. It is an act of love where each pōṟṟi carries within it a shield, a flower, a tear, a touch. Their glorification stems not from witnessing, but from identification. They do not view the Lord's actions from afar but step into it—feeling His pain, carrying His strain, and rejoicing in His compassion. They offer benediction not as spectators, but as intimate ātmābandhus—souls entwined with the Divine. And thus, they begin the hymn with what was once left unsaid: Pōṟṟi kaḷaḷaṭikaḷ—blessed be those divine feet that once walked the worlds, and now walk into our hearts.

tiruttakka śelvamum śēvagamum yām pāḍi
varuttamum tīrndu magizndēlōr em pāvāy
meaning:
O Kṛṣṇa! To fulfil the wish of peerless Devakī-devī to bear Bhagavān as her son, you were born to her, bearing the conch (śaṅkha), discus (cakra), mace (gadā), and lotus (padma) in your four arms. Yet, that very night, you became the son of glorious Yaśodā, who alone was blessed to bind, chastise, and delight in your divine līlās.

Growing up in secret at Vṛndāvana, you thwarted every wicked plot of Kaṁsa and destroyed the one who sought to destroy you. Ever compassionate to those who seek refuge, we too come to you, desiring nothing but your grace. If pleased, grant us the parai.

Our weariness melts into bliss when we sing of your unmatched wealth—coveted even by Lakṣmī—and your countless heroic deeds.
purport:
Kṛṣṇa, though born to Dēvaki, the illustrious queen of Mathurā, did not remain even for a full night with her. That same night, under the weight of divine ordainment, he was transferred to Gokula to become the foster-son of Yaśōdā, the cowherdess of unparalleled fortune. The Āḻvārs and ācāryas refer to both these exalted women as orutti—"a woman"—not out of disregard, but out of deep reverence. According to traditional etiquette, one avoids naming the most sacred persons directly, choosing instead such respectful circumlocutions. Dēvaki was the womb that bore the Para Brahman—ēkam ēva advitīyam—without undergoing any change herself, making her utterly unique among all mothers in the cosmos. She bore in her womb not a jīva with karma, but the Kāraṇa bhūta—the Supreme Cause of all creation.

Yet, it was Yaśōdā who received the full sweetness (mādhurya) of the Lord’s vātśalya-līlā, his childhood pastimes. While Dēvaki had the privilege of giving birth to the Supreme Lord in his divya-mūrti, it was Yaśōdā who got to nurse, scold, cajole, and even bind him. She played with him, bathed him, dressed him, and watched him grow—privileges denied to even the devas. Though Kṛṣṇa was born of Dēvaki, he never cried in her arms nor drank her milk. He first expressed his human behavior—crying, suckling—only after reaching Yaśōdā. Hence, even Kṛṣṇa himself regarded Yaśōdā as his true mother and addressed Nanda as his father, stammering the words “adē appā” when asked by villagers.

His descent was marked by utmost secrecy. He who is beyond time and space entered time during that unique, transcendent night—a night like no other—when Yamunā parted, chains broke, and Ādiśeṣa bore him across to safety. That divine night, oriravu, is described as “without a second” just like Dēvaki and Yaśōdā are “without equals.” The Supreme descended, bearing the symbols of his transcendence—śaṅkha, cakra, gadā, and padma—and yet, subjected himself to the distress of secrecy and exile, for the sake of his devotees. The joy of birth, the celebration due to Dēvaki and Vasudēva, was denied. There was no grand cradle ceremony, no open celebration—just silence and hiddenness. For the Lord’s avatāra is not merely a spectacle—it is an act of anugraha (grace) and anubhava (intimacy).

Kaṁsa, the embodiment of ahaṅkāra (ego), could not bear the very thought (ninaindu) of the Lord. Though he never saw Kṛṣṇa directly, he was agitated upon hearing of him through Nārada, just as the ego trembles at the truth of the Self. This isn’t merely mythic villainy—it reflects the internal struggle of the bound jīva, which resists the divine within. Kaṁsa devised numerous cruel plans to thwart destiny, sending asuras like Pūtanā, Śakaṭāsura, and Tṛṇāvarta—all reflections of various inner obstructions to bhakti. But Kṛṣṇa, out of compassion for his devotees, consumed that very fire of fear and redirected it into Kaṁsa’s heart. What once tormented Yaśōdā and the gopikās was turned into Kaṁsa’s own internal agony. The Lord, like Anjanēya who used Sītā’s grief to burn Laṅkā, transformed the anxiety of his devotees into Kaṁsa’s demise.

The gopikās, aware of this entire sequence of divine acts, say “unnai aruṭṭittu vāndōm”—“We have come here desiring only you.” Not your miracles, not your protection, not even parai (the ritual drum). Their bhakti is ananya—exclusive, unswerving. They seek not reward, nor relief, nor ritualistic outcomes—but the Svarūpa (essential being) of the Lord himself. Their act of coming—through night and dew, forsaking modesty and societal censure—demonstrates that their prīti (affection) surpasses even his dayā (compassion). If he has descended from Vaikuṇṭha for their sake, they too have left behind every comfort and identity just to be with him. Their bhakti is not transactional—it is pūrṇa, complete.

When questioned about the parai, they gently clarify: “We will receive it only if it is your will. We do not ask—your will alone matters.” This reflects the viśuddha-sattva nature of true devotion. Even if Kṛṣṇa offers something they hadn’t sought, they will accept—not out of desire, but obedience and surrender. Asking would imply agency; receiving with humility reflects the śaraṇāgati tattva.

And in the final lines, they assert: “tiruttakka selvamum, śrīvagamum, yam paṭi varuttamum, tīrndu magiḻndu”—“We are relieved of every strain and filled with bliss by singing your glory and magnificence, which even Lakṣmī herself desires.” His aiśvarya (opulence) and vīrya (valour) are such that even Śrī Lakṣmī, the goddess of wealth and prosperity, seeks shelter in him. Kṛṣṇa is not merely Śrī-nātha (consort of Lakṣmī)—he is Śriyah Śrīḥ—the wealth of Lakṣmī herself. His bhāgyam (fortune) is self-existent, inexhaustible, and ever-fresh. Singing about such a Lord removes not just fatigue, but even the trace of grief (duḥkha). Just as nāmasankīrtana (Pundarīkākṣa-nāma-saṅkīrtana) is the sustenance (pāṭhēya) for the spiritual journey, their song has become their bliss.

english_scripts:
mālē ! maṇivaṇṇā ! mārgazi nīr āḍuvān
mēlaiyār śeyvanagaḻ vēṇḍuvana kēṭṭiyēl
ñālattai ellām naḍuṅga muralvana
pālanna vaṇṇattun pāñjajanniyamē
pōlvana śaṅgaṅgaḻ pōy ppāḍuḍaiyanavē
śāla pperum paṟaiyē pallāṇḍiśaippārē
kōla viḻakkē koḍiyē vidānamē
ālin ilaiyāy ! aruḻēlōr em pāvāy
meaning: O Lord, deeply fond of your devotees and radiant like a flawless nīla-maṇi! You, who made the impossible possible by resting within a tender fig leaf—compressed, yet complete—we have come to you, intent on performing the Mārgaśīrṣa bath, as done by our noble ancestors and learned sages. If you would graciously listen, we shall present our requests: grant us śaṅkhas white as milk, echoing like your Pañcajanya, and paṣai drums—grand and thunderous—along with groups of singers devoted to your praise.
purport:
The gopikās, consumed by their own love, begin to realize that Kṛṣṇa’s affection for them is even more intense—deeper and more boundless than their own. Unlike their wavering emotions, his is vast like an ocean. So great is his fondness that it leaves him paralyzed in their absence—unable to even act to reunite with them. They, however, manage to initiate the vratam, taking effort to reach him, while he remains frozen in longing. As they awaken him, they discover not the distant, absolute God they earlier praised as Nārāyaṇa or Devadeva, but one whose true nature is defined by overwhelming compassion for his devotees. He is malē—the embodiment of affectionate fondness.

Across the epics, the Lord’s defining quality is love for his devotees. Śrī Rāma protected even Vibhīṣaṇa, Ravana’s brother, not out of duty but from joy. When Hanumān tells him of Sītā’s state, Rāma mourns that he cannot live even a moment without her. Similarly, Kṛṣṇa, out of love for the Pāṇḍavas, takes up roles unbecoming of a Supreme Being—a charioteer, a messenger—just to serve them. In truth, the Lord’s efforts to reach the Āḻvārs and his devotees surpass even their efforts to reach him.

Even his birth and upbringing among the cowherds is not merely divine leelā; it’s a secret mission, not just to escape Kaṁsa, but to avoid separation from the gopikās. He appears as one maddened with love, pulling them into the same divine madness. They see the signs of this madness in his very form—his look, his stillness, his helpless gaze. When questioned, “How do you know I love you?” they reply, “Your form does not lie—it reveals the truth within.” They address him as Manivanna—one whose complexion shines like a blue sapphire. Just as an object placed in a jewel box reflects through the jewel’s surface, his inner fondness radiates outward through his form. Even Śrī Lakṣmī is captivated, making his chest her eternal home. His form is so beautiful that people love him even if he rejects or torments them. Like a rare gem, his very nature and luster make him invaluable, precious, and worthy of devotion.

A gem is cherished by its owner, bringing life to them and prestige in society. Likewise, those who possess Kṛṣṇa are deemed alive, and the world respects them. The gem's worth is known only to those who understand its value—so too, only those who realize the true nature of God recognize his infinite worth. He, like the gem, is for others, not for himself. The one who has him desires nothing else. Hence, the gopikās fittingly address him as Manivanna. When asked about their visit, the gopikās say they seek ritual materials for the Mārgazhi bath. While its surface intention is for public welfare (rains), its deeper intent is communion with Kṛṣṇa. Though they have already surrendered to him, they still undertake this ritual—so that others, observing them, do not abandon faith or scriptural practices. Their worship becomes not obligation but kainkaryam—consecrated service.

Kṛṣṇa questions: Is this rite prescribed by the Vedas? The gopikās reply—it is rooted in ancestral tradition (ācāra), which the Dharmaśāstras uphold as greater than scriptural injunctions. The words and practices of those firmly established in dharma are the highest authority. Even Kṛṣṇa, in the Gītā, affirms that the world follows the great man’s conduct—so their practice stands as pramāṇa. The gopikās emphasize that they aren’t versed in ritualistic Vedic practices like animal sacrifice. They are cowherds, grounded in lived tradition. Their ancestors revered Kṛṣṇa as Nārāyaṇa and passed on the conviction that only he can grant the parai (drum of fulfillment). Hence, they seek not just mantras, but the dwaya-mantra—passed down and sanctioned by practice. Scripture confirms what tradition already lives.

They now offer to share their list—if Kṛṣṇa would listen. But he, mesmerized by their beauty, is lost in admiration. Noticing this, they gently rebuke him—“You are feasting on us with your eyes while we are still famished, waiting to feast on your form, words, and presence.” They seek mutual enjoyment, not one-sided. They urge him to awaken from this trance and truly listen to their needs. The first item they request is a conch—white as milk, thunderous in sound, and resembling Kṛṣṇa’s own Pāñcajanya. This conch, which once struck fear in Kurukṣetra and joy in Rukmiṇī’s heart, must now awaken the spiritual earth—the prakṛti—to release them from bondage. The conch symbolizes praṇava (Oṁ), which awakens the knowledge that the jīva belongs solely to God, cutting ties with nature and ego.

Next, they ask for large drums (parai), hollow and loud—symbolizing the word namah (“not mine”). It teaches the jīva that all action is God’s, and that the self is merely his instrument. This humility—rejection of doership—is essential to liberation. The drum, worn on the chest, echoes the centrality of “namah” in the tirumaṅtra. They request devotees to sing benedictions (pallāṇḍu) as they proceed—saints who lovingly fear for the devotees’ well-being. More than God himself, the gopikās seek the company of such saints. Fellowship with devotees not only protects but ensures union with Kṛṣṇa. The lamp they ask for represents the knowledge that they belong to such saints. Just as light reveals and guides, this conviction reveals their true path—one of belonging, not autonomy. Even Lakṣmī is this light—she shows that it is through her grace one reaches Nārāyaṇa. They request a flag and canopy. The flag—visible from afar—symbolizes consecrated service that announces one’s allegiance to the Lord. The awning protects from the dew of bhoktṛtva buddhi—the egoistic sense of enjoying service rather than offering it selflessly. This dew, if unchecked, tarnishes the soul’s natural ornament—service born of surrender.

Through their requests, the gopikās have asked for: (1) knowledge of belonging to God (śeṣatvam), (2) dependence on Him (pāratantryam), (3) company of devotees, (4) conviction of belonging to saints, (5) consecrated service, and (6) elimination of egoistic enjoyment. These are the six limbs of prapatti—the complete surrender that alone brings God. Finally, they invoke his cosmic form—the infant on the fig-leaf floating during the Pralaya. If that Kṛṣṇa, the womb of the universe, could lie upon a leaf with all worlds in his belly, surely granting these ritual materials is no feat. His omnipotence (aiśvarya) and intimacy (sauśīlya) converge in the accessible form before them. All that is needed is his mercy (aruḷ). With this last appeal, they seal their surrender.

english_scripts:
kūḍārai vellum śīr kōvindā !
un tannaippāḍi ppaṟai koṇḍu yām peṟu śammānam
nāḍu pugazum pariśināl nanṟāga
śūḍagamē tōḻ vaḻaiyē tōḍē śevi ppūvē
pāḍagamē enṟanaiya pal kalanum yām aṇivōm
āḍai uḍuppōm adan pinnē pāl śōṟu
mūḍa ney peydu muzaṅgai vazivāra
kūḍi irundu kuḻirndēlōr em pāvāy
meaning:
O Govinda! You, whose auspicious attributes are ever-abundant, are the destroyer of those who turn away from your grace.
What we seek, through our praise and by receiving the parai (divine drum), is not mere reward—but the glory of your acceptance, known and celebrated by all.

We wish to adorn ourselves for this moment of union—with bangles encircling our forearms, armlets gracing our upper arms, earrings for both the lower and upper lobes—some set with flowers, others with gems. Anklets shall chime on our feet, and over it all, we will drape ourselves in resplendent sarees.

Then, in joy and intimacy, we shall be seated beside you. Together, we will relish a sweet feast—pāyasam—warm rice pudding, enriched with milk, ghee, and sugar. Such is our delight in this divine meal that, as we eat with abandon, the rich sweetness will run down our arms, all the way to the elbows.

This, Govinda, is the bliss we anticipate—the reward of our vow: the joy of your company, the festivity of adornment, and the ecstasy of shared divine delight.
purport:
In this opening thought, Āṇḍāḷ celebrates the divine power of Govinda’s guṇas—His beauty, grace, and sweetness—which are so potent that they even conquer those who are antagonistic or uninterested in Him. Saints hesitate to approach due to their humility, lovers sulk in divine separation, ordinary souls remain indifferent, and enemies revile out of arrogance. Yet all are ultimately subdued—not by force, but by the sheer beauty of His compassion and excellence. His guṇas are the true warriors in this conquest, not weapons, and it is through them that even aversion turns into surrender.

As the gopikās continue their vrata, they humbly ask for boons—not for personal gain, but as divine sanction to serve and be adorned for their divine play. They request the “parai”—symbol of their vow—not merely as a ritual object, but as a token of His acceptance and grace. Their requests for ornaments, flowers, and silk garments symbolize their soul’s readiness to engage in līlā with the Lord, to immerse in His joy, and celebrate union through the playful, sacred music of devotion.

The detailed list of ornaments—bracelets, armlets, bangles, anklets, earrings, and garlands—are not mere finery, but spiritual metaphors. Each adornment reflects a quality bestowed by Him upon His devotees: protection, beauty, strength, and divine radiance. The flowers and garments symbolize inner purity and the sweetness of sāttvic expression. These are ornaments for the soul, not merely for the body, and represent the ātmā readying itself to play its part in the divine drama.

Their desire to sing, bathe, and rejoice in Govinda's company is not private indulgence but a celebration that unites them with all of creation. Their joy spills into rivers, trees, and cows—signs of a world harmonized by divine presence. The gopikās speak of bathing in sacred waters and singing Govinda’s glories in chorus, marking the merging of individual bhakti into collective ecstasy. The ritual becomes an offering of all nature in surrender to the Lord.

They envision sitting together with Kṛṣṇa, joyfully consuming a sweet dish—a metaphor for the bliss of divine communion. This food, simple yet rich, becomes sacred because it is shared with Him. Each grain represents grace, each spoonful divine presence. The imagery of laughter, milk flowing from mouths, and playful joy reflects the intimacy of the divine-child relationship—He is not a distant God but one who sits among devotees, laughs with them, eats with them, and becomes theirs.

Finally, the gopikās express a wish that their devotion be known throughout the world—not for pride, but so that others might be drawn to Him through their example. They yearn for the Lord's embrace not only privately but publicly, so that the world may witness the reward of true devotion. This echoes the āḻvār ideal: that one’s experience of divine love becomes the means for others' salvation. Their union with Govinda should not remain a secret—it should inspire the world to surrender.
