kaṟavaigaḻ pin śenṟu kānañjērnduṇbōm
aṟivonṟum illāda āykkulattu
un tannai ppiṟavi peṟundanai ppuṇṇiyam yām uḍaiyōm
kuṟai onṟum illāda kōvindā
un tannōḍuṟavēl namakkiṅgozikka oziyādu
aṟiyāda piḻḻaigaḻōm anbināl
un tannai cciṟupēr azaittanavum śīṟi aruḻādē
iṟaivā ! nī tārāy paṟai ēlōr em pāvāy
meaning:
We are mere cowherd girls, simple folk trailing our cattle into the forest, eating what we must, living without rules or ritual purity. We do not claim merit, discipline, or wisdom. Yet, You—Govinda—chose to be born among us, in this very gopa clan that knows nothing of sacred codes or śāstric conduct. That divine descent alone sanctifies us; it is not by any virtue of our own, but by Your grace alone that we have value. Whatever our faults may be—and they are many—it is You, the blemishless One, who stands as our completeness.

Though we may appear uncouth, our bond with You is unshakable—more ancient and permanent than lineage or law. Out of innocent love, we may have called You by names that seem small or unworthy, forgetting courtly honorifics, unaware of royal etiquette. But know this, O Lord: our love is true, even if our manners are not. Forgive us if our words have fallen short of Your divine stature. Bear with our rustic hearts, and fulfill our humble request—grant us the parai, the sacred drum that seals our vrata and marks Your favor.
purport:
The gopīs begin by asserting their absolute disqualification — they are devoid of learning, untouched by scriptural knowledge, and immersed in the simple life of cowherds. Their existence is not rooted in the disciplines of śāstra, nor have they pursued rigorous paths like karma-yoga or jñāna-yoga. They liken themselves to animals, wandering the village without understanding dharma or tapas. Yet, they emphasize that their only redeeming feature is Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s birth in their clan. Because He took birth among them, their lives gained purpose and sanctity. This confession is not self-deprecation but an affirmation of a deeper truth — that the Lord does not require qualifications, only sincerity. Their very presence before Him is not born from merit, but from His descent among them.

They openly declare that they have not performed any austerities, nor do they possess the intellectual prowess to speak of complex Vedāntic truths. They have not even engaged in the worship of lesser deities — a sign that even elemental worship is absent in their spiritual journey. Their coming to Him, therefore, is not the result of penance or spiritual practice, but simply because they recognize that He is both the path and the goal. By calling Him “Govinda,” they deliberately choose the name that emphasizes His closeness and accessibility. Unlike the majestic and transcendent “Nārāyaṇa,” “Govinda” recalls the affectionate protector of cows — their very own beloved. He is not a distant deity to be feared, but the one who herded their cattle and stole their hearts.

They emphasize that even their act of singing or praising Him is not done with the intention of attaining something. Their words of worship are not a means to an end, but the spontaneous overflow of deep love. It is not that they sing to earn grace; they sing because they cannot help but do so. Their devotion is guileless, and their hearts are simple. They disclaim any sense of being “great devotees,” stating plainly that they are not jñānis, not yogis, and not saints — merely those who sing because their hearts are full. The name “Govinda” itself is enough — for in uttering it, they feel they have reached Him. His name is their sādhana, and it draws Him closer than even the most elaborate rituals could.

The gopīs’ prayer is not a demand but a humble cry of surrender. Even though they came as a group requesting the parai, it becomes clear that the drum is only symbolic. What they truly seek is His grace, His glance, His acceptance. They wish to belong to Him — not for any worldly reward, but for His companionship. Their approach is prapatti — the path of surrender without expectation, devoid of bargaining or qualification. They see themselves as completely at His mercy. They do not have the strength to climb spiritual ladders; they simply fall at His feet. And this falling — this vulnerable surrender — is their path. They remind Him that He is known to uplift the helpless, and if He were to deny them now, it would contradict His very nature.

With humility and clarity, the gopīs urge Kṛṣṇa to remember who He is. He has never turned away those who come without support. In the epics and purāṇas, He has time and again lifted those who had no other recourse — Draupadī, Gajendra, Ahalyā, and others. The gopīs now present themselves in the same light — helpless, guileless, and fully dependent. They do not ask for honor, fame, or liberation. They seek only Him. They invoke the precedent He Himself set — that He is the refuge of the weak, the shelter of those who have no shelter. Their tone is not accusatory but devotional — reminding Him lovingly that He is bound by His own compassion.

In conclusion, they clarify once again that they seek nothing other than His acceptance and presence. Their desire is not for the drum or ritual fulfillment — it is for the Lord who uplifts the fallen. The parai becomes symbolic of His anugraha, His grace. What they seek is His smile, His glance, His touch — the nearness that makes life meaningful. This is not a prayer born from ritual obligation but from the very soul of surrender. They ask Him to accept them not because they qualify, but because He is the one who qualifies the disqualified. And thus, the refrain — “kuṟai oṉṟum illāda govindā” — becomes both a declaration of His completeness and a plea to make them whole through His grace.

tamil_scripts:
சிற்றஞ் சிறு காலே வந்துள்ளனச் சேவித்து உன்\
செபாற்றாமைர அடியே செபாற்றும் செபாருள் சேகளாய்!\
செபற்றம் சேமய்த்து உண்ணும் குலத்தில் பிறந்து நீ\
கற்றேறவல் எங்கலை செகாள்ளாமல் செபாகாது\
இற்றைப் பலற செகாள்வான் அன்று காண் சேகாவிந்தா!\
எற்றைக்கும் ஏழும் பிறவிக்கும் உள்தன்சேனார்\
உற்றேறாசேம யாசேவாம் உனக்கே நாம் ஆட்செய்சேவாம்\
மற்றை நம் காமங்கள் மாற்று ஏல் ஓர் எம்பாவாய்
english_scripts:
śiṭram śiṟugālē vandunnai ccēvittu
un poṭrāmarai aḍiyē pōṭrum poruḻ kēḻāy
peṭram mēyttuṇṇum kulattil piṟandu
nī kuṭrēval eṅgaḻai kkoḻḻāmal pōgādu
iṭrai ppaṟai koḻvān anṟu kāṇ kōvindā !
eṭraikkum ēzēz piṟavikkum
un tannōḍuṭrōmē āvōm unakkē nām āṭ ceyvōm
maṭrai nam kāmaṅgaḻ māṭrēlōr em pāvāy
meaning: Hear, O Lord, the true purpose behind our arriving before dawn, our singing your praises, and our devoted service at your radiant, golden lotus-like feet. Born into the clan of cowherds, who attend to their cattle before their own hunger, it is your dharma to honour such sincere devotion. Reject not our heartfelt offerings of love and service. We have not come merely to receive the parai and leave — our longing is deeper. What we seek is an unbroken bond with you, a kinship that transcends this life and continues through all births to come. Let us serve you alone, forever, as your consecrated servants, with no desire other than to be yours. And we pray — may no other longing ever find place in our hearts.
purport:
The gopikās arrive at Kṛṣṇa’s abode before dawn, unmindful of the darkness or the chill. This early hour, sittiram siṟukālē, symbolizes the spiritual twilight — the moment when the darkness of ignorance begins to yield to the light of God-realization. Their intense longing for union with Kṛṣṇa reflects the urgency and anguish of a true aspirant seeking God, not for material benefits but for His presence alone. The very act of coming to Him is seen as a breach of their own śaraṇāgati (complete surrender), as the ideal is to await His coming — yet their yearning overpowers protocol. They approach not as mere seekers of the paṟai (symbolic gift) but as eternal servants desiring ananya-kainkarya — exclusive, unbroken service unto Him.

They acknowledge Kṛṣṇa’s human birth in the humble community of gopas, who prioritize serving cattle before self-care, and request He not reject their heartfelt service. They highlight that their singing, serving, and longing are not to gain rewards but are acts of pure devotion, born out of intimate love. They urge Him to listen, not for their sake, but to uphold His own dharma — for He was born to receive such love and respond to such surrender. Their plea is not for gifts, nor for any heavenly boons, but to be permanently accepted as His personal attendants — to carry His flute, press His feet, hold His garments, and perform all acts of intimate service.

The gopikās declare their wish to be inseparably united with Him through all births, whether He is in His supreme Vaikuṇṭha form or among them as a cowherd. They seek every possible relationship with Him — as friend, mother, consort, or servant — fearing that limiting themselves to one form of kinship might deprive them of others. This total offering of self is akin to that of Lakṣmaṇa with Rāma, or Yaśodā’s care for her mischievous child. Even though they admit their faults in approaching and serving Him, they plead that such actions are expressions of the pain of separation He Himself has caused.

Importantly, they reject all other desires — even the desire for spiritual enjoyment — praying for pure, selfless service (śuddha-kainkarya), untainted by ego or the pursuit of pleasure. They caution against possessiveness (mamatā) and the idea of enjoying the Lord’s service for one’s own delight (bhoktṛtva-buddhi), declaring that bliss lies solely in pleasing Him. This total surrender encapsulates the essence of the Aṣṭākṣarī mantra, as the gopikās express the meanings of the syllables by affirming their identity as His alone, bound in an eternal relationship, with no other refuge or aim.

Through this pāsuram, they convey the culmination of their nōṟrāda-pōdhu (vow)— not as a ritualistic fulfillment, but as a living declaration of their soul’s purpose: to be in God’s presence, to serve Him endlessly, and to want nothing but Him, through every birth, for all time.

tamil_scripts:
வங்கக் கடல் கலடந்த மாதவலைக் சேகசவலை\
திங்கள் திருமுகத்துச் செயிலழுயார் சென்று இலறஞ்சி\
அங்கு அப்பலற செகாண்ட ஆற்றை அணிபதுலவப்\
லபங்கமலத் தண்சேரியல் பட்டர் பிரான் சேகாலத செசான்ன

சங்கத் தமிழ் மாலை முப்பதும் தப்பாகம்

இங்கு இப்பரிச உைறப்பார் ஈரிரண்டு மால் வைரத் கதாள்

செங்கன் திருமுகத்துச் செல்வத் திருமாலால்

எங்கும் திருவருள் பெற்று இன்பறவர் எம்பாவாய்
english_scripts:
vaṅga kkaḍal kaḍainda mādavanai kkēśavanai
tiṅgaḻ tirumugattu ccēyizaiyār śenṟiṟaiñji
aṅga ppaṟai koṇḍavāṭrai
aṇi puduvai ppaiṅgamala ttaṇ teriyal paṭṭar pirān kōdai śonna
śaṅga ttamiz mālai muppadum tappāmē
iṅgippariśuraippār īr iraṇḍu māl varai ttōḻ
śeṅgaṇ tirumugattu ccelva ttirumālāl
eṅgum tiruvaruḻ peṭrinbuṟuvar em pāvāy
meaning: The gopikās, adorned with otherworldly ornaments, approach Mādhava, the Lord who secured Lakṣmī by churning the ocean of milk. He, the benefactor of Brahmā and Rudra, receives their benediction. In return, they obtain the paṟai—symbol of divine reward—and the eternal privilege of Kainkarya, selfless service to Him. Āṇḍāḷ, daughter of Bhattarpirāṉ of Śrīvilliputtūr, offers this garland of thirty pāsurams, capturing the soul’s journey to the Lord. Those who recite them regularly and with devotion will receive the same blessings as the gopikās—the Lord’s everlasting grace. Śrīmannārāyaṇa, with lotus eyes and four mighty arms, will bless such devotees with joy, both now and forever.
purport:
The gopikās recall the Lord as “Mādhava” and “Keśava”—names that evoke His churning of the ocean of milk, a divine act undertaken ostensibly for the nectar but culminating in the possession of Śrī Lakṣmī. This metaphor is mirrored in the way Kṛṣṇa, under the pretext of community rituals, orchestrates events to unite with the gopikās, fulfilling their longing and His own joy. The Lord's love is such that He once labored for others’ sake—granting the nectar to the devas—but now exerts Himself for those who seek Him alone. The "ships" on the ocean suggest not only His skill in preserving all beings amid turbulence, but also signify the sādhaka’s body sailing through saṁsāra, with the Lord as both the churner and the vessel of deliverance.

The gopikās, whose faces glow like the moon, approach Kṛṣṇa adorned with ornaments bestowed by Him, reflecting their inner joy and sanctification. Unlike the sun-like brilliance of Kṛṣṇa that scorches foes, the gopikās’ moon-like beauty is soothing even to enemies. Their bliss mirrors the serenity found in sages upon seeing the Supreme. This vision highlights a transformation—external beauty now becomes a symbol of internal spiritual radiance, as divine contact purifies and glorifies the devotee. Their ornaments, gifts from Kṛṣṇa, point to the soul’s adornment through grace, and their urge to rush towards Him speaks of uncontainable bhakti.

The gopikās obtain the parai—not merely the ceremonial drum, but the symbolic fruit of divine union and eternal service. In surrender, they make no claims of spiritual merit, but emphasize the Lord’s fullness and their intimate bond with Him. Their path exemplifies śaraṇāgati—complete reliance, transparency in confessing lapses, and trust that the Lord accepts and blesses them as His own. This process, illustrated by Āṇḍāḷ, becomes the blueprint for aspirants: approach God with humility, not through effort or entitlement, but as one whose longing aligns with His grace.

Srivilliputtur, the divine land of Bhattar Pirān (Periyāḻvār), is celebrated as the world’s ornament, sanctified by its link to Āṇḍāḷ. Just as Vṛndāvana is exalted through Nandagopa, Srivilliputtur gains distinction through Āṇḍāḷ’s birth and devotion. Her father, adorned with a lotus-seed rosary, symbolizes constant remembrance of Nārāyaṇa, unlike the perishable tulasi garland. Periyāḻvār brought the Vedic essence to the world, and his daughter offers herself and her composition—the Tiruppāvai—to the Lord. This lineage and locale are not mere background but integral to the sacredness of the hymn and its message.

Āṇḍāḷ, adopting the gopikās' voice, composes a “garland of Tamil verses”—each a distilled gem of Vedantic and devotional truth. Like rain clouds giving life to the parched earth, she renders lofty Upaniṣadic secrets in sweet, simple Tamil, accessible to all. Her identification with the gopikās allows her to experience and express Kṛṣṇa-bhakti in its fullest depth. Tiruppāvai is meant to be sung collectively, evoking the joy of satsangha and divine presence. The truths once buried in Sanskrit Vedas now bloom in poetic Tamil, as Āṇḍāḷ the garland (Koḍai) binds the Lord through her devotional offering.

These thirty pāsurams, perfectly ordered, lay out a complete sādhana for God-realization—from recognizing divine grace to embracing complete surrender. They outline the aspirant’s journey: identifying auspicious moments, valuing others’ prosperity, revering saints, desiring the Lord’s qualities, and surrendering all agency. The devotee who recites with intent (ippadi sureippar) receives not only worldly joy but eternal bliss from Śrīman Nārāyaṇa—the lotus-eyed Lord with four mountain-like arms and a face glowing with love. His gracious glance bestows fulfilment now and forever. Regardless of caste, gender, or stage of life, all who approach Tiruppāvai with devotion will attain divine union and eternal service—just as the gopikās attained Kṛṣṇa and Āṇḍāḷ attained Śrī Raṅganātha.

tamil_scripts: பல்லாண்டு பல்லாண்டு பல்லாயிரத்தாண்டுபல கோடி நூறாயிரம்மல்லாண்ட திண்தோள் மணிவண்ணா !உன் சேவடி செவ்வி திருக்காப்பு
english_scripts:
pallāṇḍu pallāṇḍu pallāyirattāṇḍu
pala kōḍi nūṟāyiram
mallāṇḍa tiṇdōḻ maṇivaṇṇā !
un śēvaḍi śevvi tirukkāppu
meaning: O Lord, whose powerful bhuja-balam subdued the formidable wrestlers in Kaṁsa’s court, You shine with the brilliance of a radiant blue gem. May the divine splendour and exquisite beauty of Your lotus-red sacred feet be preserved and protected for countless crores of years. May Your supreme divinity remain ever undiminished through all ages to come.
purport:
Periyāḻvār, among all the Āḻvārs, expresses *vātsalya-bhāva* in its highest form. This composition of *Tiruppallāṇḍu* begins with the Āḻvār exclaiming, “Long live the Lord! May You live long! May You live for countless eons and ages!” This expression is the very embodiment of *vātsalya-bhāva*. Though Nārāyaṇa is the creator of Brahmā himself, and though the Vedas proclaim Him to be beyond complete description even by themselves, the Āḻvār prays that this Supreme Brahman, the *sarva-śeṣi* of all beings, should live long.

At first glance, this may seem paradoxical. To wish long life for the Supreme Being—the primordial cause of all causes—appears ironic. Yet this is the nature of *vātsalya-bhakti*. For Periyāḻvār, Bhagavān is beheld with the tender care and affection of a mother toward her child. For a mother, no matter how strong or capable her son may be, she constantly wishes for his well-being, health, and peaceful life. Similarly, though Bhagavān is the Supreme Being Himself, the Āḻvār is ever concerned for His welfare and therefore seeks to protect Him through his praises.

Hence, the Āḻvār continually glorifies Bhagavān with the benediction of *pallāṇḍu*. He blesses those shoulders of Bhagavān that uphold the entire universe, those very shoulders that vanquished Rāvaṇa and Hiraṇyakaśipu. “May those shoulders live long!” he proclaims. The Āḻvār also beholds the Lord’s lotus-red feet, the very feet that grant liberation to all beings. Gazing upon those sacred feet, he again exclaims, “May they live long!” Thus, out of boundless *vātsalya* and loving concern, Periyāḻvār offers auspicious blessings even to the One who is the eternal protector of all.

tamil_scripts: அடியோமோடும் நின்னோடும்பிரிவின்றி ஆயிரம் பல்லாண்டுவடிவாய் நின் வல மார்பினில்வாழ்கின்ற மங்கையும் பல்லாண்டுவடிவார் சோதி வலத்துறையும்சுடராழியும் பல்லாண்டுபடை போர் புக்கு முழங்கும்அப்பாஞ்சசன்னியமும் பல்லாண்டே
english_scripts:
aḍiyōmōḍum ninnōḍum
pirivinṟi āyiram pallāṇḍu
vaḍivāy nin vala mārbinil
vāzginṟa maṅgaiyum pallāṇḍu
vaḍivār śōdi valattuṟaiyum
śuḍarāziyum pallāṇḍu
paḍai pōr pukku muzaṅgum
appāñcaśanniyamum pallāṇḍē
meaning: May You, along with us, Your inseparable servants, abide for everlasting ages. May Śrī Devi, who adorns You as a living ornament upon Your right chest, be eternally preserved. May the luminous, blazing cakra in Your right hand, fierce and sharp, ever capable of annihilating foes, endure through endless time. May Your divine conch, the mighty Pāñcajanyam, whose thunderous sound pierces through the tumult of battle, resound for everlasting years.
purport:
Continuing from the previous pāsuram, Periyāḻvār persists in seeking protection for Bhagavān Himself. In this pāsuram, the Āḻvār expresses *Bhāgavata-śeṣatvam*. He not only prays for Bhagavān to live long, but also extends his blessings to the *prapanna-kūṭam*—the assembly of great devotees. Yet he adds a significant condition: they should not merely live long, but live long in eternal service to Him, never becoming separated from Him. Periyāḻvār, being thoroughly grounded in Vedānta, begins the pāsuram with the word *aḍiyōm*. By this, he establishes that all *jīvātmās* are the servants of the Lord. This is the very *svarūpa* of the *jīvātmā*—to remain *śeṣa* to Bhagavān, the *Sarva-śeṣi*. Therefore, he prays that all devotees may live long solely for the purpose of rendering service to Him in this world and beyond.

Continuing his benedictions, the Āḻvār next turns to Śrī Mahālakṣmī and prays for her well-being. He exclaims, “May Śrī Devī, who eternally resides upon Your chest, seated on the Śrīvatsa mark, also live long!” This declaration carries profound Vedāntic significance. Śrī, celebrated in the scriptures as the *puruṣakāra-bhūtā*, is the compassionate mediatrix who guides the *jīvātmās* towards *Puruṣottama*. She is never separated from Bhagavān, and therefore both together constitute the complete *Īśvara-tattva*. Indeed, it is through her grace that the world comes to recognize Nārāyaṇa as the Supreme Brahman. Periyāḻvār joyfully proclaims, “May that Mahālakṣmī live long!” He further delights in the thought that she not only resides upon His chest, but dwells there in perfect bliss. Thus he blesses both Divine Consorts together, praying that they may ever remain united and never be separated from one another.

Having offered protection to Bhagavān and Śrī Mahālakṣmī, the Āḻvār next beholds the Lord’s two divine weapons. His gaze first falls upon Sudarśana, whose radiance surpasses the brilliance of thousands upon thousands of suns. Sudarśana embodies the *saṅkalpa-śakti* of Bhagavān. The universe itself comes into existence through the mere will of Nārāyaṇa, and that divine will is symbolically represented by Sudarśana. Though this blazing discus appears terrifying to the *asuras*, it appears as the most beautiful ornament to the devotees. Mesmerized by its splendour and majesty, Periyāḻvār exclaims, “May that divine Cakra live long!”

Thereafter, he turns to Pañcajanya, the Lord’s sacred conch, and blesses it as well. Pañcajanya is renowned for instilling fear in the hearts of the wicked through its resounding call. In the *Bhagavad Gītā*, while narrating the events of Kurukṣetra to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sañjaya declares: sa ghoṣho dhārtarāṣhṭrāṇāṁ hṛidayāni vyadārayat The mighty sound of the Pāṇḍavas’ conches, led by Kṛṣṇa’s Pañcajanya, shattered the hearts of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons with fear. Yet to the devotees, that very conch is an object of immense beauty. Periyāḻvār marvels at how its pure white radiance perfectly complements the dark-blue hue of the Lord’s *tirumēni*. Held in the hand of the *nīla-megha-śyāma* Lord, the dazzling whiteness of Pañcajanya enhances the beauty of Bhagavān even further. Unable to contain his joy upon witnessing such divine splendour, the Āḻvār bursts forth in loving benediction: “May that Pañcajanya also live long!”

tamil_scripts: வாழாட் பட்டு நின்றீர் உள்ளீரேல்வந்து மண்ணும் மணமும் கொண்மின்கூழாட் பட்டு நின்றீர்களைஎங்கள் குழுவினில் புகுதலொட்டோம்ஏழாட் காலும் பழிப்பிலோம் நாங்கள்இராக்கதர் வாழ்இலங்கை பாழாளாகப் படை பொருதானுக்குப்பல்லாண்டு கூறுதுமே
english_scripts:
vāzāṭ paṭṭu ninṟīr uḻḻīrēl
vandu maṇṇum maṇamum koṇmin
kūzāṭ paṭṭu ninṟīrgaḻai
eṅgaḻ kuzuvinil pugudaloṭṭōm
ēzāṭ kālum pazippilōm nāṅgaḻ
irākkadar vāz
ilaṅgai pāzāḻāga ppaḍai porudānukku
pallāṇḍu kūṟudumē
meaning: If you are devoted to kainkaryam, the joyful service unto the Lord and the highest goal of life, come and join us. Let us carry the sacred mud and sandal paste to be distributed as prasādam during the festival. Those who seek rewards other than service to the Lord have no place among us. Free from blemishes and worldly desires, our lineage remains untainted across generations. We sing Pallāṇḍu in praise of Śrī Rāma, who destroyed the rākṣasās of Laṅkā with His divine army.
purport:
After praising the Lord, Periyāḻvār calls upon His devotees to join him in singing for the Lord’s protection. In this pāsuram, he first invites the foremost among devotees those for whom service to Bhagavān is the ultimate goal. For such devotees, serving the Lord in His *arcā-rūpa* in this world and, upon liberation, serving Him eternally in *Śrī Vaikuṇṭha*, is everything. They are known as *Bhagavad-lābhārthīs*, those who seek only serving Bhagavān.

Among devotees, the scriptures broadly classify four types. Bhagavān Himself describes them in the *Bhagavad Gītā*: chatur-vidhā bhajante māṁ janāḥ sukṛitino ’rjuna |\
ārto jijñāsur arthārthī jñānī cha bharatarṣhabha ||\
teṣāṁ jñānī nitya-yukta eka-bhaktir viśiṣyate |\
priyo hi jñānino ’tyartham ahaṁ sa cha mama priyaḥ || 7.16–7.17 ||

Among the devotees are those who seek worldly possessions (*arthārthīs*), those who seek relief from distress (*ārtas*), those who seek to know the nature of Brahman (*jijñāsus*), and those who are firmly established in that knowledge and remain immersed in the experience of Bhagavān (*jñānīs*). It is this last category that Periyāḻvār calls upon. These are the devotees who seek nothing other than service to Bhagavān. For them, serving Him is everything.

The Āḻvār invites them to come and sing the divine names of Bhagavān. He describes them as those who serve Him with both mind and body. They do not merely contemplate Bhagavān inwardly; they also engage in physical service to Him. These are the *prapannas* whom the Āḻvār welcomes into his company.

At the same time, he clearly excludes those who do not serve the Lord, those who are immersed in material pleasures and spend their lives praising and serving mortal human beings. Such people have no place in this assembly. Periyāḻvār declares that those who glorify humans instead of the Supreme Lord should not join them. Those who seek to glorify humans would not agree to seek protection for Bhagavān whole heatedly. They would indeed not let others too sing the glories our Lord. The devotees whom he calls are those who are ready to serve Bhagavān through birth after birth. For them, service is more desirable than liberation itself. Liberation is merely a natural consequence of devotion; service alone is their cherished goal.

Therefore, Periyāḻvār calls out to such devotees: “Come! Let us together praise the Bhagavān who destroyed the rākṣasas of Laṅkā as Śrī Rāma. Let us sing His glories and seek to protect our Rāma through our auspicious benedictions.”

tamil_scripts: ஏடு நிலத்தில் இடுவதன் முன்னம் வந்துஎங்கள் குழாம் புகுந்துகூடு மனம் உடையீர்கள் வரம்பொழிவந்தொல்லைக் கூடுமினோநாடு நகரமும் நன்கறியநமோ நாராயணாயென்றுபாடு மனம் உடைப் பத்தர் உள்ளீர் !வந்து பல்லாண்டு கூறுமினே
english_scripts:
ēḍu nilattil iḍuvadan munnam vandu
eṅgaḻ kuzām pugundu
kūḍu manam uḍaiyīrgaḻ varambozi
vandollai kkūḍuminō
nāḍu nagaramum nangaṟiya
namō nārāyaṇāyavenṟu
pāḍu manam uḍai ppattar uḻḻīr!
vandu pallāṇḍu kūṟuminē
meaning: O seekers of this sacred path, come without delay. Join those who live solely for the Lord and seek none but Him. Let worldly attachments fall away and let the longing for liberation awaken. Come and be among those who sing together with surrendered hearts, declaring that they seek nothing for themselves but only service to the Lord. Let this sacred message spread everywhere as we proclaim, “May You live long for countless years!”
purport:
Periyāḻvār now turns his attention to a specific group known as *Kaivalyārthis*, those who are absorbed in the contemplation of their own self and seek only *ātmānubhava*. Their aspiration is not Bhagavān Himself, but the experience of the individual self. Such seekers attain a state known as *Kaivalya*, an intermediate condition that is distinct from both worldly existence and the supreme liberation of *Śrī Vaikuṇṭha*. In *Kaivalya*, the *jīvātmā* experiences its own nature and remains free from the sufferings of material existence. Yet it does not attain the unsurpassed bliss of serving Bhagavān, nor does it experience the fullness of divine communion found in *mokṣa*. In many ways, the Ācāryas explain that attaining *Kaivalya* can become an even greater obstacle to ultimate liberation than remaining within *prakṛti*, for the soul becomes satisfied with its own limited experience and no longer aspires for Bhagavān.

Recognizing this subtle deficiency, Periyāḻvār compassionately calls out to such souls: “Come and join us! Abandon this lesser aspiration of merely experiencing the self. Realize that your true nature is not independent self-enjoyment, but eternal service to Bhagavān. Come, sing His divine names along with us and attain the highest goal!” The Āḻvār further emphasizes that service to Bhagavān is not something imposed upon the *jīvātmā*. Rather, it is the very nature of the soul itself. Service to Him is what brings true fulfilment and joy, for Bhagavān is an infinite ocean of love, compassion, and auspicious qualities. To serve Him is not a burden but the natural expression of the *jīvātmā's* true identity.

The Āḻvār acknowledges that the body is impermanent and that worldly desires are the root of suffering. However, merely renouncing material pursuits is not sufficient for liberation. One must also understand one's true identity. The *jīvātmā* is by nature the *śeṣa* of Bhagavān, existing solely for His pleasure and service. Without realizing this fundamental truth, even the attainment of *ātmānubhava* remains incomplete and falls short of the *jīvātmā's* ultimate destiny. The *jīvātmā* is *asvatantra*, while Bhagavān alone is *sarva-svatantra*. Dependence is the intrinsic nature of the jīvātmā, whereas Bhagavān remains completely independent and self-sufficient. Even the experience of *ātmānubhava* is possible only because of His presence within the soul as the *Antaryāmin*. Therefore, the Āḻvār calls out to these seekers and urges them to realize that even the bliss derived from self-experience is but a faint spark of the infinite bliss that arises from the experience of Bhagavān Himself.

Therefore, Periyāḻvār directs these *Kaivalyārthis* towards the path of true realization. He urges them to meditate upon the sacred *Aṣṭākṣara Mahāmantra*, adorned with the divine *Praṇava*. He invites them to contemplate the mantra:

Through the word *namaḥ*, the *jīvātmā* realizes, “I do not belong to myself.” It recognizes that its existence is wholly dependent upon and dedicated to Bhagavān. Through the name *Nārāyaṇa*, it understands Him to be the primordial Supreme Being, the indwelling Lord of all beings, and the cause of all causes. By meditating upon this divine mantra, great yogins transcend limited self-experience and attain the supreme abode of *Śrī Vaikuṇṭha*, from which there is no return.

Thus, Periyāḻvār lovingly calls out to the *Kaivalyārthis*: “Come! Chant ‘Namo Nārāyaṇāya’ with us. Abandon lesser attainments and join the assembly of devotees. Let us together sing auspicious benedictions and seek the protection of Bhagavān through our loving praises.”

aṇḍakkulattukkadibadi āgi
aśurar irākkadarai
iṇḍai kkulattai eḍuttu kkaḻainda
iruḍīgēśan tanakku

āyira nāmam śolli
paṇḍai kkulattai ttavirndu
pallāṇḍu pallāyirattāṇḍenminē
meaning: Having left behind those who pursue only material wealth, you have now entered the company of true devotees who seek nothing but loving service to the Lord. Come and bow at the sacred feet of Hṛṣīkeśa, the Master of all senses, the ruler of countless worlds, the protector of the virtuous, and the destroyer of evil. Let us chant His thousand names and sing, “May You live long for many years, for thousands upon thousands of years!”
purport:
Periyāḻvār now turns to another class of devotees known as *Aiśvaryārthis*. These are devotees who worship Bhagavān, not for the purpose of pleasing Him, nor for attaining *ātmānubhava*, but for obtaining temporary material benefits. Their devotion is directed towards Bhagavān, yet their aspirations remain centered upon worldly prosperity and enjoyment.

The Āḻvār addresses such devotees and reminds them of the true greatness of Bhagavān. He is not merely the ruler of a single world, but the Lord of countless universes extending beyond all measure. He is the supreme *Īśvara* of all realms and all beings. It is He who sustains and governs the cosmic order, protecting society and righteousness by destroying the forces of evil such as the *asuras* and *rākṣasas* who disturb the harmony of creation. He is also celebrated as *Hṛṣīkeśa*, the Lord of the senses. The name *Hṛṣīkeśa* signifies the One who governs and directs all the senses. When the senses are engaged in His service, He subdues and purifies them, guiding them towards their proper purpose.

Among these devotees are those who seek wealth and prosperity, as well as those who seek the recovery of wealth and comforts that have been lost. Indeed, Bhagavān alone, being the supreme *Īśvara*, has the power to grant such blessings. Yet Periyāḻvār gently instructs them that such material attainments should not be the ultimate object of their prayers. Bhagavān is the protector of all His devotees. No one desires our welfare more than He does. Out of His boundless compassion, He provides what is truly beneficial, granting what is necessary and withholding what may be harmful. Therefore, the devotee need not approach Him merely for temporary gains.

Instead, the Āḻvār teaches that service to Bhagavān alone should become the highest aspiration. In order to transform the mind and redirect it from fleeting worldly desires towards eternal service, one must constantly chant and meditate upon the countless divine names of Bhagavān. Each of His names reveals one of His infinite auspicious qualities. Through remembrance of these divine qualities, devotion gradually becomes purified of worldly motives, and the heart begins to desire nothing other than service to Him.

Therefore, Periyāḻvār urges these *Aiśvaryārthis* to chant the thousands upon thousands of names of Bhagavān. Such remembrance cultivates a divine disposition and frees the mind from attachment to temporary pleasures. By constantly glorifying the Lord, the devotee learns to seek the supreme fruit of *bhagavad-kainkarya* rather than the fleeting rewards of this world.

Thus the Āḻvār proclaims: “Let us worship that Supreme Lord, the destroyer of evil forces and the protector of all beings. Let us sing His countless names and offer auspicious benedictions for His protection.”

vandu vazivazi āṭceyginṟōm

meaning: Our lineage has rendered uninterrupted service to the Lord across many generations. Let us now praise Him and sing, “May You live long for many thousands of years!” Let us glorify the Lord who removed all our limitations and who, in the majestic lion form, destroyed the tyrant Hiraṇyakaśipu at twilight.
purport:
Called by Periyāḻvār, the *prapannas* whose sole desire is to serve Bhagavān gather together and join in singing His glories. In unison, they proclaim that they were born for the very purpose of glorifying the Lord. Ordinarily, true devotees do not speak of themselves as great devotees, for such expressions may arise from pride. However, in this instance, the assembled *Bhāgavatas* speak in this manner only to reassure Periyāḻvār that they too stand alongside him in offering protection to Bhagavān. Their intention is not self-glorification, but the affirmation that they are dedicated solely to His welfare, generation after generation.

They declare that for seven generations their families have been singing the Lord's glories and offering auspicious benedictions for His protection. They seek neither *ātmānubhava* nor material prosperity. Their only aspiration is *bhagavad-kainkarya*. Therefore, they have gathered to sing for the protection of Bhagavān and to celebrate His divine qualities.

The devotees proclaim that they sing the glories of the Lord who appeared under the sacred *Śravaṇa* Nakṣatra. They praise the Lord who incarnated as Narasiṁha to destroy the tyrant Hiraṇyakaśipu and protect His devotee Prahlāda. From generation to generation, they have continued to sing the auspicious protection of that same Narasiṁha. They behold Him not merely as the fierce destroyer of evil, but as the beautiful Divine Lion whose appearance was motivated entirely by compassion for His devotee.

In their loving devotion, they imagine that after slaying Hiraṇyakaśipu and restoring righteousness, the Lord might have become fatigued from His tremendous effort. Filled with *vātsalya-bhāva*, they therefore offer their praises as a form of service and comfort. Just as Periyāḻvār blessed Bhagavān with *pallāṇḍu*, these devotees too join in the same spirit and exclaim:

“May that Narasiṁha live long for countless ages and eons! May the beautiful Lord who destroyed Hiraṇyakaśipu and protected Prahlāda ever flourish! May He be blessed with eternal auspiciousness!”

Thus, the chorus of devotees joins Periyāḻvār in singing *pallāṇḍu*, not for any personal gain, but solely out of boundless love and concern for their beloved Lord.

tīyiṟ poliginṟa śeñjuḍar āzi
tigaz tiruccakkarattin
kōyiṟpoṟiyālē oṭruṇḍu ninṟu
kuḍikuḍi āṭceyginṟōm
māya pporupaḍai vāṇanai
āyiran tōḻum pozi kurudi pāya
śuzaṭriya āzi vallānukku
pallāṇḍu kūṟudumē
meaning: Upon our upper arms we bear the sacred imprint of the divine cakra, signifying our lineage of unwavering service to the Lord. It is He, Kṛṣṇa, wielder of the discus, who hurled His blazing weapon against Bhāṇāsura and severed his thousand arms. Let us raise our voices in praise of that glorious Lord and sing, “May You live long for many years!”
purport:
The *Kaivalyārthis* whom Periyāḻvār had previously called have now joined the assembly as well, but with a remarkable transformation. Upon their shoulders shine the sacred marks of the blazing Sudarśana Cakra and the divine Pañcajanya. These marks indicate that they have undergone the sacred rite of *Pañca-saṁskāra* under the guidance of an Ācārya. No longer content with mere *ātmānubhava*, they have embraced the path of complete surrender and service to Bhagavān.

Piḷḷai Lokācārya extols the immeasurable grace of the Ācārya. When a *jīvātmā* comes under the shelter of an Ācārya, it receives the divine *Aṣṭākṣara Mahāmantra*. Through meditation upon this sacred mantra, Bhagavān Himself becomes attainable. Once Bhagavān has become one's own, what remains unattained? Even *Paramapada*, the supreme abode, becomes readily accessible. Through the grace of Periyāḻvār and the lineage of Ācāryas, these former *Kaivalyārthis* have realized that the bliss of Bhagavān far surpasses the limited joy of self-experience.

The emblems of the Cakra and Śaṅkha impressed upon their shoulders signify an even deeper truth. They now acknowledge that they belong entirely to Bhagavān. Whether associated with the body or separated from it, the *jīvātmā* remains His possession alone. Having realized their true nature as His servants, they join the assembly in singing His glories.

The devotees now praise Bhagavān as the conqueror of Bāṇāsura. This celebrated episode is narrated in the *Harivaṁśa* and elaborated upon in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*. Bāṇa, the mighty son of Bali and a descendant of Prahlāda, imprisoned Aniruddha, the grandson of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, after Aniruddha and Uṣā had become attached to one another. In response, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma marched against Bāṇa's city to rescue Aniruddha.

Bāṇa was a great devotee of Rudra and had obtained the boon that Rudra himself would come to his aid in battle. Thus, when Kṛṣṇa arrived, a tremendous conflict arose. Yet before the Supreme Lord, all opposing forces proved powerless. Kṛṣṇa subdued the armies of Bāṇa and overcame the forces led by Rudra. The Lord bewildered Rudra and neutralized his resistance. Thereafter, He turned His attention to Bāṇa himself and severed his many arms.

However, Kṛṣṇa did not kill Bāṇa. Out of regard for Rudra's request and in keeping with the boon He had earlier granted to Prahlāda that He would not destroy his descendants, the Lord spared Bāṇa's life. He removed all but four of Bāṇa's arms and humbled his pride. As stated in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*.darpopaśamanāyāsya pravṛkṇā bāhavo mayā sūditaṁ ca balaṁ bhūri yac ca bhārāyitaṁ bhuvaḥ

The Lord declares that He severed Bāṇa's arms in order to destroy his arrogance and reduce the burden he had imposed upon the earth. Reflecting upon this divine victory, the transformed devotees proclaim: “We sing the glories of that Bhagavān, the subduer of Bāṇa. We sing for the protection of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who severed Bāṇa's arms with the blazing Sudarśana Cakra. The same Cakra whose emblem we bear upon our shoulders stands as the mark of our eternal servitude. It proclaims that we belong to Him alone. Therefore, let us sing *pallāṇḍu* to that victorious Lord and celebrate His eternal glory.”

english_scripts:
neyyiḍai nalladōr śōṟum
niyatamum attāṇi ccēvakamum
kaiyaḍai kkāyum kazuttukku ppūṇoḍu
kādukku kkuṇḍalamum
meyyiḍa nalladōr śāndamum tandu
ennai veḻḻuyir ākka valla
paiyuḍai nāga ppagaikkoḍiyānukku
pallāṇḍu kūṟuvanē
meaning: The Lord has bestowed abundant grace upon me. He provides nourishing food, grants opportunities for daily service, allows service in His royal assembly, and blesses me with sacred remnants and honours. He adorns me with ornaments and fragrant sandal paste, purifying me and transforming me into a sanctified soul. I sing in praise of Him, the Lord whose banner bears mighty Garuḍa: “May You live long for many years!”
purport:
Following the same progression, the *Aiśvaryārthis* too have now joined the assembly. Through the grace of Periyāḻvār, they have come to realize the true greatness of Bhagavān. He is the Lord of all beings, the ruler of countless universes, and the sole giver of all blessings. More importantly, they have understood that Bhagavān does not merely grant what is asked of Him. Out of His boundless compassion, He grants far more than what His devotees seek.

Periyāḻvār beautifully expresses this idea through the analogy of "ghee in rice" rather than "rice in ghee". Ghee represents the most cherished and enjoyable object of desire, the *bhogya-vastu*. Ordinary devotees approach Bhagavān seeking limited and temporary benefits. Their prayers are like asking for a small quantity of ghee to be mixed into rice. Yet when a devotee truly surrenders, Bhagavān reverses the measure. Instead of merely granting the desired object, He bestows Himself. It becomes as though the rice itself is immersed in ghee. When Bhagavān Himself becomes the reward, what remains to be sought?

Periyavāccān Piḷḷai beautifully illustrates this principle through an incident from the life of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. When Kṛṣṇa arrived in Hastināpura, many eagerly invited Him to their homes, saying, “O Lord, please come to our house and bless us.” Yet Kṛṣṇa chose to stay at the house of Vidura. Vidura did not approach the Lord with a sense of ownership or pride. Instead, he welcomed Kṛṣṇa saying, “O Lord, please make Yourself comfortable in this house, for it is not mine but Yours.” Having realized that Bhagavān is the *Sarva-śeṣi*, the true owner of all beings and all things, Vidura approached Him with complete humility. Pleased by such pure devotion, free from ego and possessiveness, Kṛṣṇa joyfully accepted his hospitality.

The transformed *Aiśvaryārthis* now understand this truth. They realize that Bhagavān knows what is truly beneficial for His devotees far better than they themselves do. Therefore, rather than seeking temporary pleasures, they seek Him alone. Bhagavān adorns His devotees with ornaments such as *kuṇḍalam* and other divine decorations that delight Him when He beholds them. He allows them to wear the sandal paste offered to Him and partake of the *prasāda* sanctified by Him. Through these acts of intimate association, Bhagavān gradually increases the *sattva-guṇa* within His devotees and enables them to perceive His divine nature more clearly. What began as devotion motivated by worldly desires is transformed into pure devotion directed solely towards Him.

Having undergone this transformation, they too join the chorus of devotees singing the Lord's glories. They proclaim: “We sing for the protection of that Lord whose banner bears Garuḍa, the mighty enemy of serpents. We sing for that compassionate Bhagavān who grants not merely worldly rewards, but the highest of all attainments. He bestows Himself upon His devotees and makes them His own. May that Lord, the bearer of Garuḍa-dhvaja, live long for countless ages and eons. May His glory ever increase! May He be eternally auspicious!”
